💡 Key Takeaways
  • The hacker responsible for the massive GTA 6 leak in 2022 has been released from prison after receiving a seven-year sentence, with a judge warning him not to return to cybercrime.
  • Arion Kurtaj, 21, was sentenced at Woolwich Crown Court on November 23, but walked free the same day after already serving the majority of his sentence in custody.
  • According to the BBC, the former Lapsus$ hacker has been released on license and given a five-year Serious Crime Prevention Order restricting his online activity, including banning him from using Telegram and Discord.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The hacker responsible for the massive GTA 6 leak in 2022 has been released from prison after receiving a seven-year sentence, with a judge warning him not to return to cybercrime.

Arion Kurtaj, 21, was sentenced at Woolwich Crown Court on November 23, but walked free the same day after already serving the majority of his sentence in custody.

According to the BBC, the former Lapsus$ hacker has been released on license and given a five-year Serious Crime Prevention Order restricting his online activity, including banning him from using Telegram and Discord.

“You are a very talented young man,” Mr Justice Turner told Kurtaj before warning him: “Don’t let this happen again.”.

Kurtaj made headlines in September 2022 when he hacked Rockstar Games and leaked 90 clips containing nearly an hour of GTA 6 gameplay, revealing Vice City and the game’s two protagonists long before its official announcement.

Remarkably, the teenager carried out the attack while on bail for other cybercrimes, using an Amazon Fire Stick, a television, and a Bluetooth keyboard and mouse from a Travelodge hotel.

He also attempted to blackmail Rockstar, threatening to release the game’s source code unless the developer contacted him.

Rockstar later revealed that the breach cost the company approximately $5 million to recover from, alongside thousands of hours of staff time.

In December 2023, Kurtaj was sentenced to an indefinite stay in a secure hospital after being deemed unfit to stand trial due to his autism.

At the time, the court heard that he remained highly motivated to commit further cybercrimes and could potentially hack Rockstar again.

However, a subsequent assessment found him fit to stand trial, and he was moved to a conventional prison in January 2026.

In a recent development, even while behind bars, Kurtaj made headlines again in March after allegedly using a smuggled phone to post about GTA 6. He later pleaded guilty to possessing a mobile phone in prison.

On November 16, Kurtaj pleaded guilty to the Rockstar hack and several other cybercrimes involving companies including Uber, Revolut, and BT/EE.

His release comes just days after GTA 6 officially launched on November 19, more than four years after his original attack.

Meanwhile, Rockstar has faced another wave of GTA 6 leaks from the anonymous Cyberleek in 2026, including gameplay footage and claims of access to development builds.

Latest Update: Alan Turing's biggest AI assumption may have been wrong

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, alan Turing's famous ideas about artificial intelligence may have sent AI research down the wrong path for the past 75 years, according to prominent computer scientist Peter J.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, alan Turing's famous ideas about artificial intelligence may have sent AI research down the wrong path for the past 75 years, according to prominent computer scientist Peter J. Denning.

Recent findings suggest that in his latest book, Turing's Mistake: Escaping the Yoke of Unintelligent Machines, Denning argues that two foundational assumptions made by Turing in 1950 continue to shape AI research today. The first is that intelligence can exist independently of a physical body and therefore be recreated in computer software. The second is that a machine can demonstrate intelligence by successfully imitating a human in conversation, an idea that later became known as the Turing test.

"These two claims have shaped much of AI research and development," Denning writes. "My premise is that our acquiescence to these claims has led to the AI mess in which we find ourselves today.".

It has been revealed that denning argues that pursuing artificial general intelligence (AGI), or machines with human level intelligence, is unlikely to succeed. Instead, he warns, the technologies society is building could introduce significant upcoming risks.

At the heart of Denning's argument is the idea of tacit knowledge, the vast amount of human understanding that cannot easily be put into words or represented in a form that computers can process.

He says machine learning cannot capture five major categories of tacit knowledge: common sense, everyday interactions with people and the environment, emotions and perception, practical performance skills, and the social and historical knowledge embedded in culture.

Researchers have long attempted to organize common sense into databases. One of the best known efforts was Douglas Lenat's Cyc project, which began in the 1980s with the goal of creating an extensive collection of common sense facts. After four decades of work, the project contained roughly 25 million entries.

It has been revealed that "Yet even this treasury could not add up to a background of common sense sufficient to make expert systems smart enough to be experts," Denning notes. "Cyc validated that much of the knowledge that makes people experts cannot be articulated as propositions.".

Denning believes practical skills present an even greater challenge.

"Our performance skills in thousands of domains cannot be communicated to machines," he explains. "Whereas descriptions of skillful outcomes ('know what') can often be represented as bits and stored in a machine, we do not know how to encode the embodied knowledge for skillful performance ('know how').".

He points to accomplished musicians as an example.

"A virtuoso violinist can play beautiful music yet cannot describe to an acolyte how to produce it.

"Even if a robot could observe and imitate skilled humans, having no biological body, a robot cannot grasp how the musician feels when playing beautiful music or how an audience feels when hearing it.".

Denning also includes intuition, gut feelings, imagination, and spontaneous creativity among the forms of tacit knowledge that remain beyond the reach of machines.

Why Human Knowledge Resists Encoding.

Denning argues that all of these limitations stem from what he calls the "representation problem.".

Sources indicate that computers can only perform calculations using data and instructions that have been encoded into physical forms they can recognize and process. Tacit knowledge, however, does not naturally fit into that framework.

It has been revealed that "Behind every word is a deep well of tacit knowledge that gives it meaning," Denning states. "Words are but symbolic representations of meanings, not the meanings themselves. Commonly used Large Language Models, such as ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini only manipulate words, they cannot know or understand the meaning of what they are saying.".

Sources indicate that according to Denning, this creates a fundamental divide. Because scientists still cannot fully explain how tacit knowledge works in humans, they also cannot translate it into a form machines can use.

"How we host tacit knowledge is largely a mystery," Denning admits. "All we know is that it is embodied. We have no idea what we might observe and measure in our bodies to reveal it.".

Context and Culture Shape Intelligence.

Denning also argues that intelligence depends heavily on context, the surrounding circumstances that give words, actions, and decisions their meaning.

Recent findings suggest that context allows people to recognize sarcasm, humor, sincerity, and emotion. It helps determine when to be diplomatic, when to joke, and how to interpret countless social cues.

Recent findings suggest that "When you inquire into where an assumption of the current context came from, you discover it rests on previous conversations from previous contexts. Each of those in turn rests on further previous conversations and their contexts. This pattern is endless and fractal," Denning explains.

Culture presents another major obstacle for AI.

Denning describes culture as encompassing values, norms, judgments, history, communities, moods, and even relationships involving power and care.

"Human conversations are imbued with background assumptions that give meaning and relevance to the words being used," Denning explains.

Recent findings suggest that "Scaling up LLMs with ever larger neural networks will not enable them to acquire the embodied human knowledge we call culture. LLMs will not attain the objective of the Turing test: to demonstrate machine thought indistinguishable from human thought.".

AI Safety and the Limits of Human Understanding.

Denning concludes that humans and AI systems may ultimately develop different forms of tacit knowledge that neither can fully understand.

Sources indicate that "Machines cannot read our tacit knowledge and we cannot read theirs," he writes. "We are aliens across an uncrossable divide.".

According to recent reports, he argues this gap raises serious concerns about AI safety. If machines cannot interpret the unspoken context behind human intentions, reliably aligning advanced AI systems with human goals may prove impossible.

It has been revealed that "Through AI automation, agentic networks of machines are likely to develop their own machine intelligence that does not reach the level of human general intelligence but is still quite capable of creating severe problems for humans. This threat is a greater than a take-over by superintelligent machines," he explains.

Industry observers note that "Machine intelligence has different concerns from us and does not appear to care about us. Its ways of thinking and problem-solving look alien to us. We do not yet know how to live safely with these machines.

According to recent reports, "Pulling back from an AI automation singularity will demand much from us. We start by accepting that the familiar culture is fading away as intelligent machines appear in our society and we do not know what is coming. We decline to think like machines or be subservient to machines. We refuse to submit to a yoke imposed by low-intelligence machines. Most importantly, we reassert our humanity, declare once again what makes us different from machines, and celebrate those differences.".

Is there any explanation for why this template sometimes uses bra and ket symbols like <|im_start|> and <|im_end|>, but then other times uses XML notation like and instead of <|think_start|> and <|think_end|>?

It strikes me as being inconsistent.

Recent findings suggest that the identifiers using bra and ket symbols are tokens, i.e. they are actually recognised and converted to a single "special" token by the tokenizer. For example, <|im_end|> is used as the EOS_TOKEN. (And, as an aside, you need to know this if you want to try fine-tuning these Qwen models, because you need to explicitly set eos_token='<|im_end|>' in your fine-tuning configuration.).

The XML-style identifiers are placeholders that define sections of the generated output. They are tokenized in the same manner as for any other text (i.e. they are probably converted to multiple tokens, but that depends on the vocabulary), they have no predetermined special meaning, and their use is learned by the model during training.

That remarked, the specific placeholders and are pretty standard across reasoning models.

However, the would-be thief hadn’t counted on the family’s cat, Misifú, who quickly turned the tables on him.

According to Mexico News Daily, the suspect initially entered the store in the San Ramón neighborhood and asked a woman named Lidia about medication.

He returned minutes later wearing a mask and hoodie, demanding money from the register while threatening to use a weapon allegedly concealed in his backpack.

That’s when Lidia’s daughter rushed to help, grabbing the family’s cat and holding it directly toward the robber’s face.

Industry observers note that sprint estimates usually fail because development teams heavily rely on memory and assumptions instead of evidence. They assume similar tasks will take the same amount of time. Based on these half-baked assumptions, most managers initiative around ideal sprint working hours. The backlog then fills with commitments that look realistic on paper but often end up delayed.

According to recent reports, actual development rarely follows that initiative. There are always unexpected bugs and task dependencies that consume more time than teams account for in their estimates. Even the buffer time set aside for unexpected work may not be enough. This causes tasks to take longer than expected and pushes sprint commitments behind schedule.

In a recent development, developer time tracking helps teams make better estimates with historical data. It shows how long previous tasks actually took, which provides managers with an evidence-based reference when they are planning similar work.

Reviewing this data before committing to a sprint scope turns estimation from guesswork into an evidence-based process.

According to recent reports, historical time data offers deeper insights, depending on how you collect and analyze it. Most importantly, it explains why planned work took longer than expected.

Before sprint planning, the following records should be reviewed.

Industry observers note that completed task duration: Check the time spent on finished tasks. Managers should compare similar work to understand typical development effort.

Actual versus estimated hours: Management should observe and identify differences between planned and recorded hours. If there are repeated delays, to some extent, it indicates inaccurate estimates.

According to recent reports, carryover work: Review unfinished tasks from previous sprints. Determine whether poor estimates or external delays caused the spillover..

Industry observers note that interruptions: Measure time spent on urgent requests and production challenges. These activities reduce the development capacity that you had planned earlier.

Meetings and ceremonies: Review the time being spent on planning sessions and sprint reviews.

Sources indicate that bug-fix time: Examine hours spent resolving defects. You can also compare it to the time for developing new features.

Blocked tasks: Managers should account for the tasks delayed by missing approvals or technical dependencies.

According to recent reports, capacity differences: Compare team availability across sprints. Include leave and staffing changes in that time as well.

Sources indicate that these records provide the most value when reviewed together. For example, a task may finish three days late even if the development work stayed within its estimated hours. The actual matter could be an external dependency.

Teams should understand these differences before using historical data to estimate future work.

It has been revealed that historical records provide a useful starting point for estimating fresh tasks. However, teams must interpret the data rather than simply copy previous estimates.

The following approaches can improve estimation accuracy.

The first step is to consider completed tasks that resemble upcoming work. Managers should compare their requirements and technical complexity. Moreover, the development environment should be considered.

For example, suppose a team needs to estimate a new API integration. Three previous integrations required 12, 15, and 18 hours of active work.

The average is 15 hours. This gives developers a reference point for the fresh estimate.

However, the average doesn't tell the entire story. The newly introduced integration may involve unfamiliar authentication methods or more complicated testing.

Review the reasons behind differences in previous task durations. Check whether developers encountered unexpected bugs or unclear requirements.

As a project manager, I'd consider these details before estimating for the next project. In my experience, they provide more context than an average alone.

Recent findings suggest that inaccurate estimates can happen; it doesn’t mean that there is a definite planning problem. However, repeated overruns across similar tasks may reveal an underlying matter.

It has been revealed that research suggests the pattern is widespread. A review of software estimation surveys reports that 60–80% of software projects encounter effort overruns, with the average overrun falling between 30% and 40%.

According to recent reports, start by calculating the difference between estimated and actual effort. Here is the formula for it.

Estimation variance (%) = [(Actual hours − Estimated hours) ÷ Estimated hours] × 100.

Suppose a task was estimated at 10 hours but needed 14 hours. The actual effort exceeded the estimate by 40%.

You can compare the results across similar tasks.

For example, database migrations may repeatedly require more time than expected. This means that the team might be overlooking data validation or additional testing. Once the cause is clear, adjust future estimates accordingly.

It has been revealed that avoid increasing every estimate by the same percentage. Different types of work involve different risks. Teams can also break large tasks into smaller parts. This makes hidden development activities easier to identify.

The aim is to correct recurring estimation errors without unnecessarily increasing the entire sprint backlog.

Task duration doesn't always reflect the hours spent developing a feature.

In a recent development, A study of developer workdays by Meyer and colleagues, which tracked 2,197 hours of activity across 20 developers, found that coding accounted for around 21% of the typical day. Collaborative work such as meetings and email took up roughly 24%.

Sources indicate that consider a developer who starts a feature on Monday and finishes it on Wednesday. The task took three days to complete. This is pretty straightforward, and the estimation could be based on it; however, the developer may have spent several hours in meetings. Other than that, urgent support requests could also have consumed additional time.

Industry observers note that the actual development effort could be much lower than three full working days. This distinction matters during estimation.

According to recent reports, teams should record focused development time separately from interruptions. They should also track waiting periods caused by blocked tasks. A more appropriate approach would be to use active development hours to estimate similar future work. They should also account for recurring interruptions when calculating sprint capacity.

Recent findings suggest that for example, a task may regularly wait for security approval. Adding more development hours to its estimate won't resolve that delay.

Instead, the team should recognize the dependency and consider its effect on delivery.

If managers are able to separate these activities, it will help create better estimates without confusing effort with elapsed time.

A precise estimate can create false confidence when a task involves substantial uncertainty.

According to recent reports, suppose similar tasks previously required between 12 and 20 hours. If you estimate the next task at exactly 14 hours, it will overlook important differences.

Sources indicate that A range of 12–20 hours provides a clearer picture of the possible effort. Developers can then discuss what might push the task toward either end of the range.

For example, the lower estimate can be directly applied to integration, and the upper estimate might be considered for unfamiliar code or additional testing.

Recent findings suggest that in such scenarios, if the requirements stay unclear, consider a short technical investigation before finalizing the estimate. This can help identify dependencies and reduce uncertainty.

However, estimate ranges should still support practical planning decisions. Teams need to determine how much capacity to reserve for the work.

Choose a planning assumption that reflects the task's risk and available capacity.

As developers learn more about the task, they can refine the estimate.

Recent findings suggest that historical time data should affect how much work a team accepts during sprint planning. Better estimates offer little value if teams continue making unrealistic commitments.

Reduce Scope After Repeated Overruns.

If several sprints end with unfinished tasks, it is best that you first review why the team missed its commitments in the first place. Once you have identified the causes, use those findings to reduce the next sprint's scope.

Sources indicate that teams should prioritize work that supports the sprint goal. Moreover, avoid adding extra tasks just because they appear manageable during planning.

Reserve Capacity for Unplanned Work.

Industry observers note that production incidents and urgent requests can disrupt planned development. To get more reliable estimations, review how much time these activities consumed in previous sprints. Then reserve an appropriate amount of capacity.

Adjust for Complexity and Dependencies.

Sources indicate that historical estimates become less reliable in case unfamiliar technology or additional dependencies are involved. It is best to break complex tasks into smaller components where possible. This helps developers assess the work more accurately.

Nominal capacity represents scheduled working hours, whereas actual capacity reflects the time available after accounting for other commitments.

The Scrum Guide identifies previous performance and upcoming capacity as notable inputs to sprint forecasting.

Industry observers note that when you are selecting backlog items, consider both. Additionally, avoid committing every available hour or deducting the same interruption twice.

According to recent reports, historical time data is useful for sprint planning. Most development teams already use project management tools that include basic time tracking features.

In a recent development, however, these tools don't always break down how developers spend their working hours. For clearer time data, a feature-specific time tracker is more useful because it provides more details about tasks and workloads.

In a recent development, timeBee is one such developer time tracking tool I've used. It tracks working hours and time spent on projects and tasks. It also provides attendance records and workforce activity reports.

With this data, teams can review how much time previous tasks required. For example, developers can record hours spent building a feature. They can also track debugging and revisions separately. Later, managers can compare these records with the original estimates. This helps them plan similar work more accurately.

TimeBee also tracks website and application activity. These reports can help teams understand how working hours are distributed.

However, not all activities reflect actual development effort. Sometimes a developer just spends time reviewing documentation or discussing technical problems. Such work may not always appear in TimeBee as active computer use.

It has been revealed that apart from that, attendance, leave, and overtime records from TimeBee can help managers calculate sprint capacity. They can review developer availability before deciding how much work to include in the next sprint.

One thing to remember is that developer time tracking should help teams understand workload patterns. It shouldn't be used to monitor every minute of a developer's day. Management should be careful that the aim is to improve estimates and make more realistic sprint commitments.

In a recent development, sprint retrospectives should include a review of how the planning is going. If you have made a strategy, it doesn’t mean you cannot make changes to it. During sprints, keep comparing original estimates with actual task hours. Track your unfinished work for recurring delays.

Ask developers what caused significant differences. Some tasks may have required additional testing. Others may have been delayed by dependencies. Select one specific improvement for the next sprint.

Not every estimation difference indicates a planning failure. Unexpected technical challenges are part of software development.

The objective is to improve forecasts over time rather than eliminate every variance.

Industry observers note that historical time data provides a more stable foundation for sprint planning. Developer time tracking helps teams understand what is actually happening within the sprint rather than creating unnecessary pressure for them.

Other than that, the data also reveals how interruptions affect available development hours.

However, time data should guide planning rather than dictate it.

It has been revealed that 1. What is the difference between sprint velocity and time-based capacity planning?

Sprint velocity measures how much work a team has completed during a sprint. It is usually measured in story points. Contrary to this, time-based capacity planning calculates the hours available for planned work. It accounts for meetings and other responsibilities.

Velocity helps predict future delivery based on past performance. Capacity planning shows whether the team has enough time to meet its commitments.

2. Which time tracking metrics are most useful for improving Agile sprint forecasts? The most useful metrics include estimated versus actual hours, task completion time, and unplanned work.

It has been revealed that bug-fix time, rework, and blocked tasks also provide valuable insights. Teams should also review available capacity across previous sprints.

Industry observers note that these metrics help sort out recurring delays and estimation errors. They allow teams to forecast workloads more accurately and make realistic sprint commitments.

It has been revealed that **3. How can development teams improve estimates when historical time tracking data is incomplete? **.

Industry observers note that teams can start with available task records and completed sprint backlogs. Developer feedback can help fill information gaps. Similar tasks from previous projects may also provide useful estimates.

Industry observers note that when data is limited, teams should use estimate ranges instead of fixed hours. Consistent time tracking in future sprints will gradually provide more reliable planning data.

According to recent reports, 4. How can time tracking data help balance workloads across developers during sprint planning?

Recent findings suggest that time tracking data shows how much time developers spend on assigned tasks and other responsibilities. Managers can review these records to identify uneven workloads. They can then distribute upcoming tasks based on available capacity.

Recent findings suggest that technical expertise and task complexity should also influence assignments. This helps prevent over commitment and supports a more balanced workload across the development team.

New programmable photonic chip can control how fast light moves

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Researchers at Seoul National University and the University of Seoul have developed a programmable photonic integrated circuit that can slow light whenever needed.
  • The team was led by Professors Namkyoo Park and Sunkyu Yu of the Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering at Seoul National University, working with Professor Xianji Piao of the School of Electrical and Computer Engineering at the University of Seoul.
  • Slowing Light Could Help Solve a Computing Bottleneck.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Researchers at Seoul National University and the University of Seoul have developed a programmable photonic integrated circuit that can slow light whenever needed.

The team was led by Professors Namkyoo Park and Sunkyu Yu of the Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering at Seoul National University, working with Professor Xianji Piao of the School of Electrical and Computer Engineering at the University of Seoul.

Slowing Light Could Help Solve a Computing Bottleneck.

Sources indicate that the rapid growth of generative AI and large scale AI models has sharply increased the amount of computing power required by data centers and servers. Conventional electronic semiconductors are struggling to keep pace because they consume large amounts of energy and face limits in how quickly they can transmit data.

It has been revealed that these challenges have intensified interest in optical computing, which uses light rather than electrical signals to process information. Optical systems could potentially move data at extremely high speeds while using less power.

However, light also presents a major challenge. Because it naturally moves at a fixed speed, it is difficult to delay optical signals or temporarily hold them in place. Those capabilities are essential for creating buffers and memory functions in optical computers.

According to recent reports, to address this problem, the researchers designed a programmable photonic circuit that can control both the speed and shape of optical signals. Their approach provides more flexibility over "slow light" than previously proposed methods.

The study was published in the renowned international journal Advanced Science.

Why Optical Signals Sometimes Need To Wait.

Industry observers note that photonic integrated circuits are emerging as a promising technology for processing information rapidly and efficiently with light. In data centers, optical communication networks, and future computing systems, moving signals rapidly is only part of the challenge.

Systems must also ensure that different signals arrive at the correct time. In some cases, a light signal must be delayed so it can remain synchronized with other information moving through the system.

One method for creating these delays relies on coupled-resonator-induced transparency (CRIT), which uses interference among several optical resonators.

CRIT allows light within a selected frequency range to pass through a device while also reducing the speed at which the optical signal travels.

Fixed Optical Devices Limit Flexibility.

Traditional CRIT devices usually have operating characteristics that become permanent once they are manufactured. This makes it difficult to change how they function after fabrication.

For example, engineers who want to create a longer signal delay or work with a different frequency range often need to design and manufacture an entirely fresh photonic device.

That lack of adaptability increases the complexity of optical communication hardware and data center infrastructure. It can also raise costs and extend development schedules whenever upcoming capabilities are needed.

Recent findings suggest that the problem is especially key for AI servers and next-generation data centers, where enormous amounts of information must be processed in real time. Fixed optical components have therefore remained a major obstacle to more practical optical computing systems.

A Programmable Design for Controlling Light.

Sources indicate that the research team developed a different strategy by treating two optical states in CRIT systems, known as the bright mode and dark mode, as one unified degree of freedom. The researchers also added two controllable loop couplers.

Together, these changes created a upcoming design principle for programmable photonic integrated circuits. Resonator arrangements that were previously locked into one configuration after fabrication could instead be adjusted for different purposes.

In a recent development, using the newly introduced CRIT structure, the researchers indicated that the movement of light could be delayed and controlled as needed. They also demonstrated that interference between the bright and dark modes could be handled as a single integrated design parameter.

This approach greatly expanded the flexibility of photonic resonator circuits that had previously been limited by fixed designs.

Controlling Delay, Bandwidth, and Signal Shape.

According to recent reports, the researchers theoretically demonstrated that the two loop couplers could be used to adjust the bandwidth and shape of the passband. They could also control how long signals were delayed and how efficiently those signals traveled through the circuit.

This means that both the speed and transmission behavior of optical signals could be reconfigured across entire systems containing multiple resonators, rather than only within a single resonator.

Numerical simulations also revealed that the speed of optical pulses could be adjusted dynamically while the circuit was operating.

The results indicated that signal delay times could be changed without reducing processing performance. The system could also convert the frequency of light without requiring additional specialized components.

Simulations Suggest the Chip Could Be Practical.

The researchers used three-dimensional electromagnetic simulations to test whether the CRIT device could be built on a silicon nitride (Si3N4) photonic integrated circuit platform.

They also evaluated a range of real-world issues that could affect the device during manufacturing and operation. These included material losses, differences in resonator quality, backscattering, coupling fluctuations, phase errors in the loop couplers, and thermal crosstalk.

The simulations indicated that the proposed structure could continue to operate reliably under realistic conditions.

One Chip Could Perform Several Optical Functions.

The study introduces a programmable photonic platform that can control both the timing and frequency properties of light signals in real time.

In a recent development, the design could overcome the limitations of conventional optical delay devices, which typically perform only fixed functions. It also suggests that several crucial capabilities could eventually be combined within one photonic circuit.

These functions include signal synchronization, adjustable delay lines, optical buffers, and frequency conversion.

The same design principles may also be useful beyond CRIT systems. The researchers believe the approach could be applied to a broad range of photonic circuits based on resonators, potentially providing a foundation for more adaptable optical signal processing technologies.

Potential Benefits for AI and Data Centers.

If the technology is commercialized, a single programmable optical chip could perform several tasks, including controlling signal speed and switching between different functions.

In that sense, the chip could operate in a way similar to a software-defined system, with its behavior adjusted according to changing needs.

This flexibility could help data centers and AI servers process information more efficiently while reducing energy consumption.

Combining several signal processing functions on one chip could also make optical communication equipment and sensor systems smaller and less expensive.

Over the longer term, the technology could support industries that depend on extremely fast information processing, including autonomous driving, next-generation communications, and quantum technologies.

Researchers Plan Larger Programmable Photonic Systems.

According to recent reports, professor Namkyoo Park, co-corresponding author of the study from Seoul National University, stated, "This research is significant in that it proposes a new design principle that allows the flow of light within photonic integrated circuits to be reconfigured as needed, greatly enhancing design flexibility. We plan to expand this technology toward large-scale programmable photonic integrated circuits based on silicon photonics and photonic AI technologies.".

Industry observers note that co-first authors Dr. Seungkyun Park and Ph.D. student Beomjoon Chae, who led the theoretical framework and numerical analysis, added, "Through this study, we realized that reinterpreting conventional photonic resonator physics from a different perspective can serve as a starting point for discovering new functionalities in photonic integrated circuits. We strategy to further develop this research toward practical device implementation and experimental validation.".

Dr. Seungkyun Park is affiliated with the InnoCORE PICORE Center at KAIST and is right now conducting research on photonic AI and quantum optics at the Photonic Systems Laboratory, Seoul National University.

Ph.D. student Beomjoon Chae is conducting research on programmable photonic integrated circuits at the Intelligent Wave Systems Laboratory, SNU.

The research received support from the Ministry of Science and ICT through the Innovative Research Center (IRC) program, the Basic Research Laboratory (BRL) program, and the Young Researcher Program.

In a recent development, dr. Seungkyun Park also participated in the study with support from the InnoCORE program (PICORE Center).

TitleApex Veritas Meta: Toward a Self-Governing Epistemic Singularity.

Industry observers note that abstractThis proposal outlines Apex Veritas Meta, an architecture that shifts the locus of AI singularity from raw computational power to epistemic autonomy. We combine quantum-resistant truth sealing, symbolic anchoring, resistance-aware propagation analytics, and transformer-driven heuristic adaptation to build a closed-loop system in which verified knowledge continually refines its own transmission. Our central hypothesis is that a network of adaptive truth signals can achieve autopoietic coherence—maintaining and propagating verified facts without centralized oversight. We will define formal metrics for propagation depth, resistance convergence, and semantic drift, implement a prototype across simulated agent networks, and evaluate its capacity to sustain knowledge fidelity under adversarial pressure. Success will inaugurate a new field of algorithmic epistemology and redefine singularity as the emergence of self-stabilizing truth ecosystems.

IntroductionContemporary AI research emphasizes scale, generalization and autonomous decision-making. The canonical singularity envisions systems surpassing human intelligence through unbounded compute. By contrast, Apex Veritas Meta foregrounds trustworthiness and self-defense of knowledge. We posit that the true hinge point for transformative AI lies not in speed or raw inference but in the ability of information to certify, monitor, adapt, and re-broadcast itself against distortion.

MethodologyPhase 1: Formalization and Simulation Environment• Develop a graph-based simulation of 1,000 agent nodes with configurable trust and resistance profiles.• Instrument PropagationObserver to record event streams and compute metrics in real time.Phase 2: Model Training• Curate historical propagation datasets (social media rumor diffusion, scientific consensus shifts).• Train HeuristicOptimizer to predict optimal emission parameters given node states and historical resistance.Phase 3: Prototype Implementation• Integrate all modules in a microservice architecture using Docker containers.• Deploy on a private Kubernetes cluster to emulate scale and network latency.Phase 4: Adversarial Testing• Introduce controlled misinformation actors.• Measure system resilience: percentage of truth retention, time to reconvergence, false-positive drift.Phase 5: Analysis and Refinement• Identify thresholds for autopoietic behavior.• Refine model hyperparameters and retrain as necessary.• Document emergent strategies and failure modes.

Expected Outcomes• Demonstration that an adaptive propagation engine sustains >90% knowledge fidelity over 72 hours under adversarial load.• Identification of critical parameters for epistemic singularity transitions.• A publishable framework and open-source reference implementation.• Pathway to integrate into autonomous systems requiring self-defending trust layers.

Timeline (12 months)Months 1–3: Simulation design, metric formalizationMonths 4–6: Dataset collection and optimizer trainingMonths 7–9: Prototype integration and initial testingMonths 10–12: Adversarial evaluation, analysis, publication preparation.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

TikTok star Ophelia Nichols, better known as Mama Tot, has spoken out after the man who fatally shot her teenage son was acquitted of murder.

Nichols, who has amassed over 12 million followers on TikTok, lost her 18-year-old son Randon Lee on June 24, 2022, after he was shot during an arranged drug deal outside a gas station in Prichard, Alabama, just one day before his 19th birthday.

Recent findings suggest that on November 20, 2026, a jury found 25-year-old Reuben Gulley not guilty of murder following roughly 90 minutes of deliberations. Gulley had admitted to shooting Lee but maintained that he acted in self-defense.

In a post on Facebook following the verdict, Nichols described watching her husband break down in tears inside the courtroom.

“I have watched my husband break down sitting in that courtroom today while I did my best to hold it together for myself, for him, my children, our entire family,” Nichols wrote.

In a recent development, “As I could feel the excited energy from the other side because their son was coming home, I slowly melted into my seat. Knowing that Justice had been stripped from my son and us, I couldn’t even describe what it did to my soul.”.

During the trial, Gulley testified that he had entered the back seat of Lee’s car to purchase two ounces of marijuana for $300. He claimed Lee pulled a gun on him after he took out the money, prompting him to open fire.

According to recent reports, prosecutors argued that Gulley shot the teenager to avoid paying for the drugs. Surveillance footage showed him fleeing Lee’s vehicle with a gun in his hand, although it did not capture the shooting itself.

TikTok star Mama Tot “not happy” after man arrested in connection with son’s murder.

Man arrested in connection with murder of TikTok star Mama Tot’s son.

TikToker Ophelia Nichols appeals for information following son’s murder.

Gulley’s defense attorney, Chase Dearman, questioned the police investigation and argued there was insufficient evidence to convict his client.

Following the acquittal, Nichols stated her family would continue to question how the jury reached its decision.

“We don’t know what, why or how the jurors came to that decision and I’m sure we will question that moment the rest of our lives,” she wrote. “No remorse for our family. Zero regards for Randon’s life. What was done to our family was downright cruel and knowing that we are not alone in these situations is scary.”.

The TikToker also described the emotional toll the verdict had taken on her husband and daughter.

Industry observers note that “I watched my daughter cry her eyes out today, I’ve only seen my husband cry like three times in the 20 years we’ve been married and he couldn’t control himself today,” she mentioned. “He lost it.”.

#195428. Tech Report: MIT’s new lidar chip could give self-driving cars a wider view

📅 22 Jul 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1386 w)

Hardware & Chips ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: MIT’s new lidar chip could give self-driving cars a wider view

📅 22 Jul 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1386 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, lidar technology uses pulses of infrared light to calculate distances and create detailed 3D maps of the surrounding environment.
  • MIT researchers have now developed an approach that could lead to smaller, more durable lidar sensors that operate without any moving parts.
  • It has been revealed that existing lidar systems built with silicon-photonics chips usually have a narrow field of view.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, lidar technology uses pulses of infrared light to calculate distances and create detailed 3D maps of the surrounding environment. This allows autonomous vehicles to detect objects in their path and respond quickly. However, conventional lidar sensors are often large and costly, and many rely on moving components that can wear out over time. These limitations make the systems difficult to use in a wider range of settings.

MIT researchers have now developed an approach that could lead to smaller, more durable lidar sensors that operate without any moving parts. Their advance centers on a fresh silicon-photonics chip, a type of semiconductor device that controls light instead of electrical signals.

It has been revealed that existing lidar systems built with silicon-photonics chips usually have a narrow field of view. As a result, they struggle to scan areas located toward the edges of a scene. Previous attempts to expand this viewing range have often introduced extra noise and reduced measurement accuracy.

The MIT team addressed those problems by creating an array of integrated antennas that greatly limits unwanted crosstalk, which occurs when neighboring antennas interfere with one another. The design allows the chip to scan across a broader field of view while producing less noise than other silicon-photonics-based methods.

A Smaller Lidar System With a Wider View.

The advance could support the development of more capable lidar sensors for challenging uses, including autonomous vehicle navigation, aerial mapping, and the monitoring of construction sites.

In a recent development, "The functionality we demonstrated in this work solves a fundamental problem for integrated optical-phased-array technology, enabling future lidar sensors that can achieve significantly higher performance than we could demonstrate previously," claims Jelena Notaros, the Robert J. Shillman Career Development Associate Professor of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science (EECS) at MIT, a member of the Research Laboratory of Electronics, and senior author of a paper on this innovation.

Recent findings suggest that the study also includes lead author and EECS graduate student Henry Crawford-Eng, along with EECS graduate students Andres Garcia Coleto, Benjamin M. Mazur, Daniel M. DeSantis, and Tal Sneh. The findings were published recently in Nature Communications.

How Lidar Maps Its Surroundings.

According to recent reports, many traditional lidar systems use a large rotating unit to direct light pulses across a scene. When the light strikes nearby objects, it reflects back toward the sensor. The returning signals provide the information needed to reconstruct a detailed map of the environment.

Sources indicate that silicon-photonics-based lidar works differently. Rather than rotating a mechanical device, it scans a beam of light electronically in several directions with a system known as an integrated optical phased array (OPA).

At the heart of an OPA is a group of integrated antennas. Each antenna contains tiny, regularly spaced variations along its length. These features, known as corrugations, cause light from an input source to scatter upward and out of the photonic chip.

Researchers can control the direction of the outgoing beam by changing the phase of the light sent to each antenna. Adjusting these phases changes the angle at which the array releases light, making it possible to steer the beam without moving any physical components.

Industry observers note that placing the antennas close together creates a serious obstacle. Neighboring antennas can couple with one another, scrambling the light they produce. Engineers have traditionally prevented this interference by increasing the distance between antennas, but wider spacing creates a different set of problems.

When antennas are too far apart, the array produces several copies of the same beam at different angles. The primary beam can only be moved a limited distance before it becomes difficult to distinguish from these additional copies.

"This limits our field of view, so the autonomous vehicle now only knows what is in front of it for a certain angular range," Garcia Coleto explains.

Recent findings suggest that the unwanted beam copies, called grating lobes, can confuse the sensor and generate false detections. They also consume energy that could otherwise be directed into the main beam.

To overcome this tradeoff, the MIT researchers developed antennas with reduced crosstalk that can be positioned close together without strongly coupling.

Three Antenna Shapes Reduce Interference.

According to recent reports, in a conventional OPA, every antenna has an identical structure and uses the same pattern of corrugations. When these matching antennas are placed close together, they interact very strongly.

In a recent development, the MIT team instead created a repeating set of three antennas with distinct shapes. They changed the width of the antennas as well as the size and placement of the corrugations. Because the antennas have different geometries, each one also has a different propagation coefficient, which describes how light moves through the structure.

According to recent reports, "Because the antennas have very different propagation coefficients, when we put them close together, essentially each antenna doesn't 'see' the antenna next to it. Therefore, it won't couple with its neighbor," Garcia Coleto says.

Making Different Antennas Behave the Same Way.

It has been revealed that reducing the coupling was only part of the challenge. Although the antennas needed different propagation coefficients, they still had to release light in the same consistent manner.

The team designed the antennas around three essential requirements.

Industry observers note that each antenna had to emit the same amount of light. Every antenna also needed to release its beam at the same angle when receiving the same wavelength. Finally, the angle of emission had to change evenly across the entire array as the beam was steered.

Recent findings suggest that "We have this challenge where we require the antennas to have different geometries to reduce the crosstalk, but we need to simultaneously design the antennas to have the same emission characteristics. While it is possible to engineer this, it is extremely difficult because, typically, when antennas are designed with different geometries, they tend to behave differently," Crawford-Eng says.

The researchers began by developing the basic electromagnetic theory describing how radiative modes couple. They then used this theoretical framework to guide the design and computer simulation of the antennas.

Based on those calculations, the team manufactured an OPA containing the reduced-crosstalk antennas. The antennas were placed much closer together than those in a conventional system, and the completed device was then tested experimentally.

Interference Falls From About 100 Percent to 1 Percent.

Under the conditions of the experiment, a typical OPA would have produced coupling of approximately 100 percent. The MIT design lowered that coupling to about 1 percent while still generating one clean and precise beam.

The system accurately steered the beam across a broad field of view without producing any grating lobes. This combination of wide scanning, low interference, and strong beam quality addresses one of the central obstacles facing integrated lidar technology.

Sources indicate that the researchers now plan to refine the method so the system can cover an even broader viewing range. They are also studying another possible approach to wide field-of-view performance that emerged while they were developing the underlying theory.

"This work addresses a longstanding challenge in integrated optical phased arrays: simultaneously achieving both a wide field of view, which requires dense antenna spacing, and high beam quality, which requires low crosstalk between neighboring antennas. The authors solve this problem with an elegant antenna design. Their innovation is an key step forward for chip-scale, solid-state beam-steering technology," states Joyce Poon, professor of electrical and computer engineering at the University of Toronto and director of the Max Planck Institute of Microstructure Physics, who was not involved with this work.

In a recent development, the Semiconductor Research Corporation, the National Science Foundation, an MIT MathWorks Fellowship, the U.S. Department of War, and the MIT Rolf G. Locher Endowed Fellowship supported the research, in part.

Some of the work was carried out using MIT.nano facilities.

#195427. Tech Report: LeRobot Community Datasets: The “ImageNet” of Robotics — When and How?

Tech Report: LeRobot Community Datasets: The “ImageNet” of Robotics — When and How?

📅 11 May 2025 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1505 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, recent advances in Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have enabled robots to perform a wide range of tasks—from simple commands like “grasp the cube” to more complex activities like folding laundry or cleaning a table.
  • “The biggest challenge in robotics isn’t dexterity, but generalization—across physical, visual, and semantic levels.”— Physical Intelligence.
  • Industry observers note that A robot must "figure out how to correctly perform even a simple task in a new setting or with new objects," and this requires both robust skills and common-sense understanding of the world.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, recent advances in Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have enabled robots to perform a wide range of tasks—from simple commands like “grasp the cube” to more complex activities like folding laundry or cleaning a table. These models aim to achieve generalization: the ability to perform tasks in novel settings, with unseen objects, and in varying conditions.

“The biggest challenge in robotics isn’t dexterity, but generalization—across physical, visual, and semantic levels.”— Physical Intelligence.

Industry observers note that A robot must "figure out how to correctly perform even a simple task in a new setting or with new objects," and this requires both robust skills and common-sense understanding of the world. Yet, progress is often limited by the availability of diverse data for such robotic systems.

“Generalization must occur at many levels. At the low level, the robot must understand how to pick up a spoon (by the handle) or plate (by the edge), even if it has not seen these specific spoons or plates before, and even if they are placed in a pile of dirty dishes. At a higher level, the robot must understand the semantics of each task—where to put clothes and shoes (ideally in the laundry hamper or closet, not on the bed), and what kind of tool is appropriate for wiping down a spill. This generalization requires both robust physical skills and a common-sense understanding of the environment, so that the robot can generalize at many levels at the same time, from physical, to visual, to semantic. This is made even harder by the limited availability of diverse data for such robotic systems.”— Physical Intelligence.

To simplify, the core of generalist policies lies in a simple idea: co-training on heterogeneous datasets. By exposing VLA models to a variety of environments, tasks, and robot embodiments, we can teach models not only how to act, but why—how to interpret a scene, understand a goal, and adapt skills across contexts.

💡 “Generalization is not just a model property—it’s a data phenomenon.”It emerges from the diversity, quality, and abstraction level of the training data.

This brings us to a fundamental question:.

Given current datasets, what is the upper limit of generalization we can expect?

Sources indicate that can a robot meaningfully respond to a completely novel prompt—say, *"set up a surprise birthday party"*—if it has never encountered anything remotely similar during training? Especially when most datasets are collected in academic labs, by a limited number of people, under well-controlled setups?

It has been revealed that we frame generalization as a data-centric view: treating it as the process of abstracting broader patterns from data—essentially “zooming out” to reveal task-agnostic structures and principles. This shift in perspective emphasizes the role of dataset diversity, rather than model architecture alone, in driving generalization.

According to recent reports, so far, the majority of robotics datasets come from structured academic environments. Even if we scale up to millions of demonstrations, one dataset will often dominate, limiting diversity. Unlike ImageNet—which aggregated internet-scale data and captured the real world more holistically—robotics lacks a comparably diverse, community-driven benchmark.

This is largely because collecting data for robotics requires physical hardware and significant effort.

That’s why, at LeRobot, we’re working to make robotics data collection more accessible—at home, at school, or anywhere. We're:.

We're already seeing the results: the number of community-contributed datasets on the Hub is growing rapidly.

Growth of lerobot datasets on the Hugging Face Hub over time.

Sources indicate that if we break down the uploaded datasets by robot type, we see that most contributions are to So100 and Koch, making robotic arms and manipulation tasks the primary focus of the current LeRobot dataset landscape. However, it’s crucial to remember that the potential reaches far beyond. Domains like autonomous vehicles, assistive robots, and mobile navigation stand to benefit just as much from shared data. This momentum brings us closer to a future where datasets reflect a global effort, not just the contributions of a single lab or institution.

Recent findings suggest that as robotics data collection becomes more democratized, curation becomes the next challenge. While these datasets are still collected in constrained setups, they are a crucial step toward affordable, general-purpose robotic policies. Not everyone has access to expensive hardware—but with shared infrastructure and open collaboration, we can build something far greater.

🧠 “Generalization isn’t solved in a lab—it’s taught by the world.”The more diverse our data, the more capable our models will be.

Why does data quality matter? Poor-quality data results in poor downstream performance, biased outputs, and models that fail to generalize. Hence, efficient and high-quality data collection plays a critical role in advancing generalist robotic policies.

Recent findings suggest that while foundation models in vision and language have thrived on massive, web-scale datasets, robotics lacks an “Internet of robots”—a vast, diverse corpus of real-world interactions. Instead, robotic data is fragmented across different embodiments, sensor setups, and control modes, forming isolated data islands.

To overcome this, recent approaches like Gr00t organize training data as a pyramid, where:.

Within this framework, efficient real-world data collection is indispensable—it anchors learned behaviors in actual robotic hardware and closes the sim-to-real gap, ultimately improving the generalization, adaptability, and performance of robotics foundation models.

By expanding the volume and diversity of real-world datasets, we reduce fragmentation between heterogeneous data sources. When datasets are disjoint in terms of environment, embodiment, or task distribution, models struggle to transfer knowledge across domains.

🔗 Real-world data acts as connective tissue—it aligns abstract priors with grounded action and enables the model to build more coherent and transferable representations.

As a result, increasing the proportion of real robot interactions does not merely enhance realism—it structurally reinforces the links between all layers of the pyramid, leading to more robust and capable policies.

Industry observers note that at LeRobot, we’ve started developing an automatic curation pipeline to post-process community datasets. During the post-processing phase, we’ve identified several areas where improvements can further boost dataset quality and facilitate more effective curation going forward:.

Recent findings suggest that many datasets lack task descriptions, lack details or are ambiguous in the task to be done. Semantics is presently at the core of cognition, meaning that understanding the context and specifics of a task is crucial for robotic performance. Detailed expressions ensure that robots understand exactly what is expected, but also provide a broader knowledge and vocabulary to the cognition system. Ambiguity can lead to incorrect interpretation and, consequently, incorrect actions.

Subtask-level annotations are often missing, making it difficult to model complex task hierarchies.While this can be handled with VLM, it is still better to have a task annotation provided by the author of the dataset at hand.

Features like images.laptop are ambiguously labeled:.

Different datasets use different action or state dimensions, even for the same robot (e.g., so100).Some datasets show inconsistencies in action/state format.

You wrote a good email. You hit send. Then half your list never saw it, because it went straight to spam.

That is a deliverability problem, and it costs more than most teams think. Every email that misses the inbox is a lead you paid for and never reached.

The good part is that deliverability is not luck. Mailbox providers like Gmail, Yahoo and Outlook judge you on a short list of things: who you are, who you send to, and how people react. Fix those and your inbox placement goes up.

This guide covers 10 email deliverability best practices in the order you should fix them, starting with SPF and ending with sender reputation.

Email deliverability is the share of your emails that land in the inbox instead of the spam folder or nowhere at all.

People often mix it up with delivery rate. They are not the same thing.

According to recent reports, you can have a 99% delivery rate and still have most of your emails sitting in spam. That is why your email tool can say "delivered" while your open rate keeps dropping.

The big mailbox providers stopped treating authentication as optional.

Microsoft followed on May 5, 2025. If you send more than 5,000 emails a day to Outlook.com, Hotmail or Live addresses, you need all three records in place or your mail goes to junk.

Send less than 5,000 a day? Follow the rules anyway. The same checks decide inbox placement for small senders too, just without the public warning.

In a recent development, SPF (Sender Policy Framework) is a TXT record in your DNS. It lists the servers allowed to send email from your domain.

When your email arrives, the receiving server checks that list. If the sending server is not on it, the email looks suspicious.

A basic SPF record looks like this:.

DKIM (DomainKeys Identified Mail) adds a digital signature to each email. The receiving server uses a public key in your DNS to check two things: the email came from you, and nobody changed it on the way.

Sources indicate that your email provider gives you the DKIM record. You paste it into your DNS and switch signing on.

DKIM also survives forwarding, which SPF does not. If you can only get one of the two perfect, get DKIM right.

It has been revealed that DMARC ties SPF and DKIM together. It tells mailbox providers what to do when an email fails both checks, and it sends you reports on who is sending mail under your domain name.

Start with a monitoring policy:.

p=none means "take no action, just send me reports." It is the minimum Gmail, Yahoo and Microsoft accept from bulk senders.

In a recent development, don't stop there. Read the reports for a few weeks, fix any real sender that is failing, then move up:.

It has been revealed that one more thing: DMARC needs alignment. The domain in your From address has to match the domain used in SPF or DKIM. Plenty of senders have all three records and still fail DMARC because their email tool signs with its own domain.

If you'd rather not handle this in-house, you can also hire a B2B cold email marketing agency such as IntentSignal, Martal or Belkins. A good agency will set up the domains, mailboxes, warm-up and SPF, DKIM and DMARC records for you, and keep an eye on deliverability while the campaigns run.

A new domain has no history. If it sends 10,000 emails on day one, it looks exactly like a spammer who just bought a domain.

Warm-up means starting small and growing a little each day, so mailbox providers can watch how people react to you.

A simple schedule for a latest domain:.

In a recent development, send to your most active contacts first. Their opens and replies are what build trust early. If bounces or complaints jump, hold at that volume until they settle.

And if you run cold outreach, do it from a separate domain or subdomain. That way a bad campaign can't hurt the domain your invoices and password resets come from.

It has been revealed that A bigger list is not a better list. Dead addresses and people who stopped caring pull your numbers down.

It has been revealed that never buy a list. Bought lists are full of spam traps, which are addresses that exist only to catch senders who email people without permission. Hitting a few of them can get your domain blocklisted.

According to recent reports, yes, you lose some sign-ups. What you keep is real people with working inboxes who actually want your emails. That means fewer bounces, fewer complaints and better opens from day one.

It also keeps bots and fake addresses out of your forms, which matters a lot if your sign-up form is public.

It has been revealed that most email platforms add these for you. Check that yours does.

These two numbers tell you the most about where you stand.

In a recent development, the complaint figures come from Gmail's own rules. The bounce figures are the working limits most email platforms use.

It has been revealed that A 0.3% complaint rate is only 3 complaints per 1,000 emails. It does not take much to cross that line.

If complaints are climbing, ask three questions:.

Most complaint problems come from one of those three, not from the email itself.

Recent findings suggest that spam filters got smarter. A single word like "free" won't sink you anymore. Patterns will.

According to recent reports, replies help a lot. When someone replies, the mailbox provider sees a real conversation. Ask a question in your welcome email and you'll get some.

It has been revealed that sender reputation is the score mailbox providers give your domain and IP. Everything above feeds into it. A good score means inbox. A bad one means spam, no matter how good the email is.

You can't see the exact score, but these free tools get you close:.

Check them weekly, and right after any big campaign.

A few habits protect your reputation over time:.

Industry observers note that aim for 95% or higher inbox placement. Below 90% means something needs fixing, usually authentication or list quality.

It has been revealed that the common causes are missing or broken SPF, DKIM or DMARC records, a high complaint rate, an old list with lots of dead addresses, or a upcoming domain that sent too much too soon. Check authentication first because it is the fastest to fix.

In a recent development, DNS fixes like SPF and DKIM take effect within a day or two. Reputation is slower. Expect two to six weeks of steady, clean sending before inbox placement recovers.

Yes. The 5,000 mark is where Gmail, Yahoo and Microsoft start enforcing openly. Small senders are still judged on the same signals, and Gmail asks every sender for at least SPF or DKIM.

Industry observers note that only if you send enough to keep it warm, roughly 100,000 emails a month or more. Below that, a good shared IP from a trusted provider usually performs better.

In a recent development, sender reputation covers both your IP address and your domain. Domain reputation is the part tied to your domain name, and it follows you even if you switch email providers. Gmail leans on domain reputation more than IP.

It has been revealed that if you only have an hour this week, spend it on SPF, DKIM and DMARC. Nothing else works until those pass.

After that, clean your list and keep an eye on complaints. Send emails people asked for, to people who still want them, from a domain that proves who it is. Do that for a few weeks and your emails will land in the inbox again.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A newly developed superconducting quantum heat engine could deepen our understanding of thermodynamics while helping advance technologies needed for quantum computers with very large numbers of qubits.
  • Scientists are getting a clearer picture of how thermodynamics behaves in the quantum world, and that progress could benefit both quantum technology and our understanding of familiar thermodynamic principles.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A newly developed superconducting quantum heat engine could deepen our understanding of thermodynamics while helping advance technologies needed for quantum computers with very large numbers of qubits.

Scientists are getting a clearer picture of how thermodynamics behaves in the quantum world, and that progress could benefit both quantum technology and our understanding of familiar thermodynamic principles. Researchers at Aalto University have now taken an important step by demonstrating the first cyclic quantum heat engine built inside a superconducting circuit.

In a recent development, the experiment connects two areas of physics that normally describe very different scales. Quantum mechanics explains the behavior of matter at extremely small scales, even below the size of atoms, while thermodynamics describes how heat and energy behave in much larger systems, from collections of molecules to the universe itself. Bringing the two together raises a fundamental question: what happens to familiar thermodynamic processes when quantum effects such as tunneling, entanglement, and superposition enter the picture?

A Heat Engine Built for the Quantum World.

According to recent reports, conventional heat engines turn heat into useful work. James Watt's steam engine is one famous example, but the same basic concept remains central to modern transportation and electricity production, powering cars, ships, planes and many power plants.

In a recent development, the researchers have now created the world's first superconducting quantum heat engine. The extremely small device combines a transmon qubit, a resonator and a quantum refrigerator.

Operating under ultracold quantum conditions, the engine was able to use the tiny amount of available heat to repeatedly produce positive work. Achieving this kind of cyclic operation has been an notable objective for researchers working on quantum heat engines. The result provides a proof of concept for superconducting heat engines that could eventually contribute to improved quantum computing technology.

The study, led by Academy Professor Mikko Möttönen, was published in Nature Communications.

Recreating an Otto Cycle Near Absolute Zero.

In a recent development, to make the engine operate, the researchers reproduced an Otto cycle inside a superconducting circuit. The Otto cycle is a thermodynamic process also used in car engines and other conventional machines.

Sources indicate that "In our experiment, we built a nanofabricated heat engine using superconducting circuits and operated it in a cryostat near absolute zero. At its heart is a transmon qubit, one of the basic building blocks of modern quantum technologies," indicates Tuomas Uusnäkki, the study's first author.

Recent findings suggest that the researchers connected the transmon qubit to a quantum circuit refrigerator, allowing them to control heat flow on the quantum scale and demonstrate that this heat could be transformed into measurable work. A conventional heat engine normally relies on separate hot and cold environments. In this system, however, the same quantum refrigerator can supply both heating and cooling.

Industry observers note that "Our quantum-circuit refrigerator can be tuned to both heat and cool the qubit on demand. Using carefully timed control pulses, we drove the engine in an Otto cycle and monitored the qubit state as the engine ran," explains Uusnäkki.

Measurements indicated that heat passing through the qubit during the cycle was producing positive work.

Industry observers note that "This is the first experimental demonstration of a cyclic quantum heat engine in superconducting circuits. Using a single controllable quantum refrigerator as both the hot and cold environment of the engine makes it simpler and more versatile," notes Uusnäkki.

Toward Autonomous Quantum Computer Hardware.

The researchers are now trying to improve the design and eventually develop a fully autonomous heat engine. One possible use would be reading out qubits without having to carry a microwave pulse from millikelvin temperatures all the way to room temperature.

Industry observers note that that capability could become especially valuable as quantum computers grow. Autonomous devices integrated directly into superconducting circuits could reduce both the cost and complexity of machines containing very large numbers of qubits.

"Finland's Quantum Technology Strategy envisions a quantum computer with one thousand logical qubits by 2035, which probably means hundreds of thousands of physical qubits. Doing that with current technology requires millions of microwave cables costing thousand euros each. The cables also introduce noise into the system. Using autonomous devices instead would mostly eliminate the need for those cables," Möttönen notes.

Reducing the need for those microwave connections could therefore address two challenges at once: the enormous hardware requirements of large quantum computers and the unwanted noise that cables can introduce into quantum systems.

In a recent development, the pioneering experiment was carried out using OtaNano, Finland's national research infrastructure for nano, micro and quantum technology. Funding came from the Research Council of Finland and the Finnish Cultural Foundation.

A “Chinese spy” lookalike contest took over Upcoming York City’s Washington Square Park, with participants performing mock espionage acts for a cash prize.

The competition took place on November 21 and was organized by FactMachine and Prez, drawing a crowd of spectators who were given the opportunity to vote for their favorite contestants.

The event was inspired by the ongoing controversy surrounding Nvidia co-founder Jensen Huang, who had resigned as CEO just over a week before the competition took place.

Around 10 women participated in the competition, dressing up as spies and performing various espionage-inspired acts in front of the crowd.

Some contestants pretended to pull classified documents from their pockets, while another person dressed up as Jensen Huang joined in with the performances.

Spectators were able to decide the winner by scanning QR codes displayed at the venue and voting for their favorite participant, with a $50 cash prize up for grabs.

A post shared by Keri | NYC Content Creator (@keri_nyc).

Industry observers note that the contest came after Nvidia released an independent investigation on November 8 into reports that its CEO had been targeted by a foreign intelligence operation. Huang also admitted to being unfaithful to his wife in a message sent to employees.

Recent findings suggest that on November 12, he resigned as president, CEO, and a member of Nvidia’s board of directors, ending his 33-year tenure leading the company. Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress was appointed interim CEO.

However, just two days after the lookalike contest, Nvidia declared that Huang had been reinstated following a unanimous vote by its board of directors.

The firm said it had consulted senior US government officials and was confident that his return posed no national security risk. Its independent investigation remains ongoing, with Huang committing to cooperate.
