📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that my best attempt at summing up Grand Theft Auto 6 came from a conversation with a friend about something else entirely. This friend was telling me about a theory they'd recently heard, and half agreed with, that just so happened to layer over this game perfectly. Americans, they remarked, paraphrasing, have found a newly introduced 'third place': the car.

Industry observers note that I'm slightly skeptical of the obsession with third places these days - love the concept; less convinced that societal bonds are collapsing because today's men aren't spending enough time at their barber's. But here it felt just right: GTA 6 is, of course, a game both about America and about the personal vehicle. The clue's in the name. And as you play GTA 6, you realise, over and over, that the car is where so much of this game happens. It's where you take calls that lead to missions or story developments; where you pick up, hang out with, and chat to your partner; where you race away from police, gangs, wild animals and weirdos. Where you do much of your discovery of this properly, disorientatingly, astoundingly big and detailed world. Where you'll be when you find the most 'emergent events'. And, more than it's ever been before, the car is now an essential partner in itself; a place to stow weapons, disguises, and stolen goods - a companion it feels almost impossible to do without.

I could go on about this. GTA 6 is a game of perpetual motion, as protagonists Jason and Lucia do their best to outrun a world that so often feels a step ahead - and which often culminates in some of the most exhilarating, astonishing chase sequences ever built in a video game. GTA 5, its Los Santos-set predecessor, was aware enough of the importance of the car to name an in-game canyon after Reyner Banham, the British architectural critic who described Los Angeles' freeway system, one of the city's "four ecologies", as "Autopia". So yes: the car is the third place, in modern America and in GTA 6. The place of self-actualisation between work and home - two points that, for GTA 6's protagonists in particular, seem to always be in a state of flux. Maybe the car's their true home. For the longest time I really thought that idea summed up GTA 6 quite nicely. Until I didn't.

Reducing GTA 6 to just the car, I realised, looking at it through only that one lens, forces you to be too narrow. You miss too much of it. What about the romance? The sensuality? The people and the natural world? And so what I've come to settle on instead - and honestly I expect this to change many more times over the coming days and weeks too, as even more of this horizonless game rolls back to reveal itself - is that GTA 6 just doesn't have a single thread to pull on. No one thing that, when properly grasped, suddenly draws it into a manageable shape.

Recent findings suggest that I've no doubt we'll all try. People have, for whatever reason, always reached for the most reductive ideas when they talk about Grand Theft Auto in particular. Maybe it's a natural response to something too big and unwieldy to instantly get your head around: to seize the first acceptable idea and declare it just 'x'. To admit something is too complex for you to immediately summarise is far less comfortable than simply dismissing it on the spot.

Whatever it is, GTA 6 isn't just anything. For one, every thing it is also seems to have an opposite. It's vast - incomprehensibly vast - but also overloaded with miniscule detail. It's about substantial ideas, themes, places - America, society, love - and also about individuals. It's ridiculous and puerile, and also sometimes mature. Tender and violent. Deep and shallow. Novel and, in places, surprisingly familiar. It's both a big adventure playground of video game activities and a focused story of suffocating intensity. Whatever foible might arise, the game presents you with a ready-made answer - often quite literally: you can turn off notifications about your relationship status in the menu if you just want to ignore that part. You can switch to the old controls (GTA 6 has seen a bit of a control overhaul), from the first screen you're shown. Or simply tear off in the opposite direction to whatever it is that dissatisfies you and do something else. If there's an idea to reduce this game to, then, the best I can manage is this: maybe Grand Theft Auto 6 is a game designed to be irreducible.

None of that is to say it's perfect. It's easy to stand in front of something like this and just bask in the awe of it, forgetting to stop a moment and step back. The awe is all part of the point, of course, and GTA 6 is nothing if not truly awesome, but there are also nits to pick. But then you step back again and they tend to fade away. GTA 6 will not be for everyone. But no game has made a better attempt at being everything.

According to recent reports, GTA 6's story begins with Jason and Lucia. Discussing it beyond that is, frankly, almost impossible to do with any kind of substance without also spoiling it. For all the precipitous leaks, Rockstar has kept its story's two most essential moments - its beginning and its end - entirely secret, and without those two moments we're only really left with euphemisms.

Jason and Lucia are on the run, after a seemingly simple fetch quest goes awry. Who they're running from, or why they're being chased quite so hard, remains agonisingly beyond their field of view. But what is clear, right from the off, is exactly why they're so determined to escape. And amongst all this Rockstar has achieved something kind of momentous, when it comes to Grand Theft Auto: we've got real and very human stakes.

What else can be said? Well, let's go back to Rockstar's decision to begin so explicitly with Jason and Lucia. This is a story about a relationship. You can nurture or neglect it, but fundamentally that relationship - however strong - is at the heart of things.

The fact that Grand Theft Auto 6, of all games, is in many ways a game about love, and arguably the first blockbuster video game to be quite so explicitly a love story, is notable enough on its own. These are the games of rampages, wanted levels, hookers and hot coffee - the series which, in its most recent entry until now, featured effectively zero women of note or meaningful substance. Immediately there's a kind of tension forming as you play: I've sat down with this thing, fully prepared to steal a tank and squish beachloads of ultra-realistic civilians like playdough. But should I pick up some flowers first? The secret is that tension, like a lot of GTA 6's many opposites, is kind of the point.

Buying flowers, for instance, is one of the game's early, albeit optional missions. You begin GTA 6 proper playing solely as Jason for a short while, as he waits in his hazy, barefoot, margarita-soaked island hometown for Lucia to be released from prison. The two have been separated, their relationship effectively and conveniently reset - what kind of impression do you want to make when you finally see her after all this time? While the urge might be to test out those new wanted mechanics or - as recent memes would have it - race across the map to the first stripclub you can find, suddenly you have an altogether different to-do list.

Pick up some groceries. Get those flowers. Grab some clothes for Lucia to change into. Maybe finish those odd DIY jobs you've left half-started around the place so, y'know, your bedroom actually has a wall. Ever since GTA 4, and Roman Bellic's slightly desperate calls to go play darts and shoot some pool, Rockstar has leant further and further into the mundane. But here the studio has gone many steps further, past the Sopranos of GTA 5 and poker of Red Dead Redemption 2, full-tilt into slice-of-life. The result, mercifully, is anything but dull - all these situations, familiar as they may be, are really moments for irony, humour, character, just as they are in life itself. That, and a welcome chance to catch your breath amidst the bombast, which accelerates from these early missions exponentially.

It has been revealed that that early, to-do list mission is like a lot of other moments in GTA, in that it's a case of Rockstar not-so-subtly dropping hints. This time, it's "we are going to play with your priorities". If there's a constant in GTA 6, you realise, it's that there often seems to be a nagging thought in the back of your mind as you progress. Should I be prioritising this right now? Is that optional thing worth the effort? Will this choice matter? How? It's such a prominent thought as you play, the actual act of devising what systems this game is using as you progress is as interesting in itself as how those systems end up working. Or to put it more simply: figuring this game out for yourself is really part of the fun.

Industry observers note that back to Jason and Lucia. The other thought I kept returning to is how profound a bond I started to form with them. I have to admit: I've tended not to care much about video game characters, frankly. Even in the obvious games, where voice actors have started to attract almost cult-like followings, I've never really got it. The closest any game has got to making me cry is in Football Manager 23, when I lost the Champions League final in the dying minutes to PSG. But with Jason and Lucia, suddenly I think I get it. I put much of this down to the performances - they are spellbinding - but really it's all interconnected, a factor of the extreme levels of development craft, from animation to cutscene direction, and of several relatively simple, but smartly executed systems layered on top (more on those later).

It has been revealed that lucia's performer - unveiled at last as Manni L. Perez - is astoundingly natural, charismatic, authentic in her delivery. The range of this character takes her from fierce to afraid, giddy and giggly to imperiously strong, or petal soft. And despite those extremes of emotion, and GTA characters' historic knack of scenery-chewing, she is never a caricature; between those two far ends lies the entire spectrum, too. Jason, prosaic and inarticulate - arguably even shy - feels destined to be underappreciated by comparison, but there's something to his performance also. Next to the sheer dazzle of Lucia, you need a straight-man to play off. And so where she might shine with sass, or protectiveness, or playful faux annoyance for a laugh, Jason might offer an eye roll, a sigh, or some other exasperation under his breath. He's also - at least with the relationship at its strongest - a surprisingly fine example of the strong, yet thoroughly non-toxic man; gentle and considerate, reassuring and attentive. Occasionally I have to catch myself, before I start believing GTA 6 - again, of all games - might genuinely be the game to offer the most persuasive model of a positive relationship to the kids who play it. (Again, aside from all the killing and stuff).

Sources indicate that and those quieter aspects are a necessary foil - in fact, they're really a place where Rockstar exercises some rare subtlety. Some of GTA 6's funniest moments - between the significant, obvious, admittedly still very funny gags for this childish mind (be sure to look out for all the game's many WAiNK locations!) - come from almost imperceptible glances and asides amongst the chaos. Together, both protagonists feel somewhat aware of the ludicrousness of the world around them, even more than they are simply a part of it.The two stars' relationship - and I chose to lean into this all the way, full 'wife guy' Jason and guard-down Lucia - is developed through minutiae. In a way, it comes just as a real relationship does. Little touches, side eyes, in jokes. After a mission together with some classic, larger-than-life GTA character or other, they'll occasionally have a little debrief, in the way a real couple might the morning after a particularly lurid double-date. They'll check-in, chit-chat, hang out, discuss hopes for the future, fears about what might happen, skepticism that they'll ever escape this constant whirlpool. And how you've behaved so far will dictate how the other might respond, with reassurance and commitment or something else.

Sources indicate that small gestures will add up, and both parties have to contribute. You can hold hands whenever you're together, open car doors for each other, send check-in texts or invitations to hang out. But it gets even more menial than that. Sometimes it's just sitting on the sofa together, watching TV or talking about nothing in particular (on the topic of TV: GTA 6 has a number of fully fledged TV shows, from Weasel News to actual, fully realised cartoon animations with multiple episodes; it also has four fully playable video games, including a pastiche arthouse walking simulator and twin-stick extraction shooter). Other times, sure, it's a particular kind of passion ignited by the unique thrill of a violent, climactic mission. This couple can be a burning cocktail, if you want them to be, born of extreme external danger and the safety of each other's embrace. And in their most tender moments, handled with genuine attentiveness and sincerity, it's intoxicating.

None of this, crucially, feels like a chore. Instead it feels almost irresistible, the easiest and most natural role play, created in part by Rockstar smartly prompting you with certain icons in moments, incentivising you with the tease of branching narrative - the idea in the back of your mind that there's some kind of outcome, somewhere in here, if things go a certain way. In others, they leave it to you: if I hadn't approached Lucia in the kitchen one early-game morning and pressed L2 to see what interactions came up, I wouldn't have noticed I had the option to offer her a lift to work, another little moment to bond.

Recent findings suggest that all together, it's a picture of what many great relationships - maybe minus the rampages - become as a whole. A series of grand memories made together, sure - across rooftop bars, helicopter rides, and sunsets at the beach, maybe a couple of bank robberies and killing sprees - but also hours upon hours of touches, jokes, hugs, nicknames, shared friends, cups of coffee, dancing, laughter, or long, quiet journeys in the car. It is without doubt the most believable, captivating relationship I've ever played.

Sources indicate that I could talk forever about this pair, not just in their relationship but as characters, extensions of GTA 6's thematic world. At various moments in my time with the game, for instance, I found myself wondering about Lucia's experience of the world, and how Rockstar uses its famously detestable NPCs - individually written and constructed in the thousands, another quietly stunning factor in this game - to occasionally play the role of, for instance, leering older men. How villains love to taunt her as "mamacita", while Jason affectionately nicknames her "mami". Or through a bizarrely affecting, bittersweet friendship she develops with a gentle(-ish) giant - and also another, not-so-gentle giant for that matter, in a mission that takes a turn. And in the casual racism she simply rolls with, just an everyday annoyance. And Jason too, in turn, in how he's sexualised and objectified in his own way, reduced in various moments to a weapon, a meathead, a walking gun, the staff. How the two of them wrestle with their position of desperation, poverty and precariousness in the world of Leonida, a microcosm of Rockstar's take on the United States.

I should probably start talking about that world. Where to begin? Let's start with the obvious stuff: GTA 6's map is absolutely massive. I haven't tested this directly, but the leaked maps are more or less accurate, and the comparisons in terms of size - multiple GTA 5's within GTA 6's map of Leonida - are about right. After dozens and dozens of hours with it there are still little areas, islands, and archipelagos I haven't explored, and many more spots so rarely visited they still feel entirely fresh when I drive through them again.

It has been revealed that at one point, amongst the forest of the national park up in Leonida's northern third - trundling down one winding dirt track among many, trees in all directions - I actually found myself slightly lost. At least for a moment, anyway, until I plonked down a map marker and the GPS sorted me out. GTA 6 asks more of you than any previous GTA game, but it's also a retraction from the intentional clunk of Red Dead Redemption 2. You'll never be truly stuck or stumped; there's no sense of toil.

A quick example: the Scooter Bros (remember those?!) return here in a delightful reference, now acting as an official in-game phone app that lets you summon an owned vehicle for a fee, or up to three times a day if you unlock the app's "unlimited" version for a one-off cost. They can also repair your car or recover it if, like me, you have a habit of landing it on its roof. You can also fix it up at the returning Pay 'n' Spray's and all-latest gas stations - which, thankfully, you really don't need to visit for refuelling all that often. (When you do, it's often worth the time: this is a great window for an emergent event to pop up - more on those, too, later.).

According to recent reports, soon after that little diversion in the woods, up on the scraggy peak I'd originally set out to reach, a wave of fog rolled in, bringing visibility eerily close amongst colonial-era ruins, crumbling log cabins, and the rusted-out tracks of disused, Old West mine carts. Hikers strolled by with a nod. Then, a firewatch tower I'd sought to climb for a proper view offered me the start of one of several mysteries GTA 6 has laid out here for players, continuing the series' long-running tradition. Later that evening, after finding and raiding an encampment of drug runners, being chased, found, and chased again by police, nosing around a nudist colony, then an eerily romantic lover's lookout (plus another bizarre encounter I won't spoil), I drove my couple home, to the city in the south, country radio giving way to electronica, and thunderclouds rolled in, soaking the hills and fields and miles upon miles of tarmac as much with atmosphere as with the rain itself.

It has been revealed that time and time again you'll find yourself in moments like this, not really doing anything or going anywhere - or suddenly abandoning plans for something stranger, more curious. But crucially still passing through the world, typically from the seat of a car. Right near the beginning of the game, in the first miniature moment of free roam with Jason - a short car journey home from wherever it was I was doing some fresh-from-prologue activity - I hit a perfect example of this. Rockstar clearly knows the value of the first drive: night, rain on the asphalt, Vice City FM on the radio, red tail lights flaring the lens. That's one I've never grown tired of, and probably never will: the tail lights. A kind of universal symbol of America's bigness, your tiny position in the queue of thousands, amongst this sea of snaking red stars against the darkness. All this together an absolutely superlative vibe.

I expect everyone will find their own little fascination like this. All of these things come as a result of Rockstar's ludicrous budget and infinite runway, but also an obvious determination to use that almighty privilege to its fullest. This studio has always been emphatically, maybe fanatically focused on detail, and now it's had the greatest opportunity to exploit that obsession that might ever be afforded to a developer. And so detail is everywhere; from the way Jason's t-shirt creases as he walks or rumples in the wind, to the noise and gust kicked up by helicopters; hair that flows impossibly like water, water that actually looks like water, sweat on skin, and sweat on bottles, and dusted condensation on cars. One of the very first things I wrote down in my notes on this game, as Lucia paced the hallway of her prison, was about a patch of mismatched paint on the wall.

Recent findings suggest that this is not a patch of paint designed to be noticed. It's in the foreground for a fraction of a second as Lucia heads into another room, but it stuck for precisely that reason. This is the product of someone looking intensely at the environment as they attempt to recreate it and realising how notable imperfections are to simulating reality. Clearly someone's scuffed, scratched, or graffitied something outside of this office, and the penitentiary system has felt the need to paint over it in some vain declaration of order. And then tight budgets, like a crumbling English council once again repainting a playground fence, have dictated the colour of paint that'll be used - likely whatever was to hand - to cover up these little marks of rebellion.

Recent findings suggest that I looked at this and wrote it down. And then a few hours later, as I was whizzing around this world evading cop cars, hopping out to make a mad dash for cover, I realised how pointless that was. I'd already been darting by piles and piles of this stuff. Back alleys filled with rubbish - glorious rubbish, the most decadent scrap metal, buckets of mulch, and sacks of rotting food waste you've ever seen - and tables covered in piles of tat. Back offices stacked with papers, posters, family photos, files, mugs, notices, trophies, pens, and all kinds of amalgamated bric-a-brac that forms a picture of a real office in the mind.

Recent findings suggest that the point is: at first, as Rockstar gently guides you from place to place, gradually layering the systems onto one another, easing you into this ocean of water by toe, ankle, knee, waist, you think it's doing that thing where video games front load fidelity to set the tone, maybe flex a little, before easing up after hitting you with some significant and glorious view. Then you realise this is just what this game is like. It's everywhere. A huge amount of this map is, in the nicest possible way, kind of pointless. It's things - a disused motel, a lumber mill - which have no mission or character attached, and are instead there predominantly because in a real world they would be there, and therefore, to Rockstar, they must be there.

It has been revealed that in some moments, if you're like me, it might genuinely create a kind of sadness: the sheer, incomprehensible amount of things that have evidently been slaved over by literally thousands of humans (some of whom, notably, currently locked in an employment tribunal with Rockstar over alleged union-busting) that will almost certainly be missed. Things you'll fly by in an instant as you whip the camera round the room in search of valuables or escape routes, never to return, worker hours piling up like grains of sand on Vice City's heavenly beach. It's so easy to focus on breadth and scale when talking about GTA 6's world. The volume. The "content". But what matters more I think is this miniscule detail. There's a point where detail, in a simulated world, tips over into effective infinity, where your brain just learns to let it glide on by. A point I never thought an open world game could ever truly reach - and yet here we are. In turn it creates almost a kind of obligation to linger - linger, that is, in a game built to be experienced from behind the wheel of a supercar. Another point of brilliant tension.

Speaking of, let's get into some mechanics, where all these tension points are at their strongest. GTA 6 works like this: Jason and Lucia's story is spread over a prologue and then several chapters. The world is open more or less from the off, not dissimilar to GTA 5, and yet the game, to borrow a term from Rockstar, is "stratified" in how it gradually rolls out its systems and greatest rewards. In other words, there's a little bit of progression to get through before what feels like the true GTA 6 reveals itself.

And the real drive here, insofar as there is one, is earning money. GTA 6 is easily the purest expression of life as an actual thief that Rockstar has attempted to make. Theft is at the heart and all along the spine of Jason and Lucia's story. From the setup of the game's prologue to the inciting incident its entire, lengthy first chapter builds to, and then well beyond it, all the way through to the finale. Over time, for instance, you'll have a perpetual optional objective: to top up your joint savings account to higher and higher targets, essentially building a flight fund or future life, whatever it may ultimately be. Likewise at various points you'll need to spend a certain amount of money with someone or on something to progress. And throughout, money is ultimately the gatekeeper to the game. Money is the "bridges" of previous GTAs, if you like: in the very early game you can, as far as I could tell, go more or less anywhere. But to actually do anything worthwhile and engage with Leonida's many, many activities, you'll need to both progress the story and get a bank account, the latter of which our dear off-the-grid, dishonourably-discharged minor criminal Jason has so far opted against.

Over and over then, you'll find yourself scraping together cash, and gradually GTA 6 offers newer, more rewarding and more complex means of doing so. At first it might be via minor drug deals, collected and delivered via your boss' bi-plane, or discovering a small-time criminal operation to rob out the back of a local liquor store. Then it might be stealing some low-tier cars to flip to a fresh-found fence, or busting bigger drug operations and gang hideouts. These are a rare example of Rockstar seemingly taking outside inspiration - criminal operations, marked on your map in yellow once discovered, are essentially Ubisoft-like outposts. At first I wondered if that might be a drawback, but then separate the idea and execution itself from the stigma and I don't think so. They're dense scenarios that essentially offer a more combat-focused route to money, and a texture-forward slice of the game's criminal world. In the simplest terms they're also quite fun, and a nice break from all the other forms of theft.

Theft continues beyond that still. You soon learn how to stick up minor stores and restaurants, and rob people at gunpoint on the street. Then it's pawn shops, jewellery stores, payday loan businesses. Then before you know it you're ripping ATMs out of walls with a tow truck, hurtling down the highway with this massive metal cube still attached like a bouncing, sentient steel piñata on the run, until it cracks open for you to feast on its delicious insides. Then you're yoinking supercars or - and oh, this is the good stuff - robbing full-fledged banks at will.

This is where a lot of the various systems teased in previews - all of which sounded, on the surface, kind of awkward to me - weave into what the game is trying to do. There are several here, all overlapping in their own way and typically evolving - but not outright replicating - ideas first brought in via Read Dead Redemption 2. The combined impact is a sense of constant decision-making, tension once again between the immediacy of steaming in somewhere and tearing away from the cops, and the satisfaction of a slightly more restrained proposal.

In a recent development, to stick with money, it operates in a kind of tiered system. At the bottom you have cash, which has a $20,000 limit per character and which can be lost in its entirety, particularly when you're wasted or busted. Once you've unlocked your BuckMe (yep) account - a kind of PayPal parody - cash can be deposited at ATMs into a much safer kind of basic shared current account. Even that is at risk of charges of some kind when you're killed or arrested - I've yet to reverse engineer what dictates these, but they're at worse in the low thousands, typically less. Then above that is your savings account, again shared across Jason and Lucia, where your money is at its safest but also, crucially, irretrievable once deposited.

The physical act of collecting money is now an action, too, as opposed to something you can simply run over and vacuum up. You need to manually collect it from characters' bodies, from the counter after being placed there by a panicked cashier, from inside safes you crack, and so on. Sometimes it might be in a locked container - such as when you bust open an ATM - which you'll need to shoot first to access. Sometimes it's stored behind a bank's vault door, which only opens in a very specific circumstance, meaning a narrow, heist-like window needs to be exploited in order for it to be reached. And when you're stealing anything other than clean cash - namely jewellery, marked bills, and drugs - you'll store it in a stash bag.

That feeds into two other systems here, which both operate around a sense of ownership, in vehicles and weapons. Stash bags contain all your loot until they're filled, and then they need to be sold to a fence - with different fences offering more or less for certain goods, or not taking some at all - before you can actually access the profit. You can drop these bags when you're hit by a car or knocked off a bike (or, ahem, fumbling with the controls for a second), and likewise hand them off to your partner to carry or even independently sell for you. You can also store them in your car's trunk, where they're slightly safer, but also then take slightly longer to access if, say, you're switching vehicles mid four-star cop chase along the freeway.

Sources indicate that and cars and weapons also follow a similar system in turn: stolen cars are now only temporarily yours; safe when stored in a parking spot but at risk when out in the world, until you pay to register them with a fence (or, later in the game, at Pay 'n' Sprays). But owned cars are yours forever, even when destroyed, as long as you have enough garage space to store them - garage space that, you realise, costs more and more money to procure. The same goes for weapons: found weapons are essentially borrowed, and lost when you're killed or arrested. But owned weapons - ones you buy, or unique, custom ones you discover - are yours forever, recoverable even if lost or left behind.

This then, in turn, ties into the upcoming police and 'wanted' system. Now it's much more realistic: police can spot or receive reports of you and take note of several factors, from facial appearance to clothing, whether you're with your partner, what weapon you have on you and what vehicle you're driving. And when it comes to things like robbing stores and banks, there's a system for whether you're spotted on locally stored CCTV, which can be destroyed, or fancier cloud-based footage which can't.

In a recent development, all kinds of things then play into this, from whether you walk into a place with a "longarm" gun - automatically putting guards on high alert - or a concealed pistol, to whether you're committing a crime somewhere fancy or rough. I got a strong sense that my crimes were being far less attentively dealt with in Vice City's poorer neighbourhoods. There are also two rings of attention drawn on the map when you're wanted, dictating how intensely a police search for you is concentrated, and different kinds of star ratings too, via a system called heat. These indicate whether police can see you, have a description of you, or are simply looking for a criminal for the crime you performed in that area. Even after you successfully escape, heat - dictated by whatever police might know - remains over the entire region of your crime, the size of that area and rate of its deterioration depending on just what exactly that crime was.

It has been revealed that finally, the criminal profile system is another tangent on its own, but once again it all folds together. It's a tiered honour system ranking you from "Professional" at one end to "Irredeemable" at the other, that last one the only point from which your reputation can never be recovered. Incapacitations instead of kills - which crucially are satisfying and easy to achieve with a bit of concentration - as well as completing objectives more subtly or achieving cleaner getaways from crimes, will tilt you towards Pro status. Driving that tank over those civilians or, heaven forbid, kicking a dog takes you the other way. If this sounds burdensome, again I'd say you really shouldn't worry: I naturally found myself with both Jason and Lucia as Professionals at the end, mostly thanks to shooting lots of cops in the groin. Your necessary actions during missions or when under attack don't impact it in the same way, I gather. It feels closer to a case of illustrating the role play on offer here, and ultimately committing to the consequences of that, than it does any kind of struggle to manage.

Sources indicate that all in all, the effect with the overall game is similar: less that GTA 6 becomes hard work - as I'd feared myself, and as Rockstar intentionally made Red Dead Redemption 2, to its thematic benefit in many ways - and more that, now, a greater amount of what you're doing is gamified. A robbery is in itself a game: whether you go in loud or quiet, together or separate, or focus on cracking the safe or looting the registers. As is how you divide up the bags between you, or whether your getaway is done together or separately to split cops' attention; whether you use your own car or a stolen vehicle, and if you're smart enough to park another one somewhere out of sight nearby for a sneaky changeover. You can also pack changes of clothes in your car to help disguise your identity.

Sources indicate that and all that's introduced, ingeniously, via the main missions of Jason and Lucia's story. If you were ever in doubt that GTA might have lost its edge, amongst all these soft and cuddly themes and grand ideas - that it might be sacrificed at the altar of realism and narrative heft - you can put that worry firmly aside. The low-brow humour, parody, larger-than-life characters, out of body experiences, 90s film references or cops-n-robbers bombast are all here, and all about as good as they've ever been.

In fact, really, in a lot of cases they're quite a bit better. The highlights are hard to pick out without spoiling again - many of the best arise from moments where you wonder if the game will go there, before it inevitably does. Others involve movie references that feel more overt than ever - Lucia openly quotes John McClane at one point, lighter in hand - but while some of this can feel a tad predictable, the sheer spectacle is often spellbinding.

It has been revealed that the best moments, aptly, come in car chases, where tyres are eviscerated by gunfire and speeding 4x4s suddenly dip, flip, and crash into one another with a sensational boom. Clearly some magic has been worked under the hood here to ensure that when they crash out, they do so with a kind of cinematic, organic-looking stuntman style, swerving into other vehicles in the chasing pack, across lanes into trucks and lorries, over highway partitions, wrapping around trees or catapulting off bridges. The new focus system - bullet time, on a specific, buffable meter - highlights weak spots such as engines and tyres for you to aim at for generally non-lethal take-outs, helping you with yet another system I'll get to in a moment. But really that system is kind of secondary here: I started shooting at these spots because, more often than not, it rewarded me with something awesome.

It has been revealed that main missions and the bigger character-based, optional side missions work similarly to how they've done before in GTA games. A location is marked on a map and you head there, or call someone, or wait for a call, and once you arrive things kick off, elements of the open world closing somewhat as self-contained scenarios within the sandbox open up. There are few low points, as the first act glides through a wistfully carefree, low-key criminal life before the game shifts to the snowballing momentum of its crooks-on-the-run melodrama. There are multiple heists, which are naturally high watermarks - massive moments of catharsis and chaos that propel the couple forward across some newly introduced Rubicon after hours and hours of sub-mission preparations. There are episodes with every vehicle, every ludicrous modern American scenario, every body part you could imagine. You'll be dragged through all kinds of Floridian subcultures, naturally, from sleepy key life and everglades hicks to rusted-over rural towns, biker gangs, strip clubs, record labels, towerblock drug kingpins and, erm, bodybuilders. And then plenty beyond that.

Rockstar is as ever ruthless with the skewer. The targets remain broad, from Miami's upcoming wave of non-indigenous crypto bros to wellness Bali girlies aiming to be their very own #SheEO. But there's also a maturity here, believe it or not, even if it's slightly tucked away between the dangling wangs and murderous– actually I won't spoil that one. I've found no cases of Rockstar punching down - although rest assured no progressive, gentrifying hipster goes unscathed - and there is a subtle, but absolutely present awareness of the world in which Rockstar is now operating. In one moment the concept of using dirt on a senator is discussed, at which point Jason wisely remarks that dirt must be pretty spectacular, given what they've already gotten away with these days.

The changes here are small, ultimately, and while there's a whole essay of its own to be written about the concept of parody, my sense is Rockstar has played this just right. GTA 6 has essentially taken the 'mirror' approach, in simply concentrating the extremes of the current world - so often deemed impervious to satire - by putting them all together in a single place, then reflecting them back at the world they came from. Florida is often described as a kind of heightened America - America Plus, the country's Ultimate Edition - and Leonida is just a heightened Florida. With an awful lot of very silly puns.

Away from the main missions and primary sidequests, Rockstar's made another seemingly subtle, but kind of revolutionary tweak. Aside from more static activities - the races, sports, pastimes, and the rest - the other source of missions in GTA 6 is what the game calls emergent events. These are entirely missable - though I think they re-present themselves eventually - and occur essentially as overheard goings-on just out of shot. They could be anything from one-off opportunities or minor punchlines to entire quest chains and conspiracies.

According to recent reports, for instance: driving around Vice City you might find a guy doing his best Florida Man impression by livestreaming himself to his Snapmatic following while standing on the highway overpass wall above a high drop. Then, inevitably, he slips and you might be able to pull him up or might - as I may or may not have done - fumble the controls and have him plummet to his death. You might watch a bunch of amateurs rob a payday loans store and get blasted by the marked bills' exploding dye. Or a group of masked, heavily-armed professionals rob a cash truck or minor bank. A weirdo might flag you down and trigger a whole load of nonsense happening next, or the cops might be arresting someone and leave a supercar and bag of coke happily unattended while they try to run off. Even beyond that, there's also just weird stuff lying around, without anything specific tied to it. I once spent a worrying amount of time in conversation with a pioneering member of the Hollow Earth Society. Then got a good laugh when I next paid him a visit.

It's a cracking system, in part because it reinforces a sense of continuous, organic weirdness around every corner, and in part because each of these feels like a kind of invitation. Once you do a couple and find yourself blackmailing a guy who in turn blackmailed GTA's in-game Amazon equivalent for a cut of his lawsuit winnings, or spraying manure on a spurned farmer's ex-lover's house, or running over some numpty protesters trying to set an actual bear loose on the freeway, it's hard not to stop at every distant argument or out-of-pocket comment that crosses your airwaves. Rest assured, if you think I've spoiled anything here: there are scores of these events, many of which I've yet to encounter or investigate, and many of which are far weirder and more curious than these.

According to recent reports, all this feeds back into a sense of choice, which is a challenge to accurately describe, thanks to both how difficult it is to figure out when and how one might have mattered, and when a moment of the story might have diverged. But choices, combined with the strength of your relationship and your criminal profile, and other factors I'll intentionally decline to mention here, all have an impact. One particularly great achievement of Rockstar's, in fact, is in making you wrestle with those choices, within missions and without, in this state of blindness to their outcomes. Even whether they're significant at all is often unknown - in many cases the variables, permutations and forks are still unknown to me now, after all this time - and yet also, once again without spoiling any moment at any point, the studio has still made whatever outcomes you might encounter feel as resonant as any I've experienced. Forgive me for dodging any examples and insisting you take my word for it.

In a recent development, away from missions themselves, of which there are of course many, and there are so many more things to do beyond them. You can dive for treasure across dozens of underwater sites. You can bird watch, animal watch, fish, and hunt for game. You can customise guns and cars to extreme ends - please do the street racing side missions for a, ahem, lovely example of custom wrapping - and customise your characters just as much. The fitness system is great, with a surprising number of superbly animated gym and bodyweight exercises and, naturally, walking BBLs who hit on Jason as he demonstrates perfect form.

Recent findings suggest that it's also uninvasive, I found, thanks to clearly marked, and relatively long, windows around maintaining your current status, but there's still a level of detail here. Your body composition is dictated by both cardio and strength training, but also what you eat and how often. You can ignore it and just look like an average person, or pay attention for meaningful buffs to health, focus, stamina, and appearance - and naturally the world around you reacts to that in comments from passers-by and, I suspect, small details of certain missions changing too.

Industry observers note that there's more! There's racing - at racetracks and mud tracks; in street races and off road courses; with bikes, cars, drones, and the rest. There are stunt jumps, naturally, and basejumps too. There are places to meditate. There's a system around not just fishing but using the right bait, multiple series of collectible trading cards to hoard or sell, various collectible books and magazines, meteorites, golden doubloons, and 'key valuables' found at gang hideouts including one-off guns, cars, and jewellery like fancy watches. There are clubs, bars, strippers, love hotels, diners, coffee houses, stores of clothing and shoes, hairdressers, and beyond. You can play an alarmingly realistic version of pool. Or listen to the radio of course - there are roughly double the stations you've seen revealed so far - or numerous talk demonstrates and podcasts, including entire true crime dramas and series. You can ride jetskis, pose in rented supercars, order cocktails at swanky pools and go on dates to rooftop restaurants or crusty marina dive bars. There are DJs and live performances, including a cover band with the most accurately depicted, finger-specific fretting of a guitar solo I've ever seen in a game.

The overall effect - yet another overall effect! I'm aware I keep doing this but I just have simply no other way of summarising it all - is of a genuine open-world playground, but crucially rather than a somewhat directionless soup of content, there is thematic sense to all of it. One of GTA 6's many messages, as foreshadowed on one of its most potent trailers, is a sense of embracing the moment while it lasts - of presentness and gratitude for things that might be accessible even without the substantial financial grind. And, surely, of what a joy it is to experience them with someone else.

According to recent reports, what you realise is you're pairing all this stuff to do - ultimately, variations on simply hanging out - with the fact that so much of Jason and Lucia's relationship is delivered in quiet, hang-out moments. And as so many of their other relationships - with parents, adopted parents, friends - come in the same way, this picture starts to form. From an apartment sofa to the Vice Beach waves, GTA 6 is ultimately just a place to be.

According to recent reports, in fact, in many ways it's a kind of evolution of the hangout game itself. The gentle, wistful, nostalgic guitar strums from Justice's background score as you idle on the map or menu. The dedication, through all those years of what I imagine to be Rockstar's incessant tinkering with sounds and performances and tiny visual touches, to an authentic sense of place. I could melt into this world. I think about the amount of people about to play this game, and the way it invites you to submerge yourself in it like a hot bath, and wonder if the axis of the entire hangout genre - maybe the biggest paradigm shift in video games of the last two decades - might have suddenly been shifted again. The comfort of continuously mic'd up pal chatter replaced here with a kind of sublime isolation.

It has been revealed that there are, as I mentioned, a few very little flaws I could pick at. Some of the missions for Dre-Quan, a record label-owning friend of Jason involving a newly invented rap group for the game, were fun in their own right, extraordinarily well produced and an essential part of the whole, but also just a little throwaway in a sense. There seemed to be little tie-in from those to the progress of the actual story, leaving them feeling a little more like lavish side missions than a part of the main event, contributing to a little mid-game narrative sag. The controls, while a marked improvement from Red Dead Redemption 2 - I fear I'll never make it to heaven after the amount of times I accidentally punched that horse - could still be tighter. Shooting is less wafty than it has been for some time, forgoing auto-aim for aim-assist (though settings can be heavily tinkered or restored to those of GTA 5), and GTA is now a proper third-person cover shooter in its action moments, with better snapping to cover and dashing between it, which suits it perfectly. But there were still moments where the controls wobbled. Walking three steps along a narrow beam to open a small container without falling off felt like the hardest thing the game asked me to do in its entire runtime.

What else? Not much, frankly. On the technical side, I had one hard crash in my entire time with the game, which did cost me about 25 minutes of a mission, and one moment where an NPC got stuck trying to enter my car and I had to reload to a checkpoint made seconds earlier.

I also wish there were more save slots - GTA 6 does away with mission replayability, which might prove controversial. As you play it you'll realise why that makes sense, but I also longed for more room than the 15 given to load back in at various moments and replay something specific - often for no other reason than that moment being an utter banger. Performance-wise, yes it plays at 30fps, even on a PS5 Pro, but Rockstar's frame pacing - I have to assume it's this; I'm no tech expert here - is so good that it feels resoundingly smoother than a typical game that runs at the same rate. Put aside the arbitrary number and ask me purely how it feels, and I'd tell you it feels smooth. How that fares on other consoles, particularly the Xbox Series S, will be worth considering.

A little more philosophically, it's also not a perfect narrative, arguably because it never really could be. The middle of the game is phenomenal in its mission variety and excitement, though perhaps where Jason and Lucia's characters are pushed slightly to the background, when I wish their relationship - or lack of it - had even more time in the narrative spotlight. For all its dramatic heft, GTA 6 also can't purely be a drama, and so there is inevitably some tonal whiplash between an intimate love scene, say, and a quest involving chasing a man with a fake English accent wearing nothing but a comedy man thong around the poshest part of town. The point, instead, comes back to how all those strange and implausible bedfellows combine.

And this is the magic. Every modern Grand Theft Auto is considered now to be a kind of product of its time. Nico Bellic's story is labelled a tale of the immigrant experience of the American Dream, amongst the post-9/11 world of Fresh York and the war on terror. I always thought of GTA 5 as something prodding at a crisis of masculinity, after the financial crisis, and a kind of early 2010s complacency and drift. These aren't the only things they're about, obviously. GTA 5 is also The Sopranos and an ode to LA and the split of the id, ego, and superego, and of course a broad, hours-long, occasionally mis-targeted piss-take. But by virtue of being games depicting the world as it was in some way, they also become a reflection of it.

It has been revealed that what is Grand Theft Auto 6, then? I know I said it's irreducible, but I can't help it. For now, after the car, I'm coming back to money. How Jason and Lucia keep attempting the famous bootstrapping of American meritocracy, keep picking themselves back up from zero, keep scrabbling and clawing their way out of the vortex, and how the so-called land of opportunity keeps telling them it's possible to climb up and out the top of it, away from worry and pain, up to the balcony and the penthouse and the helipad on the roof, all the while with its other hand constantly pushing them back down. At every tier of life savings, after every major score and narrow escape, the goal posts move back, and the enemy reorganises itself again. It might be trite, but it feels essential to point out nonetheless, that GTA 6 is a product of capitalism at its most extreme: the most extraordinary amount of wealth ever directed at an entertainment product and, surely, the one to achieve the most extraordinary number of sales. It is about the most capitalistic place on earth, and the place within it that features perhaps the most extreme disparity of wealth, as its hypercars scream past the homeless.

Sources indicate that GTA 6 is a reflection of the outer world and a part of it. And at its heart, its fragile and desperate humans play a rigged game, while attempting to walk the narrow line between exhausted desperation and the empowering wish-fulfilment of crime. You might wonder, as Jason and Lucia often do, whether they're always going to be doomed. And then later, whether that matters, when the beauty of it all is in the struggle.

A copy of Grand Theft Auto 6 was provided for this review by Rockstar.

Tiny Agents in Python: a MCP-powered agent in ~70 lines of code

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Inspired by Tiny Agents in JS, we ported the idea to Python 🐍 and extended the huggingface_hub client SDK to act as a MCP Client so it can pull tools from MCP servers and pass them to the LLM during inference.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that FRESH: tiny-agents now supports AGENTS.md standard. 🥳.

Inspired by Tiny Agents in JS, we ported the idea to Python 🐍 and extended the huggingface_hub client SDK to act as a MCP Client so it can pull tools from MCP servers and pass them to the LLM during inference.

MCP (Model Context Protocol) is an open protocol that standardizes how Large Language Models (LLMs) interact with external tools and APIs. Essentially, it removed the need to write custom integrations for each tool, making it simpler to plug new capabilities into your LLMs.

In this blog post, we'll show you how to get started with a tiny Agent in Python connected to MCP servers to unlock powerful tool capabilities. You'll see just how easy it is to spin up your own Agent and start building!

Spoiler : An Agent is essentially a while loop built right on top of an MCP Client!

This section walks you through how to use existing Tiny Agents. We'll cover the setup and the commands to get an agent running.

First, you need to install the latest version of huggingface_hub with the mcp extra to get all the necessary components.

Now, let's run an agent using the CLI!

The coolest part is that you can load agents directly from the Hugging Face Hub tiny-agents Dataset, or specify a path to your own local agent configuration!

If you don't provide a path to a specific agent configuration, our Tiny Agent will connect by default to the following two MCP servers:.

It has been revealed that the following example indicates a web-browsing agent configured to use the Qwen/Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct model via Nebius inference provider, and it comes equipped with a playwright MCP server, which lets it use a web browser! The agent config is loaded specifying its path in the tiny-agents/tiny-agents Hugging Face dataset.

According to recent reports, when you run the agent, you'll see it load, listing the tools it has discovered from its connected MCP servers. Then, it's ready for your prompts!

do a Web Search for HF inference providers on Brave Search and open the first result and then give me the list of the inference providers supported on Hugging Face.

You can also use Gradio Spaces as MCP servers! The following example uses Qwen/Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct model via Nebius inference provider, and connects to a FLUX.1 [schnell] image generation HF Space as an MCP server. The agent is loaded from its configuration in the tiny-agents/tiny-agents dataset on the Hugging Face Hub.

Generate a 1024x1024 image of a tiny astronaut hatching from an egg on the surface of the moon.

Now that you've seen how to run existing Tiny Agents, the following sections will dive deeper into how they work and how to build your own.

Each agent's behavior (its default model, inference provider, which MCP servers to connect to, and its initial system prompt) is defined by an agent.json file. You can also provide a custom PROMPT.md in the same directory for a more detailed system prompt. Here is an example:.

According to recent reports, agent.json The model and provider fields specify the LLM and inference provider used by the agent. The servers array defines the MCP servers the agent will connect to. In this example, a "stdio" MCP server is configured. This type of server runs as a local process. The Agent starts it using the specified command and args, and then communicates with it via stdin/stdout to discover and execute available tools.

You can find more details about Hugging Face Inference Providers here.

Modern LLMs are built for function calling (or tool use), which enables people to easily build applications tailored to specific use cases and real-world tasks.

In a recent development, A function is defined by its schema, which informs the LLM what it does and what input arguments it expects. The LLM decides when to use a tool, the Agent then orchestrates running the tool and feeding the result back.

InferenceClient implements the same tool calling interface as the OpenAI Chat Completions API, which is the established standard for inference providers and the community.

Recent findings suggest that the MCPClient is the heart of our tool-use functionality. It's now part of huggingface_hub and uses the AsyncInferenceClient to communicate with LLMs.

The full MCPClient code is in here if you want to follow along using the actual code 🤓.

Key responsibilities of the MCPClient:.

​​Here’s a glimpse of how it connects to an MCP server (the add_mcp_server method):.

Sources indicate that it supports stdio servers for local tools (like accessing your file system), and http servers for remote tools! It's also compatible with sse, which is the previous standard for remote tools.

The MCPClient's process_single_turn_with_tools method is where the LLM interaction happens. It sends the conversation history and available tools to the LLM via AsyncInferenceClient.chat.completions.create(..., stream=True).

First, the method determines all tools the LLM should be aware of for the current turn – this includes tools from MCP servers and any special "exit loop" tools for agent control; then, it makes a streaming call to the LLM:.

It has been revealed that as chunks arrive from the LLM, the method iterates through them. Each chunk is immediately yielded, then we reconstruct the complete text response and any tool calls.

Once the stream is complete, if the LLM requested any tool calls (now fully reconstructed in final_tool_calls), the method processes each one:.

It first checks if the tool called exits the loop (exit_loop_tool). If not, it finds the correct MCP session responsible for that tool and calls session.call_tool(). The result (or error response) is then formatted, added to the conversation history, and yielded so the Agent is aware of the tool's output.

With the MCPClient doing all the job for tool interactions, our Agent class becomes wonderfully simple. It inherits from MCPClient and adds the conversation management logic.

The Agent class is tiny and focuses on the conversational loop, the code can be found here.

Industry observers note that when an Agent is created, it takes an agent config (model, provider, which MCP servers to use, system prompt) and initializes the conversation history with the system prompt. The load_tools() method then iterates through the server configurations (defined in agent.json) and calls add_mcp_server (from the parent MCPClient) for each one, populating the agent's toolbox.

The Agent.run() method is an asynchronous generator that processes a single user input. It manages the conversation turns, deciding when the agent's current task is complete.

Quantum computing’s “dark horse” just proved it can go universal

📅 25 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1180 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A practical quantum computer must eventually be able to handle any type of quantum algorithm, much like a conventional laptop can run many different kinds of software.
  • Scientists from the University of Chicago Pritzker School of Molecular Engineering (UChicago PME), Harvard, Stony Brook University, and Quantinuum created and tested a full set of operations based on non-Abelian anyons.
  • "We demonstrated a so-called universal gate set -- meaning that if you store information in these emergent versions of quarks, and you move them around, you can do any quantum computation you might want to do," remarked Ruben Verresen, assistant professor of molecular engineering at UChicago PME and a co-author of the new study published in Nature.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A practical quantum computer must eventually be able to handle any type of quantum algorithm, much like a conventional laptop can run many different kinds of software. Researchers have now demonstrated a latest way to reach that level of flexibility using unusual quantum objects known as non-Abelian anyons.

Scientists from the University of Chicago Pritzker School of Molecular Engineering (UChicago PME), Harvard, Stony Brook University, and Quantinuum created and tested a full set of operations based on non-Abelian anyons. Their results provide the first experimental demonstration that this approach can support the broad range of operations required for universal quantum computing.

"We demonstrated a so-called universal gate set -- meaning that if you store information in these emergent versions of quarks, and you move them around, you can do any quantum computation you might want to do," remarked Ruben Verresen, assistant professor of molecular engineering at UChicago PME and a co-author of the new study published in Nature.

A Possible Shortcut Around Costly Quantum Error Correction.

The strategy could do more than help create a general-purpose quantum computer. It may also offer a more efficient route toward reliable quantum machines.

Sources indicate that quantum computers are extremely vulnerable to errors, so researchers typically protect information by distributing it across many physical qubits. These error correction methods can preserve data, but they usually do not provide every operation needed to perform universal quantum computation on that protected information.

Sources indicate that to fill the gap, engineers often rely on specially prepared resources called "magic states." Producing them usually requires an intensive purification process known as distillation, which can consume a large fraction of a quantum computer's available qubits. The new results suggest that non-Abelian anyons may offer a way around that expensive step.

Industry observers note that "Non-Abelian codes are a dark horse in the race to quantum error correction," mentioned Henrik Dreyer, managing director and scientific lead at Quantinuum's Munich office and a co-author of the study. "In this work we show the first universal gate set in a non-Abelian code, which demonstrates that fault-tolerant computations can in principle be done without resorting to magic state distillation or cultivation, which are the most expensive operations in standard quantum error correction codes.".

Why Non-Abelian Anyons Are Different.

In a recent development, ordinary qubits encode information using two basic states, along with quantum combinations of those states. Non-Abelian anyons work in a fundamentally different way.

These anyons do not appear as ordinary standalone particles in nature. Instead, scientists create them inside quantum circuits by entangling many conventional qubits into a collective state that behaves as though it were a new type of particle with its own unusual rules.

"The way I think about these codes is they're creating little universes -- alternative universes, but ones that reflect some of the properties of our own," Verresen said.

Sources indicate that each non-Abelian anyon carries an internal state that changes when one anyon is moved around another in a process known as braiding. The sequence of those braiding operations matters (that's what non-Abelian means), allowing information to be encoded and manipulated in ways that are unavailable to ordinary particles.

Because the information is spread across many entangled qubits rather than stored in a single location, it can also be naturally protected from some of the small disturbances that frequently disrupt conventional qubits. Braiding the anyons can also perform computational operations.

Why Braiding Alone Was Not Enough.

In 2024, a research team that included Verresen used a Quantinuum trapped-ion computer to create anyons associated with a symmetry group called D4 -- the rotations and reflections that leave a square unchanged -- demonstrating this form of non-Abelian order on quantum hardware for the first time.

That experiment demonstrated that the unusual particles could be created and manipulated, but braiding them alone was not sufficient to carry out every operation required for universal quantum computing.

In a recent development, "In that work, we didn't demonstrate that those emergent forces were enough to do quantum computation," remarked Verresen. "That particular universe we created was not powerful enough.".

Fusion Unlocks Universal Quantum Operations.

For the newly introduced study, the researchers switched to another symmetry known as S3 -- the rotations and mirror-image flips that leave an equilateral triangle unchanged -- and created the corresponding anyons on Quantinuum's H2 trapped-ion processor using 54 entangled qubits.

In a recent development, the S3 system had the properties needed for universal quantum computation, but only when braiding was combined with another operation called fusion. During fusion, two anyons are brought together and the resulting state is measured.

The underlying concept was proposed theoretically in 2003 by Carlos Mochon, then a student of John Preskill at Caltech. Turning that theoretical idea into an experiment that could actually run on quantum hardware, however, required extensive additional theoretical and experimental work.

The researchers used pairs of anyons to encode "topological qutrits" which store three possible levels of quantum information instead of the two levels used by ordinary qubits.

Recent findings suggest that by combining different braiding and fusion operations, the team demonstrated three key tools: one entangling gate produced through braiding and two different measurements created through fusion. Together, those operations can in principle produce any quantum operation, including operations that braiding alone could not achieve.

Beyond their possible computing applications, these unusual quantum states could also help researchers investigate fundamental aspects of physics.

"It is gratifying to see ideas we have spent our PhD work thinking about realized in the lab, and it has been made possible by remarkable advances in quantum hardware over the past few years," remarked Anasuya Lyons and Chiu Fan Bowen Lo, graduate students at Harvard University in the group of Ashvin Vishwanath who helped lead the work.

Toward Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computers.

The researchers also demonstrated that non-Abelian anyons could directly produce a magic state using topological operations -- sidestepping the costly distillation process used in most quantum systems.

The experiment did not yet include active error correction. Instead, the researchers focused on testing the individual building blocks of the method and confirming that they could create a magic state consistent with theoretical expectations.

Recent findings suggest that "So far, we've ignored the question of error correction. Here, it's more like a proof of principle," Verresen noted.

It has been revealed that the next major step will be combining these operations with active error correction. If that can be achieved, non-Abelian anyons could eventually become a practical basis for large-scale, fault-tolerant quantum computers. Verresen is already working with other PME researchers on latest techniques for stabilizing non-Abelian quantum memories.

Materials provided by University of Chicago. Original written by Sarah C.P. Williams. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Rockstar Games has partnered with Panini to release real-life GTA 6 trading cards based on the collectibles players can find scattered throughout Leonida.

There’s no shortage of things to collect in Grand Theft Auto 6, with Rockstar taking a page out of Red Dead Redemption 2’s book by including hundreds of trading cards for players to hunt down.

There are 480 cards across 18 different sets, ranging from fictional sports stars to comic book characters and nightclub dancers, with players able to sell their rare finds at pawn shops for some extra cash.

Now, just days after GTA 6’s record-breaking launch, Rockstar is giving collectors a chance to rip open packs in real life.

Grand Theft Auto VI official trading cards, coming soon from @PaniniAmerica and @RockstarGames. pic.twitter.com/H1VrYVXTm5.

On November 24, Panini unveiled its partnership with Rockstar Games to produce the first officially licensed Grand Theft Auto trading card collection, set to launch in December 2026.

Dubbed the GTA VI: Sports Trading Card Collection, the set will recreate cards featuring fictional athletes and teams from Rockstar’s universe.

According to Panini’s product listing, each hobby box will contain four packs of four cards, with collectors pulling an average of two Rookies, one Retro, one Illustrated, and four Special Silvers per box.

Much like real-world sports cards, there will also be rare color variants and numbered parallels, including Bronze Legend cards limited to 49 copies, Silver Legends limited to 25, and coveted one-of-one Gold cards.

Industry observers note that you just know all the down bad GTA 6 players who have fallen head over heels for goth stripper Vicki, will be clamoring for her card. However, the collection may be limited to sports cards for now.

The collaboration is the latest example of Rockstar bringing its fictional world to life, having already created a real-life Grotti Cheetah worth £1 million and teamed up with the Miami Heat for Vice City merchandise.

Panini has yet to announce pricing, an exact release date, or international availability, but considering how much money GTA 6 merchandise has already fetched on the resale market, those one-of-one cards could end up being worth a pretty penny.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, the day is finally here: Grand Theft Auto 6 is available to play worldwide. It's destined to become the largest video game release of all time, and probably one of the biggest entertainment releases of all time. So we're doing a launch day live blog to chart its arrival in the world.

Have you played it yet? I'm curious how many people stayed up until midnight in their region to give the game a go. I couldn't manage it but my college-age son was contemplating it. And if you have played it, what do you think - what are your early impressions? Is this what you were waiting for?

More broadly, I wonder about the impact GTA 6 will have on the wider world. I've already seen nearly all mainstream news and media outlets attempt to cover the game - and many other kinds of businesses - so will GTA 6 make people reappraise video games?

Sources indicate that moreover, exactly how big will the launch be? The record books are ready to be written in, but what exactly will be written? And how will other games fare in GTA's wake - better, or worse? There's lots to consider as the ripples spread around the world.

We'll pull-in stories and developments, and your comments, as we chart the arrival of Rockstar's game around the world. Let's get to it.

Our live coverage of this event has finished.

Industry observers note that an historic day in gaming and there's loads to unpack. But to begin with, this: did you take a day off to play GTA 6, and have you played it yet?

Rockstar's marketing department has gone all out.

Recent findings suggest that the marketing push by Rockstar to have GTA 6 imprint on real-world cities has been impressive to see. There have been festivals in Miami, Selfridges dedicated a portion of its department store to selling GTA merch, but there's more than this besides. The London Standard summarised much of the activity in London in a video on Instagram.

A post shared by The Standard (@thelondonstandard).

Rockstar employment tribunal verdict could take weeks.

The din of release is in danger of drowning out the Rockstar employment tribunal that came to a close this week in Scotland. Former Eurogamer video producer Chris Bratt - now co-owner of People Make Games - has been following the case closely, and reported yesterday that a verdict in the case could take "weeks".

It has been revealed that he quotes Judge Lucy Wiseman as saying: "I cannot give a time frame for producing the judgement in this case. What I will say is that I will use my best endeavors to get that judgement out as rapidly as I possibly can.".

And that's it for the Rockstar tribunal! We await the judge's decision, but how long will it take? Judge Lucy Wiseman: "I cannot give a time frame for producing the judgement in this case. What I will say is that I will use my best endeavors to get that judgement out as rapidly as I possibly can.".

Yesterday, we independently confirmed that most, if not all, of the fired Rockstar employees are credited in the GTA 6 credits - which are, according to Chris Tapsell, our reviewer, an enormous thing in their own right.

Here’s how significant it is, news-wise:.

Yesterday, my mother _(whose single dabble in gaming over the years can be described as,“working out the way to bypass the Brontosaurus Guarding Causeway in the text adventure Time Machine, is to GIVE it the Ship’s Biscuit found aboard the Marie Celeste”)_ texted me to ask if I was “ready for tomorrow?”.

I instantly assumed I’d made or hinted at some strategy to do something with her and subsequently forgotten.

BUT, NO. She was asking if I was ready for GTA. A product I have never mentioned in her presence in all my many years.

So if you’ve got the over-seventies non-gamers talking… I’d say you’ve cracked it.

Goodness! And will your mother also be playing it?

My inbox is flooded with all kinds of brands trying to get in on the GTA 6 hype.

The most recent one? Petrol prices. "Having to refuel your car in GTA 6 adds another layer of realism to the game, but it's something real-life drivers have to think about every time they get behind the wheel," noted Beth Fountain, fuel expert at somewhere called Interfuels.

"With petrol and diesel prices remaining high, filling up can take a significant chunk out of someone's monthly budget, particularly for those who rely on their vehicles for work or regular travel.

"While players might find the latest mechanic frustrating, it's a reminder of how much we depend on fuel in everyday life and how promptly those costs can add up.".

There's another one from Just Eat, the food delivery manufacturer, which has apparently made a real controller with Just Eat order button on it for you to order food while gaming. It's not specifically GTA 6-linked but it's jumping on that bandwagon. The controller is apparently synced to your Just Eat account. Imagine mashing that by accident and having an accidental feast turn up.

"When you're deep into a high-stakes gaming session nothing kills the moment faster than having to pause the action just to sort out food. With the Just ChEAT Button, Just Eat has unlocked the ultimate hack to evade the kitchen, enabling gamers to stay just where they are and locked into play," noted Just East UK and Ireland marketing director Tina Koehler.

It's not clear where you can buy this controller or how much it costs. It's described as "limited edition". I wonder if that means only one has been made.

The goofy things people are already doing in GTA 6.

Many people are playing GTA 6 already of course and doing expectedly bizarre things in it. From lobbing hammers like Crocodile Dundee lobs cans of tinned food, to dropkicking people, to attempting to dive through a car window while oiled up and in one's pants - Connor has rounded up some of the goofiest clips around.

You are brilliant, Eurogamer readers!

I just want to resurface the winning entry to the GTA memories competition we ran at the tail-end of last week, because it's funny and uplifting, and I still smile about it.

My favourite GTA memory is introducing my nan to Vice City.

She'd never played a video game before, so I told her she could pretty much do whatever she wanted.

She spent the first 20 minutes driving around obeying traffic lights and apologising whenever she bumped into another car.

Then she accidentally punched someone.

I don't know what happened, but something just clicked.

Within half an hour she'd stolen a police car, run over several pedestrians and was shouting at the telly because the police wouldn’t leave her alone.

My grandad came in to see what all the noise was about.

Without even looking up she just remarked, "I'm wanted for murder, Barry. Put the kettle on.".

Genuinely one of the funniest afternoons of my childhood.

I'm on the management team for a charity and they've scheduled their AGM for tonight at 6pm. Of all the dates! I've had to weigh up not doing my duty for selfish video game reasons.

According to recent reports, I must be growing up because I've decided that going to the AGM is the right thing to do and that GTA 6 probably isn't that good, anyway. Right?

In a recent development, well! Allow the Eurogamer comments to decide. I think you should set GTA 6 up in another room in the building you're holding the AGM in, and find excuses during it to nip out and play. It'll be like a Mrs Doubtfire moment. Nothing can go wrong.

Recent findings suggest that another email from a shopping comparison site, Idealo, and this time about PS5 Pro demand, which has apparently leapt by 57 percent week on week because of GTA 6. This, by the way, is exactly what the industry was hoping would happen - that GTA 6 would reinvigorate console sales, which were slumping, not least because of their unprecedented rising prices. Apparently the price of PS5 consoles is rising in step with this demand.

"Grand Theft Auto debuts are major cultural moments, and GTA 6 is already having a noticeable impact on the wider gaming market, particularly when it comes to console demand," Katy Phillips from Idealo mentioned.

"We're seeing a significant increase in interest in the PS5 Pro, with demand jumping by 57 percent in the week leading up to launch. At the same time, the price of the console has climbed by more than £450 since the end of October.".

GTA 6 videos you might find helpful.
