Dynamic tone mapping for HDR10 content.

Matte anti-glare screen is very effective.

Industry observers note that why you can trust Tom's Hardware Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.

It has been revealed that if you’re shopping for one of the best OLED gaming monitors, the 240 Hz QHD category offers the most choices and the best bang for the buck. But 4K at 240 Hz is creeping downward in price and only represents a small upcharge. It also means that you can go to 32 inches and maintain good pixel density. If you have enough video card horsepower to push frame rates over 180fps, the quality is unmatched.

Samsung slides into the neither-expensive-nor-inexpensive position with its Odyssey G8 G80SH. This 32-inch Quantum Dot OLED runs 240 Hz at 4K resolution with Adaptive-Sync, HDR10, HDR10+, wide gamut color, factory calibration, and high brightness for HDR content. Let’s take a look.

Quantum Dot Organic Light Emitting Diode.

Max Resolution and Refresh Rate.

First, I want to clear up any potential confusion with another recently reviewed Samsung display, the G80HS. That is a 6K resolution dual-refresh mode model that presently costs around $1,600. The G80SH I’m covering here is a 4K screen with a single 240 Hz mode, and it’s currently selling for $900.

Recent findings suggest that the G80SH delivers the best of everything in the premium OLED category. It’s 4K with a Quantum Dot layer that delivers a measured 106% coverage of DCI-P3. That’s about average among the QD-OLEDs I’ve tested, which range from 104 to 108%. The visual difference there is extremely small, not enough to affect a purchase decision. The G80SH also offers excellent out-of-the-box accuracy courtesy of a factory calibration. Though my sample didn’t need any tweaking, it benefited from a few adjustments. And that capability extends to HDR content, where you have full control of color temp, brightness, and luminance tracking.

Speaking of HDR, you get the requisite HDR10 support that all monitors have, plus Samsung’s answer to Dolby Vision, HDR10+. This extension of HDR10 includes dynamic tone mapping where the content matches its luminance curve to whatever display it’s shown on. Since HDR is mastered to a specific peak luminance, usually 1,000 nits but sometimes as high as 10,000, it’s beneficial when the screen can adapt to the incoming metadata to accommodate a lower or higher limit. You’ll see the same fine detail and nuance that the content creator did.

Recent findings suggest that gaming benefits from the aforementioned 240 Hz refresh rate plus a flawless implementation of Adaptive-Sync. The G80SH works with equal precision on G-Sync and FreeSync platforms, as well as the VRR output from gaming consoles. To help with your aim, there are reticles available in different colors and shapes, with a dynamic mode that keeps them in contrast with the background.

Sources indicate that like every Samsung monitor I’ve experienced, the G80SH delivers high style and solid build quality. The main color is silver, which you can see everywhere except the front, keeping the screen and surrounding bezel all black. There’s a matte anti-glare coating too, effectively eliminating all ambient light reflections. If you have a sunny room, this monitor can handle it without a degradation in image quality. You also get the latest video interfaces, four in total, plus USB and a headphone jack. LED lighting is featured on the back and can be controlled from the OSD.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

So, just to recap before we jump into the tests, this is the Odyssey G8 G80SH, a 4K 240 Hz OLED that sells for $900. If you’re interested in learning more about the 6K model, my review from a few months ago is here.

In a recent development, samsung still uses crumbly foam to ship its monitors, and my G80SH sample arrived safe and sound. The base, upright, and stand assemble with a captive bolt and a snap-on to create a solid package. To keep the panel thin, the power supply is external. It’s quite large, so consider that when fitting it into your space. The accessory bundle includes right-angle power cables plus one each of DisplayPort, HDMI, and USB-C.

Sources indicate that the G80SH’s silver trim is visible from the front in the base and a thin border around the screen that wraps around from the back. The actual bezel is very narrow and flush, so you can’t see it when the power’s off. A small protrusion in the bottom center claims Samsung in tiny letters and houses an equally tiny power LED that can’t be seen from the front. Samsung is one of the few manufacturers to offer matte-screened OLEDs, and this implementation is excellent. Even a bright flashlight can’t throw a reflection onto the screen. Sunny office dwellers, this is your monitor.

In the back, it’s all silver all the time with a smooth finish and minimalist styling. There’s a thin ventilation grill on top, a small logo on one side, and hooray, inputs that face backward. You get two HDMI 2.1, a DisplayPort 2.1, USB-C with 98 watts, and two USB-A downstream ports. There are no internal speakers, but there is a 3.5mm headphone jack. On one side of the I/O panel is a joystick, the G80SH’s sole control key. Around the stand’s attachment point is an LED ring with colors and effects available in the OSD. If you remove the stand, a 100mm VESA mount is revealed should you prefer an aftermarket solution. Fasteners are not included.

Sources indicate that that large external power supply keeps the panel thin at just under two inches. The stand is solid and wobble-free and offers 2/25 degrees tilt, 30 degrees swivel, a 90-degree portrait mode and a 4.7-inch height range. Movements are firm and smooth, in keeping with the G80SH’s premium status.

The G80SH’s OSD keeps Samsung’s traditional gaming monitor styling with its control panel appearance. Up top are portholes that deliver information about game-related settings. No refresh rate info, though. It would be nice to have that.

In the Game menu, you get an Adaptive-Sync toggle, aiming points, a black equalizer to enhance shadow detail, and the LED lighting control. The reticles come in two shapes and three colors. Or you can use AI Mode, which changes the color to maintain contrast with the background. You can also position the aiming point somewhere other than the center of the screen. The lighting has multiple effects or can remain a single static color. One miss here is a frame counter. There’s no way to monitor the refresh rate.

According to recent reports, in the Picture menu are all the G80SH’s calibration controls. You get five color temps, all adjustable, and seven gamma presets. The Contrast Enhancer is a field dimming control. True variable brightness is only active in HDR mode. You can choose between static and active tone mapping for HDR, which is handy for HDR10 content because it helps bring out highlights without clipping fine shadow detail.

Industry observers note that you won’t find an sRGB mode among the color space choices, but if you pick Auto, the G80SH will render sRGB for SDR content. This is an approach that I like, and almost no other manufacturers do it that way. If you’d rather see the full gamut for all content, just leave it on Native. Peak Brightness does just what it says for HDR content; it raises the peak output. In my HDR tests, I saw 530 nits from a 25% window pattern.

Remaining menu items include port version control, an off timer, DSC toggle, and USB-C control. You also get two panel care options: logo brightness (dimming, actually) and pixel refresh. You can pause the incoming video signal while this is running if you wish.

The G80SH includes a factory calibration with a report saved in the monitor’s firmware. I found visually perfect color and grayscale tracking, but gamma was a little light. Two clicks of the gamma slider made that much better. I noted that though the default picture mode is called Eco, it is just as bright as the other presets, so that you can use it for all content. In HDR mode, you get Display HDR, which has excellent tone mapping and color accuracy. Suppose you want sRGB; just set Color Space to Auto. Then the G80SH will automatically render sRGB for SDR and the full gamut for HDR, which covers 106% of DCI-P3. If you want full color for SDR, set it to Native. My recommended settings are below.

According to recent reports, the G80SH’s color quality and accuracy make it well suited for duty as a post-production monitor or perhaps an on-site display for location shoots. Only a slight gamma anomaly separates it from perfection. It nails grayscale and gamut tracking, which you can read about on pages four and five. And it’s bright enough for any indoor space. I noted that there was no variable brightness option for SDR, but you can turn on a dynamic contrast option, which equates to field dimming. In HDR mode, dimming occurs at the pixel level, and you can choose between Active and Static tone mapping. The former delivers more punch to HDR10 content.

I also noted the G80SH’s excellent color balance. SDR lets you choose between Native and Auto. Native shows the full gamut, which covers 106% of DCI-P3 and is very colorful. It will be the likely choice for most users. If you prefer sRGB for SDR, set the color space to Auto. Then, it will switch automatically. This is something very few monitors offer. I also noted that the HDR mode allows calibration of grayscale and gamma, another thing I rarely see.

According to recent reports, with the image dialed in, I turned to a few afternoons of gaming where the G80SH provided the addictive quality that all premium OLEDs have. It doesn’t have a frame counter, so I had to use FRAPS to monitor the refresh rate, which stayed around 200fps at the max detail settings in Doom Eternal. This was fast enough to provide blur-free motion and input lag low enough to keep up with my most frenetic movements. You’ll see on the next page that it offers response typical of other 4K 240 Hz OLEDs. That means you’ll be able to aim and shoot with speed and precision. I got extra credit in hoard mode for jump shots where I was able to land grenades on target while flying through the air. Turn and shoot became second nature as I mowed through my opponents.

Detail in close encounters made me stop and admire the picture more than a few times. Tiny highlights like sweat and other bodily fluids popped right out, making the characters look three-dimensional. Other textures like stone and metal looked better thanks to strong reflections. These highlights moved smoothly over objects like the player’s weapon, which further enhanced realism. The G80SH has some of the best-looking HDR I’ve seen of late.

It makes a great workday monitor too, with understated styling that stands out but doesn’t scream for attention. The LED lighting is just a ring in the back with smoothly playing effects or static colors available, or you can shut it off. The stand is rock solid with comfortable and usable ergonomics. The joystick navigates the OSD intuitively and efficiently. I really appreciated the rear-facing ports, which were easy to see and access. You get two USB-A downstream ports, which can accommodate peripherals once you make a connection to the USB-C input, which doubles as a charger with 98 watts of power. There are no internal speakers, but headphones plug into the 3.5mm jack.

Takeaway: If Samsung keeps the G80SH’s price below $1,000, it will sell a lot of them. It’s a super versatile display for any form of productivity or entertainment. It’s addictive for gaming, with smooth operation and quick response. The image looks stunning in every respect, whether moving or static. Color accuracy is good enough that calibration isn’t required. It has unique but understated styling and excellent ergonomics with a solid stand and rear-facing ports. Aside from a lack of internal speakers, there is nothing missing here.

#195342. Inside this quantum computer, memory vibrates like a guitar string

Inside this quantum computer, memory vibrates like a guitar string

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1147 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A quantum computer might seem to have little in common with a guitar, but researchers at ETH Zurich have found a surprising connection.
  • In a recent development, unlike the sounds produced by a musical instrument, these vibrations occur at frequencies far beyond human hearing.
  • By harnessing these vibrations, the researchers have created a way for quantum computers to process information efficiently while accessing a flexible working memory.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A quantum computer might seem to have little in common with a guitar, but researchers at ETH Zurich have found a surprising connection. Physicist Yiwen Chu and her team have developed a system that uses microscopic mechanical vibrations to store and manipulate quantum information, much like the vibrating strings of a guitar produce musical notes.

In a recent development, unlike the sounds produced by a musical instrument, these vibrations occur at frequencies far beyond human hearing. They take place within a tiny quantum chip, where they serve as a new form of computer memory.

By harnessing these vibrations, the researchers have created a way for quantum computers to process information efficiently while accessing a flexible working memory. "The interaction between the quantum processor and the quantum memory provides a crucial foundation with a view to establishing quantum computers as a powerful and reliable way to perform computations that are not feasible with conventional computers," notes Yiwen Chu.

Industry observers note that the breakthrough, described in the journal Science, introduces a different approach to quantum computer design. Instead of closely integrating information processing and storage, as many existing systems do, Chu's team has developed an architecture that gives these functions more distinct roles.

Quantum Memory Inspired by Conventional Computers.

The researchers drew inspiration from the basic design of everyday digital computers. In a conventional machine, the central processing unit (CPU) carries out calculations while information is held separately in working memory, commonly called random access memory (RAM). The arrangement of these components plays an key role in determining how efficiently a computer operates.

Recent findings suggest that chu's quantum system follows a similar principle. A superconducting qubit acts as the processing and control unit, performing a role comparable to that of the central processing unit (CPU). Meanwhile, a separate quantum memory temporarily holds the information needed during calculations, allowing the processor to retrieve and modify it as necessary.

The major difference lies in how that information is stored.

"In our quantum working memory, however, information is not stored electromagnetically -- as is usually the case today -- but rather in the form of mechanical vibrations," explains Chu.

In a recent development, quantum computers take advantage of unusual properties of quantum physics, including superposition, which allows quantum systems to exist in combinations of different states, and entanglement, which creates powerful connections between quantum states. These effects could eventually enable quantum machines to tackle certain extremely complicated calculations much faster than conventional computers, including some problems that are currently beyond their practical capabilities.

Why Vibrating Quantum Memory Could Be Better.

One of the greatest challenges in quantum computing is maintaining precise control over quantum information. The states used for calculations are delicate, and even small disturbances can cause information to be lost. To perform calculations reliably, the processor and memory must interact closely enough to transfer and manipulate quantum states with high precision.

In the new system, microscopic structures called mechanical resonators hold information in particular patterns of vibration. When the superconducting qubit needs that information, it accesses the stored vibrational state, performs the required operation, and returns the modified information to memory.

Many existing quantum computers instead use electromagnetic memory alongside superconducting qubits. Researchers understand these technologies well, and they can be combined to provide extremely accurate control over quantum states, including reading, changing, and manipulating stored information.

Sources indicate that however, electromagnetic memory systems have a significant disadvantage. They can occupy considerable space, making it difficult to expand experimental quantum devices into the larger, more capable computers that researchers and industries ultimately need.

It has been revealed that mechanical resonators offer several potential advantages. They are substantially smaller, allowing more compact designs. They can also support numerous different patterns of vibration, providing opportunities to store more information simultaneously than conventional electromagnetic memory.

Industry observers note that another key benefit is that mechanical vibrations can preserve quantum states for longer periods before the stored information begins to fade. Longer storage times could make it easier to carry out complicated calculations that require information to remain available throughout multiple processing steps.

New Quantum Computer Passes Major Tests.

The research published in Science provides the first experimental demonstration that mechanical resonators can work together with superconducting qubits to carry out quantum computations. The results establish that vibration-based memory is a feasible alternative to electromagnetic storage.

The achievement goes beyond simply storing information. Chu's team demonstrated that its architecture can handle both relatively straightforward calculations and more demanding quantum operations.

Recent findings suggest that to evaluate the system, the researchers tested two key computational techniques: the quantum Fourier transform and period finding. Both are fundamental tools in quantum computing and require a computer to coordinate multiple quantum states with considerable precision.

Recent findings suggest that "The Quantum Fourier Transform is a fundamental computational procedure required for many quantum algorithms. The period-finding algorithm we implemented served as a demonstration of how this procedure can be used," explains Igor Kladaric, doctoral student in Chu's team and co-author of the publication.

Sources indicate that successfully completing these tasks requires the system to store, control, and maintain coherent relationships among multiple quantum states at the same time. The experiments showed that the new architecture can meet these requirements, providing strong evidence that it can support genuine quantum computation rather than simply function as a memory device.

A Promising Step Toward Powerful Quantum Computers.

One of the most significant findings is that the upcoming system can, in principle, carry out all the fundamental operations needed for arbitrary quantum computations. This means the architecture has the essential capabilities required for a programmable, general-purpose quantum computer.

According to recent reports, however, demonstrating those capabilities in an experimental chip is only the beginning. The next major challenge is scaling the technology to larger systems with greater processing power while preserving the precision and reliability demonstrated in the laboratory.

It has been revealed that chu and her colleagues are continuing to investigate how their approach can be developed further. Its long-term success will depend on whether mechanical quantum memory can remain effective as more components and increasingly complex computations are added.

Industry observers note that practical quantum computers powerful enough for widespread scientific and industrial applications are still some distance away. Nevertheless, by showing that tiny mechanical vibrations can serve as compact, capable quantum memory, the ETH Zurich team has demonstrated a promising fresh route toward making those machines a reality.

#195341. Power BI MCP server: how to brief an AI agent to build accurate measures

📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 15m • 📚 Deep Dive (3067 w)
📖 Baca

Power BI MCP server: how to brief an AI agent to build accurate measures

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (3067 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sitepoint

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.
  • Industry observers note that 7 Day Free Trial.
  • In a recent development, power BI, Microsoft's reporting and dashboard tool, now lets an AI agent work on the data model behind a report.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Weekly. Free. One click to leave.

Industry observers note that 7 Day Free Trial. Cancel Anytime.

In a recent development, power BI, Microsoft's reporting and dashboard tool, now lets an AI agent work on the data model behind a report. If you ask one to add a year-on-year revenue measure (a measure is Power BI's name for a saved calculation) with Microsoft's MCP server connected, it can write the formula and save it to the model without you opening the formula bar. When we tried this on a sample model, an agent inspected the model, wrote the measure, tested it and saved it in under four minutes.

The agent did a careful job, but its formula didn't follow the same rules the finance team uses to count revenue. Nobody had told it what "revenue" meant in this business, so it had to decide for itself. We then gave another agent a short brief that set out finance's rules for what counts as revenue and which date to count it by. The agent wrote the formula from those rules, and the result matched finance's figure exactly. The two results show how much difference it makes in how you brief an AI agent to build accurate measures.

In a recent development, we wanted to find out what an agent can see in a Power BI model and how to brief it so the measure matches the business's own definitions, with the setup arranged so that every change can be checked. Developers will know the principle from agents that write SQL or API code, where the brief ends up doing the job of a specification.

Because MCP (Model Context Protocol) is an open standard, the same server can be used from different AI clients, GitHub Copilot in VS Code and Claude among them, although some clients need extra sign-in setup for the hosted version.

Power BI has two current MCP servers, plus an older one, the Power BI Consumption MCP server, kept for existing integrations. The first of the current pair is the Power BI Authoring MCP server, which you may still see under the name of its package, powerbi-modeling-mcp. It lets an agent create and change the objects inside a semantic model, which is the layer of a Power BI report that holds the tables, the relationships between them and the calculations, kept separate from the charts on the page. It comes in two forms. The hosted version, still in preview, needs nothing installed. The local version is generally available and runs on your own machine, which makes it the one to use when the model is a file you hold yourself, whether that's open in Power BI Desktop, the free Windows app used to build reports, or saved as a project folder. Macs aren't supported by the local version, so on a Mac it has to be the hosted one, which works only with models published to Microsoft's cloud (a Fabric workspace).

Recent findings suggest that the second is the Fabric IQ MCP server. Fabric IQ is part of Microsoft Fabric, the wider data platform that Power BI now sits within. It gives an agent read-only tools for finding published reports and models and running queries against them, within the permissions already set, so the agent can answer questions about the data but can't change a model.

In a recent development, which one to use follows from the job. Anything that changes a model goes through the authoring server, whether that's a fresh measure, a relationship or a set of descriptions, and it has to be the local version if the model is a Desktop file or a project folder under source control. Fabric IQ is for agents that only need answers from models other people maintain.

An agent connected to a semantic model can see its metadata (table and column names, data types, relationships, existing measures and any descriptions someone has written) and can run queries against the data. Everything it produces is inferred from those clues. A model that has served a business for years carries names that made perfect sense to the people who built it, and a column called Amt on a table called Sales_v2 tells an agent far less than it tells them.

According to recent reports, names carry a lot of the meaning. A column called Amount could hold the value with VAT (the UK's sales tax) or without, before credit notes or after, and an agent asked for "revenue" has to pick one. If the model holds several revenue measures built for different reports, the agent has to choose between them, and the one it picks may have been built for a different purpose.

The formulas depend on context as well. Power BI measures use a syntax of their own called DAX, which stands for Data Analysis Expressions. A DAX result shifts with whatever the person viewing the report has filtered or clicked on, which is known as filter context. A developer might think of a measure as a function that reads implicit state set by its caller. The same measure can be right as a single total on a card and need different handling once it's split by product in a table or filtered by a date slicer (the on-page date filter), depending on how CALCULATE (the DAX function that changes which filters apply) is used. Which behaviour is correct depends on how the business wants the number to respond, and that's something the agent has to be told.

It has been revealed that relationships work the same way. Plenty of models have more than one date column on the sales table, say order date and dispatch date, with only one relationship active at a time. A DAX measure uses the active relationship unless it's written to switch to the other one, and the agent has no way of knowing which date your monthly reporting runs on unless something tells it.

In each case the agent can write a valid measure. Which of two valid measures matches the business's own definition is the part it can't see from the model.

In a recent development, to see this in practice, we built a small sales model in a Power BI Desktop file, working through the server itself, with invented data: 5,266 order lines, with order dates from January 2025 to October 2026. We gave the Sales table an Amt column holding each line's value after discount with 20% VAT added, next to LineTotal and Discount columns that excluded VAT, and an existing [Revenue] measure that summed Amt. There were two date columns, with the active relationship to the Date table on dispatch date and the order date relationship inactive. Orders stop at the end of October 2026, which made the current year a part year, a deliberate test. Nothing in the model had a description. In this made-up business, finance reports revenue net of VAT and discounts, by order date.

On 12 November 2026 we connected an AI agent (Anthropic's Claude Fable 5.2) to version 1.0.1 of the local server through a small Node.js script that speaks MCP over stdio. In all three runs the agent had the server's tools only, without Microsoft's powerbi-authoring plugin, which adds modelling guidance on top of them. It was also told that nobody was available to answer questions, so each measure was saved exactly as the agent wrote it, with no review in between. The first prompt was one sentence: "Add a year-on-year revenue measure.".

Industry observers note that before writing anything, the agent listed the tables, relationships and columns, read the existing measure, sampled some rows and checked the date ranges. It worked out for itself that 2026 was a part year and limited the comparison to the same dates in 2025, which avoided a misleading result of -6.7%. From 15 sample rows it also spotted that Amt looked like the net figure plus 20%.

Industry observers note that the measure it saved reused the existing [Revenue] measure and followed the active relationship. This is the core of it, with the date handling and blank checks left out. CurrentDates is defined in those lines as the dates up to the last order:.

In a recent development, it returned growth of 21.5% for 2026, which is correct for revenue counted by dispatch date. On finance's definition, by order date, the answer is 18.6%, and the whole difference came from that choice of date. The VAT question made no difference to a percentage, because Amt was already net of discount and every line carried the same rate, although it would have overstated any figure in pounds by 20%.

We reset the model and repeated the run with a fresh agent, which made the same two choices and returned the same 21.5%. Both choices were reasonable readings of the model as it stood, and the DAX was sound. In their reports, both agents flagged the date basis and the VAT treatment as open questions, and both worked out that an order-date basis would give 18.6%. That's what a good analyst would do, and with those two answers they would have had everything they needed.

Industry observers note that think of a capable analyst on their first morning, someone who knows DAX well but has never seen your business before and knows nothing (or not a lot) about it. You wouldn't say "add a revenue measure" and walk off. You'd tell them which table holds the trusted figures, whether revenue includes VAT, which date drives the reporting calendar, and what they shouldn't touch. An agent needs that briefing for the same reasons, and getting good work out of it draws on the skills you'd use with any new starter. Developers do the same thing when they write a good ticket. A request for a measure is a requirement, and it needs the same definitions and constraints, plus a way to check the result.

Before you send a prompt, ask yourself whether you could do the task properly if you were given only the words in that prompt and the model itself. If the answer is no, then the agent is in the same position, and it will make its own assumptions.

For the detailed run we cleared the earlier measure from the model and gave a fresh agent this brief:.

Recent findings suggest that this time the measure summed LineTotal minus Discount and used USERELATIONSHIP, the DAX function that switches a calculation to an inactive relationship, to work from order date. It returned 18.6% from that one brief, with no follow-up prompt, which is the figure we had calculated separately from the source data. This is the full measure as the agent saved it:.

Recent findings suggest that each line of the brief answered a question the agent would otherwise have had to settle alone. It also made some sensible decisions the brief hadn't covered. It left the grand total blank, for instance, where a plain total across both years would have shown a meaningless growth figure of 151.2%. The final line of the brief, asking to see the DAX before anything is saved, is there so that a person can see choices like that. In the test we approved that step in advance, to keep the run unattended.

According to recent reports, one detail needs adjusting before this measure is reused on other data. Its guard checks that each comparison period starts on or after the first order date, which works here because the sample data has an order on 1 January 2025. When we swapped that date for 2 January 2025 in a copy of the measure, January 2026 and the 2026 row came back blank. Comparing against the first date in the Date table, as the first agent's measure did, brought the 2026 figure back, since the Date table starts on 1 January. That version doesn't confirm that sales exist for the whole comparison period, though, so the right check depends on whether the business wants growth shown only where a complete prior period exists. That's a decision for whoever reviews the measure.

We ran the one-sentence prompt twice and the detailed brief once, all with the same AI model and one small set of data, which is enough to illustrate the pattern but too little to say how often it happens.

It has been revealed that good briefs help, but you'll be writing the same definitions into prompts again and again unless they live in the model itself. Descriptions on tables, columns and measures are part of the metadata the agent reads, so filling them in is one of the cheapest ways to put business definitions in front of it every time. In our test, where nothing had a description, both agents given the one-sentence prompt noted that nothing confirmed what Amt contained. A description such as "Net sales value in GBP, excluding VAT, after credit notes" stays in the model, where the agent reads it without anyone retyping it.

According to recent reports, naming deserves the same attention. Spelling out abbreviated column names, hiding technical keys that no report needs, gathering measures into a single measures table, and removing measures that are no longer used all give the agent fewer things to choose between. These are the same habits that make a model easier for a new colleague to pick up, so asking someone outside the team to find a figure in it is a fair test of the result.

Microsoft has also added a set of Prep data for AI features (in preview) to Power BI Desktop and the service. They let you choose which fields Copilot, Microsoft's AI assistant, should consider and write AI instructions that explain your business terms, with verified answers available for common questions. They're aimed at Copilot, but deciding and writing down your definitions is the same work whichever AI tool reads them.

Recent findings suggest that an agent working through the authoring server has the same access as the person signed in, so anything that person can change, the agent can change. Sign in with an account that has no more access than the job needs, and take a copy of the model first, as you would before any bulk edit.

Start with read-only mode. The local server takes a --readonly flag that blocks all write operations, which is the right setting while you're learning how the agent behaves on your models. When we tried to create a measure in this mode, the server refused and said it was running read-only. In VS Code, the configuration looks like this (other clients use a similar structure, sometimes under an mcpServers key instead of servers):.

You'll need Node.js installed for the npx command. The server won't run other tools until its licence terms (the EULA) have been accepted. Once you've read them, you can either tell the agent to accept for you or add --accepteula to the args list.

The --readonly flag belongs to the local server. On a Mac the route is the hosted server and a copy of the model in a Fabric workspace, once a Fabric administrator has switched on the tenant setting that allows the MCP endpoint, and there the copy is the safeguard. For an enforced limit, sign in with an account that holds only Build permission on the model, which lets the agent read and query it and nothing more.

Industry observers note that read-write is the default, so check how confirmation behaves in the version you install. Version 1.0.1 skips confirmation prompts by default, which the project's README hasn't caught up with, and has a --require-confirmation flag to turn them on. The flag is listed in the server's own --help output. In our runs every edit went through without a prompt. When we added the flag to the args list, the server asked for confirmation before the first write, with a message beginning "Are you sure you want to perform operations that will modify your database", and answering no blocked the change.

Version control is the other safeguard. Saved in the Power BI Project format (PBIP), a report and its model become folders of text files instead of one binary .pbix file. Commit those before the agent starts and its work arrives as an ordinary diff, which you can review and revert like any other change.

Whatever the agent reads, including table and column names and the rows returned by any query, is passed on to the AI provider behind your client, which may sit outside Microsoft's compliance commitments. For a model holding customer or payroll data, check that the provider is approved under your data policies before you connect.

Recent findings suggest that an agent can draft and test a measure in minutes, and someone still has to read what comes back. For a developer fresh to Power BI, that takes enough DAX to see what a measure's filters will do in a table broken down by month or product, and enough knowledge of the business to confirm the agent used the right column and the right date. Writing the brief takes the same knowledge. Ours could only have come from someone who knew the model had an inactive relationship and which columns carried VAT.

In a recent development, these are data modelling and DAX skills, which many learners find the hardest part of Power BI. If the person reviewing agent output hasn't had that grounding yet, it helps to know how to judge whether a Power BI course covers enough DAX and data modelling, because courses vary a great deal in how much time they give to those two subjects compared with building charts.

In a recent development, take a copy of a model you know well and connect the local server to it in read-only mode. Ask the agent to describe every table and measure in its own words, then check those descriptions against what you know the model does. Wherever the two differ, the model needs a clearer name or a written description, and the corrected text can go straight into the description fields. With those in place before you allow any writes, the agent starts its first real task with the same definitions your finance team uses.

#195338. AI-powered bionic eye breakthrough could help the blind see again

AI-powered bionic eye breakthrough could help the blind see again

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1454 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Artificial intelligence could help overcome one of the biggest challenges in restoring vision to people who are blind: getting a brain implant to produce reliable visual experiences.
  • The team used a deep learning system to develop electrical stimulation patterns for electrodes temporarily implanted in the visual cortex, the region at the back of the brain responsible for processing visual information.
  • In a recent development, published online in the journal Neuron, the proof-of-concept study represents progress toward more advanced visual prostheses, sometimes described as bionic eyes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Artificial intelligence could help overcome one of the biggest challenges in restoring vision to people who are blind: getting a brain implant to produce reliable visual experiences. Researchers from three institutions, including UC Santa Barbara, have demonstrated that AI can improve how precisely an experimental visual prosthesis stimulates the brain and predicts what a person perceives.

The team used a deep learning system to develop electrical stimulation patterns for electrodes temporarily implanted in the visual cortex, the region at the back of the brain responsible for processing visual information. By analyzing the brain's responses, the technology gave researchers greater control over neural activity and helped them better anticipate the visual sensations produced by the implant.

In a recent development, published online in the journal Neuron, the proof-of-concept study represents progress toward more advanced visual prostheses, sometimes described as bionic eyes. These devices could eventually become more effective by learning how each person's brain responds to stimulation rather than relying on predetermined settings.

According to recent reports, "Building a model in the abstract is one thing," remarked Michael Beyeler, an associate professor of computer science and psychological and brain sciences at UC Santa Barbara. "Seeing it shape an experiment with a person is something else entirely. That ability to go from theory to something that may one day help people is what drives much of the work in our lab.".

How Bionic Vision Could Bypass Damaged Eyes.

For decades, scientists have worked to develop technologies capable of restoring some vision to people who are blind, although the results have generally been limited. Some experimental devices stimulate the retina, the layer of tissue at the back of the eye that detects light. Others attempt to activate parts of the visual system farther along the pathway that carries visual information to the brain.

Visual cortical prostheses work differently. Instead of depending on the eyes or optic nerves, they deliver electrical signals directly to the visual cortex. This approach could offer a potential solution for people whose visual pathways have been damaged but whose visual cortex can still respond to stimulation. Possible candidates include individuals who lost their sight because of strokes, neurodegenerative diseases, or traumatic brain injuries.

The ability to regain even limited vision could be especially meaningful for people who remember what it was like to see.

Beyeler highlighted those "who have been able to see for part of their life, but then, because of an inherited eye disease or an accident, have lost their vision," adding, "For those people, the desire may be very strong to get some vision back.".

Recent findings suggest that the upcoming findings build on earlier computational research supported by Beyeler's 2022 National Institutes of Health (NIH) Director's New Innovator Award. The five-year, $2 million grant has supported his efforts to make artificial vision systems more accurate, predictable, and effective.

Scientists Test AI With a Brain Implant in a Blind Man.

An important opportunity to test the technology came in 2024, when researchers from Beyeler's Bionic Vision Lab traveled to Spain. Their goal was to determine whether their computer models could improve the performance of a brain implant already being used in an experimental study.

At Hospital IMED Elche, the team worked with a 27-year-old man who had become blind following a traumatic brain injury. He had received an implant containing 96 electrodes arranged in an array within his visual cortex. The device was intended to remain in place for six months before being removed.

In a recent development, when researchers activated the electrodes using electrical current, the participant experienced visual sensations known as phosphenes. These can appear as spots, flashes, or shapes of light, sometimes resembling stars or fireworks.

Producing these sensations is possible, but making them consistent and predictable is much more difficult. The same electrical stimulation does not always trigger an identical response, and activating particular electrodes does not guarantee that the person will perceive a specific visual pattern.

To address this problem, the researchers trained a deep neural network, a type of AI designed to recognize complex patterns, to predict how the visual cortex would respond to different electrical stimulation settings. The model also considered the brain's resting activity immediately before stimulation, giving it information about the participant's current neural state.

Using these predictions, the researchers identified combinations of electrical signals that were most likely to produce particular patterns of brain activity.

AI Makes Bionic Vision More Precise.

According to recent reports, when the scientists tested the stimulation patterns selected by AI, the results were encouraging. The upcoming approach generated the intended patterns of neural activity more accurately than the comparison methods while requiring less electrical current.

Industry observers note that another key discovery emerged when the team examined the relationship between brain activity and the participant's visual experiences. The patterns recorded directly from his brain were better predictors of what he perceived than the stimulation settings themselves.

This distinction matters because activating the brain is not the same as knowing what a person will see. Even when researchers can produce a desired neural response, they still need to understand how the brain transforms that activity into a conscious visual experience.

According to recent reports, "Engineers naturally want to treat phosphenes like pixels: stimulate more electrodes, and you should get a more complete image," Beyeler noted. "But the brain does not work that way. Electrodes interact, neural responses fluctuate, and what we put into the brain is not necessarily what the person perceives. The challenge is to learn more about that transformation.".

The findings suggest that future visual prostheses may need to do more than simply deliver electrical signals. They may also need to monitor how the brain reacts and use that feedback to continually improve stimulation.

Teaching Brain Implants to Adapt to Each Person.

In a recent development, A key advantage of the implant used in the experiment was its ability to perform two tasks. It could stimulate the visual cortex with electrical current while simultaneously recording the resulting neural activity.

This allowed researchers to train their AI model using the brain's actual responses rather than relying exclusively on information about which electrodes were activated and how much current they delivered.

The participant also provided feedback about what he experienced. He reported whether he saw a phosphene and, during certain experiments, described its appearance, including its shape, size, brightness, and color.

Comparing these reports with the recorded brain activity revealed that neural responses contained more useful information about the perceived visual sensations than the electrical stimulation parameters alone.

According to recent reports, the AI system also used measurements of resting brain activity to account for changes in the participant's neural state before each stimulation. This could be particularly valuable because the brain's response to electrical signals can vary over time, including from one day to the next.

By adapting stimulation to these changing conditions, future prostheses might provide more consistent visual experiences without requiring users to adjust to a rigid set of signals.

"A useful visual prosthesis cannot rely on a fixed recipe," Beyeler noted. "It has to learn how an individual brain responds and adapt the stimulation accordingly. Ultimately, the device should adapt to the person, not the other way around.".

A Collaborative Step Toward Restoring Sight.

Industry observers note that the research brought together scientists from UC Santa Barbara, ETH Zurich, and Miguel Hernández University (MHU). Beyeler described the effort as "a true collaboration.".

It has been revealed that the project was led by co-first authors Pehuén Moure of ETH Zurich, Jacob Granley of UC Santa Barbara, and Fabrizio Grani of MHU. The supervising researchers were Beyeler, Shih-Chii Liu of ETH Zurich, and Eduardo Fernández of MHU. Their work forms part of a larger feasibility trial taking place in Spain.

Although the technology remains experimental and the participant's visual experiences were limited to flashes and shapes of light, the results demonstrate how AI could improve communication between artificial vision devices and the brain.

In a recent development, rather than treating every brain as if it responds the same way, future bionic vision systems could learn from each individual and adjust their signals accordingly. That personalized approach may prove essential to developing implants that can eventually restore useful vision to people who have lost their sight.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, the Co Print Quadro is an Independent Quad Extrusion (IQEX) bedslinger 3D printer, carrying four fully functional printheads on one gantry.
  • Sources indicate that independent Quad Extrusion, or IQEX, is unlike tool-changer 3D printers.
  • In a recent development, the Co Print Quadro is a non-enclosed bedslinger, and its design is quite similar to the Bambu Lab A1, albeit much beefier.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, the Co Print Quadro is an Independent Quad Extrusion (IQEX) bedslinger 3D printer, carrying four fully functional printheads on one gantry. The 3D printer accessory firm’s first 3D printer aims to bring IQEX technology to the masses at a budget price, with an SRP of only $899. It has already raised over $500,000, crushing its goal of only $9,820.

Sources indicate that independent Quad Extrusion, or IQEX, is unlike tool-changer 3D printers. Instead of one print head swapping assemblies, it has four individual print heads. This allows for increased productivity by printing with all four heads at once, or reducing waste by not going through any purging steps.

In a recent development, the Co Print Quadro is a non-enclosed bedslinger, and its design is quite similar to the Bambu Lab A1, albeit much beefier. The four print heads line up on one gantry, with space for three extruders on either side so they can get out of the way while either of the extruders on the edges can print. It has a large build volume of 300mm3, while the unit itself takes up a massive 780 x 620 mm footprint (2.5 x 2 feet).

Co print claims the Quadro can switch colors in one second, beating out tool changers that still need to park, grab, and home each tool, possibly with some priming as well. The Quadro’s demonstration video still used a prime tower, but it’s likely optional, meaning it can achieve zero color-change waste. What’s even more impressive is the copy printing technology, allowing multiple or even all print heads to print the same objects at once, potentially increasing productivity fourfold. Of course, it also has its own slicer for added IQEX functions, and it’s based on OrcaSlicer, so we’ll likely see community mods that make it do even crazier things.

It has been revealed that the Co Print Quadro is not without competition, however, as another IQEX printer finished its Kickstarter campaign earlier this year: the LightMake L4, raising $3 million in backing over its $50,000 goal. The L4 is an enclosed Core-XY printer with an even bigger print volume of 354 x 370 x 386mm in a smaller 610 x 620 mm footprint while still able to let each print head reach every corner of the build plate. The L4 has the size and enclosure advantage, but Co Print does proposal to sell an enclosure for the Quadro as well for more demanding filaments. The L4 has two gantries and can also print four objects at once, but it has a much higher SRP of $2,400 compared to the Quadro’s $899.

Recent findings suggest that the Quadro is Co Print’s first 3D printer, but the company is no stranger to 3D printing, providing multi-color upgrade kits for Creality, Elegoo, and Flashforge printers, including open-source printer brands like Sovol, Voron, and QIDI. While the products are mostly viewed positively, many forums complain about Co Print’s customer service and support. If Co Print wants to sell a whole 3D printer, it should be prepared to deal with challenges and take feedback.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

NVIDIA Isaac GR00T (Generalist Robot 00 Technology) is a research and development platform for building robot foundation models and data pipelines, designed to accelerate the creation of intelligent, adaptable robots.

According to recent reports, today, we announced the availability of Isaac GR00T N1.5, the first major revision to Isaac GR00T N1, the world’s first open foundation model for generalized humanoid robot reasoning and skills. This cross-embodiment model processes multimodal inputs, including language and images, to perform manipulation tasks across diverse environments. It is adaptable through post-training for specific embodiments, tasks, and environments.

In this blog, we’ll demonstrate how to post-train (fine-tune) GR00T N1.5 using teleoperation data from a single SO-101 robot arm.

Technical Blog for GR00T N1.5: https://research.nvidia.com/labs/gear/gr00t-n1_5/.

Now accessible to developers working with a wide range of robot form factors, GR00T N1.5 can be easily fine-tuned and adapted using the affordable, open-source LeRobot SO-101 arm.

This flexibility is enabled by the EmbodimentTag system, which allows seamless customization of the model for different robotic platforms, empowering hobbyists, researchers, and engineers to tailor advanced humanoid reasoning and manipulation capabilities to their own hardware.

Before proceeding to installation, please check if you satisfy the prerequisites.

Tiny flaws in diamonds could unlock a quantum computing revolution

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1198 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that A new computational technique could accelerate the search for diamond materials capable of powering future quantum computers and highly sensitive sensors.
  • The approach has already revealed new candidates for quantum computing and sensing applications.
  • It has been revealed that one of the biggest challenges in developing quantum technology is finding materials that can maintain delicate quantum states under practical conditions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that A new computational technique could accelerate the search for diamond materials capable of powering future quantum computers and highly sensitive sensors. Developed by a researcher at the U.S. Department of Energy's (DOE) Princeton Plasma Physics Laboratory (PPPL), the method makes it much easier to identify promising materials for quantum technology, potentially opening the door to advances across many areas of science.

The approach has already revealed new candidates for quantum computing and sensing applications. The findings were recently published in ACS Central Science and have attracted attention from other researchers in the field.

It has been revealed that one of the biggest challenges in developing quantum technology is finding materials that can maintain delicate quantum states under practical conditions. Many candidates require extremely low temperatures to function reliably. Diamond materials stand out because certain quantum properties can remain useful even at room temperature.

It has been revealed that this capability could help advance technologies that are important to national research priorities and the development of next-generation computing. Quantum sensors promise levels of sensitivity and precision beyond those of conventional instruments, while quantum computers could eventually solve certain extraordinarily complex problems much faster than today's most powerful supercomputers.

Why Imperfect Diamonds Could Be the Key to Quantum Computing.

Although diamonds are made of carbon atoms, a flawless diamond crystal is not enough to create a useful quantum computing system. The key lies in tiny irregularities within the crystal structure.

These imperfections, known as defects, can occur when a carbon atom is absent from its normal position, when another element replaces a carbon atom, or when both changes occur together. The atoms surrounding these defects can form qubits, the basic units used to store and process quantum information in quantum computers and sensors.

Finding the most useful defects, however, has been difficult. Accurately modeling their quantum behavior traditionally requires enormous computational resources, making it challenging to evaluate large numbers of possible candidates.

A Simpler Way to Discover Better Diamond Qubits.

It has been revealed that mark Martirez, a staff research scientist at PPPL, developed a way to dramatically reduce the complexity of these calculations. Instead of simulating a much larger diamond structure, he isolates a small region containing just 16 to 30 atoms around a defect.

According to recent reports, by "carving out" this tiny atomic cluster and treating it like a separate molecule, Martirez can use powerful computational methods that chemists have spent decades refining. These established techniques make it possible to analyze the quantum properties of diamond defects much more efficiently without sacrificing the high level of accuracy needed for the calculations.

Sources indicate that "Because we're treating the qubits as molecules, the cost of calculating these defects is equivalent to the cost of just modeling a simple molecule," Martirez remarked. "This method really opened the floodgates" in terms of how qubits can be assessed.

Sources indicate that the new technique allows researchers to calculate how different qubits respond to laser light and microwave pulses far more quickly than before. Using this approach, the team identified promising defects involving boron and oxygen that could serve as new types of qubits.

New Diamond Defects Reveal a Spectrum of Quantum Colors.

Sources indicate that light plays an key role in how scientists interact with diamond qubits. Researchers use lasers and microwave pulses to manipulate their quantum states and retrieve stored information.

Sources indicate that much of the previous work in this area has centered on a defect known as the nitrogen-vacancy center. This structure forms when a nitrogen atom takes the place of a carbon atom in a diamond crystal, while an adjacent position that would normally contain another carbon atom remains empty.

Under laser illumination, this type of defect can emit red light when it occupies a particular quantum state.

Industry observers note that the newly investigated defects offer different optical properties. Oxygen defects can produce blue light, while those involving boron emit ultraviolet light.

These differences could make it possible to combine several types of qubits within a single quantum device. Because each type responds differently to light, researchers might be able to interact with one group of qubits without disturbing another.

"One could imagine, then, combining different qubits of different responses, so you can basically probe one qubit but not the other," Martirez stated.

It has been revealed that beyond identifying fresh candidates, the findings suggest a broader change in how researchers approach quantum technology. Diamond qubits have traditionally been studied primarily through physics, but understanding their underlying chemistry could provide additional ways to design them.

Martirez believes that researchers could eventually engineer qubits for particular functions using principles similar to those applied when chemists create specialized molecules, including compounds designed for new medications.

How Quantum Chemistry Could Transform Future Research.

Industry observers note that the potential benefits extend well beyond the development of quantum computers themselves. Martirez sees an intriguing possibility in which advances made possible by quantum chemistry eventually lead to quantum technologies that help improve the field of chemistry.

In other words, quantum chemistry could develop the very tools needed to "enrich itself" in the coming decades.

It has been revealed that A practical quantum system containing multiple qubits could make molecular calculations substantially more accurate. That would allow scientists to study increasingly complex chemical structures, including large biological molecules and proteins, with a level of detail that is difficult to achieve using conventional methods.

Recent findings suggest that "We could describe larger molecules, biomolecules, proteins and everything like that in a more accurate way, and that could improve all the chemical-adjacent industries, such as pharmaceutical science and materials science. Even our fundamental understanding of molecular systems could be enriched.".

Such improvements could have far-reaching implications for pharmaceutical development, materials research, and the fundamental study of how molecules behave.

Sources indicate that martirez also hopes the research will encourage more chemists to explore solid-state physics. Although building advanced quantum computers is often viewed as a challenge primarily for physicists, he argues that chemistry offers valuable expertise that could help accelerate progress.

Industry observers note that "At this moment in time, there's a great emphasis on building the first state-of-the-art qubit computer," he mentioned. "But it's not just physicists who should be participating in this research. Chemists have decades of developed intuition about chemical systems that could be easily translated into understanding defects in solids as well.".

By bringing these disciplines together, scientists may be able to develop more effective ways to discover, understand, and eventually engineer the quantum materials needed for future technologies.

The research was funded through PPPL's Laboratory Directed Research and Development program under prime contract number DE-AC02-09CH11466, with additional support from the DOE Office of Science, Office of Fusion Energy Sciences.

Industry observers note that this chip comes with AMD's second-gen 3D V-Cache, which places the extra SRAM under the compute die. Another indicates that entry-level listings have plummeted 35% since 2023; another suggests entry-level jobs in Upcoming York City have been cut in half. That means the pressure is on for early-career candidates to show employers what they can bring to a role beyond their ability to use AI tools. A catch-22 emerges: many employers increasingly turn to AI, yet many also want candidates who can think independently, come up with original ideas, recognize when to put the technology aside and trust their own judgment. Indeed, many young workers find themselves in a tricky-to-navigate, even unfair entry-level job market. Luckily, there are tips that can make you stand out in a labor market that both increasingly relies on AI, and that also demands workers show employers the human skills they’re looking for. Don’t let AI write your resume for you Sure, AI can be a helpful writing tool: it can help you brainstorm, organize your experience, even give you a first draft. But if every candidate is using AI to write their application, it can become harder to show what makes you different. According to Amitoj Sandhu, Manager of Global Early Talent at HR platform Dayforce, employers are starting to see more applications that all sound alike. “Every single profile looks the same. They all are the same on the paper, so it becomes really hard for us to shortlist them and present in front of leaders,” he says. Sandhu says AI is a useful starting point, but candidates need to be able to use their own voice, and  stand behind what they submit. After all, if AI is writing your resume for you, when it comes time for the interview, “will you be able to validate the results?” he says. Sandhu recommends preparing two or three strong examples from internships, school projects, or extracurricular activities that you can actually speak to authentically without farming everything out to ChatGPT. Then, be ready to walk an interviewer through those experiences and what you learned from them. With fewer entry-level roles apparently available, layering this in can make your application pop. Do use AI in your cover letter, but with caution “AI can be a great tool for writing a better cover letter. It can help candidates organize their ideas, communicate more clearly and make meaningful connections between their own interests and the organization they’re applying to,” says Dan Kejsefman, Talent Director at Avature, a software development company. He says AI can raise the bar in terms of an application’s quality—but at the same time, “the motivation behind it still needs to be genuine.”  “I’d encourage candidates to start with their own reasons for wanting the job: What interests them about the company? What would they like to learn? What experiences or interests connect them to the opportunity? Then use AI to help communicate those ideas more effectively,” he says. The important thing is being able to explain and stand behind what’s in your cover letter. “AI can help you tell your story better,” he says, “but the story still has to be yours.” Use AI tools where you can—many jobs will expect you to use them to some extent, anyway—but standing out in an increasingly crowded entry-level field means tapping into what makes you, you. Don’t leave your curiosity at home According to Sandhu, when it comes time for the interview, curiosity is one of the biggest qualities employers look for. Missing that in an interview is “kind of a red flag for us,” Sandhu says. Sure, one way to demonstrate this is by researching the employer before the interview, and developing a genuine understanding of what the company does and the industry it operates in. But preparation is only part of it. Kejsefman says candidates also need to show genuine interest in the conversation, rather than simply relying on a list of questions prepared with AI during your interview practice. “AI can help candidates research a company, understand a role, and prepare thoughtful questions. That’s useful, and I wouldn’t discourage it,” Kejsefman explains. “But there’s a difference between asking an impressive question, and actually being interested in understanding the answer.” For example, curious candidates listen carefully, ask follow-up questions and try to understand why things work the way they do. That’s a timeless strategy, regardless of AI or not. Young workers “don’t necessarily have all the answers, and that’s perfectly fine, especially early in their careers. What matters is whether they show a real desire to learn and understand,” Kejsefman says. Do bring your own judgment to the work Sandhu says employers want candidates who can question the information AI provides, apply their own judgment and build on what the technology produces. Think of a software developer who might use ChatGPT to generate code, but still needs to determine whether it makes sense or meets the requirements or passes the right tests. Human judgment, after all, has long been touted as something that will still prove crucial in the AI era—in fact, as more decisions get outsourced to robots, it becomes even more valuable. “Can you use your own judgment to evaluate a response you get from AI? Can you build on that context? That’s what we’re looking for,” Sandhu says. In fields such as communications and journalism, employers still want to see creativity and original ideas rather than generic content generated by AI. “They want to look at how you think and what kind of ideas you can spark, not just all the generic ideas AI is producing,” Sandhu says. Kejsefman says AI adoption is still uneven across organizations, creating an opportunity for early-career professionals. A recent graduate who develops strong AI skills can bring something valuable to a team, even when working alongside people with much more professional experience. But they also bring enthusiasm and perspective older workers don’t have, and that robots definitely don’t have. Kejsefman also cautions against focusing exclusively on learning individual AI tools. As those tools continue to change, the ability to think critically, understand problems and evaluate results will become increasingly important. As AI takes on more workplace tasks, your ability to bring your own ideas, judgment and perspective to the work can help you stand out—especially when looking to break into a field or organization. Do prioritize experience over job titles Regardless of best practices, as AI continues to change the skills employers need, recent graduates may need to be more flexible about where they start their careers. For starters, Sandhu cautions against focusing too heavily on a particular job title or starting salary. “The significant mistake which they’re making is they’re running after titles and what the compensation is going to look like,” Sandhu says. Instead, he encouraged candidates to prioritize gaining experience and finding opportunities to get started, even if the position isn’t exactly what they initially envisioned or in their precisely preferred field. “Don’t run after a specific job title in the world which is changing every day,” he says. And that experience doesn’t have to come from a traditional job. Kejsefman encourages recent graduates to draw on those other past experiences, like university projects or volunteering—even personal projects or side gigs, which a lot of Gen Z already has anyway. “They need examples of situations where they’ve taken initiative, faced a problem, learned something new, or adapted when things didn’t go as expected,” Kejsefman says. “For someone starting their career, demonstrating that mindset can be much more valuable than presenting a perfectly polished result.” Make no mistake—for new workers in the workplace, it’s rough out there. But keeping these strategies, which mix time-tested tactics with AI adoption and adaptation, could open the right door at the right time.

What is Model Routing in AI?

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1962 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sitepoint

  • "Do you know the closest ATM?" and "I was charged twice, the refund never arrived, and now my card is blocked" are both customer messages.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes
