How Nvidia employees feel about Jensen Huang’s return

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1478 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The public reaction to Jensen Huang’s return has been mixed at best, raising the hackles of lawmakers and corporate governance experts.
  • Recent findings suggest that the public reaction to Jensen Huang’s return has been mixed at best, raising the hackles of lawmakers and corporate governance experts.
  • In videos that are circulating across social media, Huang received a hero’s welcome at Nvidia headquarters, where his employees lined the walls cheering for him.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The public reaction to Jensen Huang’s return has been mixed at best, raising the hackles of lawmakers and corporate governance experts. Even the stock price took a bit of a dip after surging by over 30% on Monday. Within the tech giant, however, the mood appears to be considerably lighter. In videos that are circulating across social media, Huang received a hero’s welcome at Nvidia headquarters, where his employees lined the walls cheering for him. Between chants of “Jensen! Jensen!” and “We love you, Jensen,” he addressed his staff in a display of contrition. “I’m terribly sorry for putting all of you through all of this,” he mentioned. “I’ve made some very terrible mistakes, and I’m going to work on coming back.” After an employee threw her arms around Huang in a tight hug—lasting over 10 seconds—he continued: “Thank you all for the second chance. I’m going to be a better CEO the second time around.” Many Nvidia employees have taken to LinkedIn to express their relief over Huang’s return, seemingly overlooking the indiscretions that led to his ousting. They heaped praise on their newly reinstated CEO, describing him as the “heartbeat of Nvidia” and “one of a kind.”  One employee even invoked Charles Dickens, paraphrasing the opening of A Tale of Two Cities: “It was the worst of times, it is the best of times. It was the season of Darkness, it is the season of Light. It was the winter of despair, it is the spring of hope. We had nothing before us, we have everything before us.” Another employee claimed he always knew Huang would return to Nvidia: “When Jensen stepped down, many said their goodbyes and thanked him for his legacy. I stayed quiet—not out of indifference, but because deep down I knew there is only one boss, and he would be back.” A former robotics engineer at Nvidia—who quit rather publicly after Huang’s resignation—congratulated him on X and admitted he made a hasty decision. “Looking back, I may have moved too quickly, and I don’t want to rush into another major decision. For now, I’d like to take some time to rest, reflect, and think carefully about my future. As part of that, I’m open to exploring the possibility of returning.” These reactions line up with previous reports about employee sentiment after Huang stepped down: According to Wired, many employees demonstrated immediate support for him internally, asking the board to reverse the decision. More than 10,000 current Nvidia employees, or about a quarter of its workforce, signed a petition to reinstate Huang as CEO. Still, there are some employees who seem to feel differently—perhaps those who have been the target of Huang’s outbursts and creative insults, as reported by The New York Times recently. In a Wired report this week, several current and former employees expressed frustration over the turn of events, in part because they had hoped Huang’s exit would usher in some long overdue changes. A number of employees were disturbed by Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy and at least one inappropriate relationship with an employee. Beyond that, however, they also felt that Nvidia condoned abusive behavior and echoed previous claims that Huang belittled employees at times. (In an internal post, one employee asserted: “If Jensen comes back, I’m not doing any HR trainings ever again.”) Workers also told Wired that the focus on unity and the “one team” ethos discouraged employees from challenging leadership. Even employees who have few misgivings about the culture may now find themselves questioning Huang’s leadership. One engineering leader openly grappled with his feelings about Huang in a LinkedIn post he shared before the CEO was reinstated. “Some believe his contributions to Nvidia and the industry are so extraordinary that he deserves another chance,” he wrote. “Others argue that making exceptions for powerful leaders sets a dangerous precedent. I’ve wrestled with this question all week. My opinion has probably changed every single day. And I’ve realized something. I don’t have a clear answer.” As evidenced by the reception to Huang yesterday, this may not be the prevailing view among employees. But whether or not other employees have lost faith in Huang, there are now open questions about how—if at all—the company aims to address the myriad problems that have been exposed by the events of the last few weeks.

If you want a new rig before the holidays, then this 4K-ready gaming PC from Newegg would be a solid option. You can pick up this CyberPowerPC machine with specs that include the AMD Ryzen 7 7800X3D and Nvidia GeForce RTX 5070, along with 32GB of DDR5 RAM and a 1TB SSD, for $2,099.99.

● Check out this deal at Newegg.

According to recent reports, in the current market, that's a competitive price for a machine with a strong spec sheet. With this rig, you're getting the AMD Ryzen 7 7800X3D CPU. While this isn't quite top spec these days, AMD's 3D V-cache technology means that it continues to be a formidable option for gaming that few can rival. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, we're thrilled to share that Groq is now a supported Inference Provider on the Hugging Face Hub! Groq joins our growing ecosystem, enhancing the breadth and capabilities of serverless inference directly on the Hub’s model pages. Inference Providers are also seamlessly integrated into our client SDKs (for both JS and Python), making it super easy to use a wide variety of models with your preferred providers.

Groq supports a wide variety of text and conversational models, including the latest open-source models such as Meta's Llama 4, Qwen's QWQ-32B, and many more.

Sources indicate that at the heart of Groq's technology is the Language Processing Unit (LPU™), a upcoming type of end-to-end processing unit system that provides the fastest inference for computationally intensive applications with a sequential component, such as Large Language Models (LLMs). LPUs are designed to overcome the limitations of GPUs for inference, offering significantly lower latency and higher throughput. This makes them ideal for real-time AI applications.

Groq offers fast AI inference for openly-available models. They provide an API that allows developers to easily integrate these models into their applications. It offers an on-demand, pay-as-you-go model for accessing a wide range of openly-available LLMs.

Recent findings suggest that you can now use Groq's Inference API as an Inference Provider on Huggingface. We're quite excited to see what you'll build with this newly introduced provider.

Read more about how to use Groq as Inference Provider in its dedicated documentation page.

See the list of supported models here.

Recent findings suggest that the following example shows how to use Meta's Llama 4 using Groq as the inference provider. You can use a Hugging Face token for automatic routing through Hugging Face, or your own Groq API key if you have one.

It has been revealed that install huggingface_hub from source (see instructions). Official support will be released soon in version v0.33.0.

Recent findings suggest that for direct requests, i.e. when you use the key from an inference provider, you are billed by the corresponding provider. For instance, if you use a Groq API key you're billed on your Groq account.

Recent findings suggest that for routed requests, i.e. when you authenticate via the Hugging Face Hub, you'll only pay the standard provider API rates. There's no additional markup from us, we just pass through the provider costs directly. (In the future, we may establish revenue-sharing agreements with our provider partners.).

Crucial Note ‼️ PRO owners get $2 worth of Inference credits every month. You can use them across providers. 🔥.

We also provide free inference with a small quota for our signed-in free owners, but please upgrade to PRO if you can!

It has been revealed that we would love to get your feedback! Share your thoughts and/or comments here: https://huggingface.co/spaces/huggingface/HuggingDiscussions/discussions/49.

Groq’s integration as an Inference Provider on Hugging Face delivers ultra‑low latency and high‑throughput LPU‑powered inference for cutting‑edge open‑source LLMs — a game‑changer for real‑time AI deployments.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Business culture has long lionized bold, disruptive leaders.
  • Business culture has long lionized bold, disruptive leaders.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Business culture has long lionized bold, disruptive leaders. But these days, at least, Americans are yearning for some stability. In a survey conducted shortly after the midterm elections, 82% of Americans said they prefer leaders who “get things back to normal rather than shake things up” and 82% also said they prefer a “stable and predictable” life. The New York-based global public relations firm Burson interviewed about 1,600 Americans across party lines. The poll was published November 14. An overwhelming 90% of respondents also said they want honest, calm, consistent leadership, and 75% said they lose respect for CEOs who change positions under pressure. It is easy to interpret these findings as a reflection of current public opinion about President Donald Trump. Trump’s penchant for disruption and his brash businessman image helped him win the White House twice, but the outcome of the midterms—and the results of the Burson survey—indicate that the public has grown tired of the chaos. In a separate Associated Press poll, about two-thirds of the roughly 100,000 midterm voters surveyed thought Trump has the wrong priorities, while 7 in 10 said Congress hasn’t been doing enough to check the president’s power. As Fast Company reported earlier this month, the midterm results also illustrate the risks organizations face when they become overly dependent on a single charismatic leader. Successful leaders can make subordinates increasingly reluctant to question their judgment, even when circumstances change. “At some point, you have to ask whether people are following your vision, or simply afraid to challenge it,” leadership expert Adam Mendler said.

According to recent reports, sending a document for signature is the easy part of an e-signature integration. One POST request and the signer gets an email. The work that actually breaks in production happens afterwards: knowing when the document was signed, trusting the notification that told you so, handling the same notification twice, and getting the final PDF into storage before the download link expires.

Sources indicate that this tutorial builds that whole loop in Node.js with Express. An event in your app (a deal is approved, a client is onboarded, a task moves to "ready to sign") sends a contract from a template. When the signer finishes, a webhook arrives, your server verifies it, and the signed PDF plus its audit trail get saved without anyone touching them.

According to recent reports, the code uses Firma.dev, the e-signature API I work on, because I needed a real API to make the examples runnable. The patterns are not specific to it, though. Signature verification, idempotent handlers, short-lived download URLs, and reconciliation jobs show up in almost every webhook-driven integration, and the same structure applies whether you're receiving events from a payment processor, a CI system, or another signing provider.

There's a fifth part that tutorials usually skip: a reconciliation job that catches anything the webhooks missed. We'll build that too, because webhooks are a notification mechanism, not a delivery guarantee.

Set three environment variables:.

Before sending anything, wrap the HTTP calls in one place. This is where authentication lives, and it's also where you handle 429 Too Many Requests once instead of in every caller. Most APIs, this one included, return a Retry-After header on a 429, so the client should honour it rather than guessing a backoff.

Industry observers note that the 503 branch matters later. When a document has just been completed, the final PDF and its completion certificate take a moment to generate, and the download endpoint states so with a 503 and a Retry-After instead of handing you a half-built file.

The trigger depends on your product. It might be a route handler, a queue consumer, or a CRM automation calling into your service. What matters is that the function doing the sending is small and takes plain data:.

Two design choices are worth calling out.

It has been revealed that use a single create-and-send call when you can. Many signing APIs split this into "create a draft" and "send the draft." That's useful when a human needs to review the document first, but for automation it creates a window where your process can crash between the two calls and leave an orphaned draft. A combined endpoint makes the operation atomic from your side.

In a recent development, store the provider's ID on your own record immediately. Webhook payloads reference the signing request, not your deal or customer. Without that mapping you'll end up searching by email address, which falls apart as soon as one client signs two documents.

Here's the first place integrations quietly go wrong. Webhook signatures are computed over the exact bytes the sender transmitted. If Express parses the body as JSON first, you lose those bytes, and re-serialising the object won't reproduce them (key order, whitespace, and number formatting can all change). Signature checks then fail intermittently, which is the worst kind of failure.

The fix is to use express.raw() on the webhook route only, so the handler receives a Buffer:.

Industry observers note that most webhook providers sign payloads with HMAC-SHA256 using a shared secret. The details vary, so read your provider's docs for the exact header format, but the scheme here is common: the header looks like t=1731456000,v1=5f2b..., and the signed string is the timestamp, a dot, and the raw body. Stripe uses a very similar format, and the Standard Webhooks spec describes the same idea as a vendor-neutral convention.

Each line here defends against something specific.

The OWASP guidance on cryptographic storage covers the other half of this: the secret belongs in an environment variable or secrets manager, never in the repository.

Every serious webhook system delivers at least once, not exactly once. If your endpoint is slow, returns a 5xx, or the network drops the response, the sender retries. Firma.dev, for example, makes up to three attempts per event (immediately, then after at least five minutes, then after at least an hour) and treats anything other than a 2xx as a failure, including redirects. Other providers retry more aggressively. Either way, your handler will eventually see the same event twice.

The defence is to record each event's unique ID and skip ones you've seen. In the server above that's alreadyProcessed and markProcessed. For a demo, a Set works:.

In production, use your database and let a unique constraint do the work, so two concurrent deliveries can't both pass the check:.

It has been revealed that also notice the order in the route: respond with 200, then do the work. Many providers time out deliveries after a few seconds (five, in this case). Downloading a PDF and uploading it to object storage can easily take longer than that, and a timeout counts as a failure, which triggers a retry, which triggers duplicate work. Acknowledging fast and processing asynchronously avoids that loop.

setImmediate is fine for a tutorial, but it has a real weakness: if the process dies after sending the 200 and before finishing the work, the event is acknowledged and lost. In production, push the event onto a durable queue (BullMQ, SQS, a jobs table) before responding. Step 7 covers the safety net for whatever still slips through.

Now the actual business logic. You'll usually see several event types (sent, viewed, a signer signed, declined, expired, completed). Only one of them means "the document is final":.

Three things in here are easy to get wrong.

In a recent development, don't treat "a signer signed" as "the document is done." With multiple signers, each one triggers its own event, and a per-signer "all complete" flag can be true on more than one of them. Key your storage logic off the single completion event.

In a recent development, don't persist the download URL. Pre-signed URLs expire (this one carries an expires_at). Saving the link to your database and serving it to users later produces broken links a few minutes or hours later. Download the bytes and store them in storage you control. Swapping the fs.writeFile calls for an S3 PutObject or a Google Drive upload is a drop-in change.

Store the audit trail, not just the PDF. If a signature is ever disputed, the PDF highlights what was signed, and the audit trail shows who signed it, when, and from where (timestamps, IP addresses, the sequence of views and signatures). That evidence is what makes an electronic signature defensible, which brings us to the legal side.

In a recent development, retries are finite. Endpoints go down during deploys. Some providers auto-disable a webhook after enough consecutive failures, and events aren't guaranteed to arrive in order. Any one of these can leave a completed document sitting unsaved.

Recent findings suggest that A small scheduled job closes that gap. Keep a list of signing requests your app considers "pending," and periodically ask the API for their real status:.

Sources indicate that since storeSignedDocument overwrites by ID, running it twice for the same document is harmless. That's the property you want from every step in a webhook pipeline: doing it again shouldn't change the result.

None of this is legal advice, but a few facts shape how you build.

According to recent reports, in the US, the ESIGN Act and the Uniform Electronic Transactions Act (adopted by 49 states) give electronic signatures the same legal standing as handwritten ones for most commercial documents. ESIGN also has requirements around consumer consent and record retention, which is part of why you store the final PDF yourself rather than relying on a third-party link.

In the EU, eIDAS defines three levels: simple (SES), advanced (AdES), and qualified (QES). SES and AdES cover most business contracts. QES requires a qualified trust service provider and certificate-based identity, and some documents (certain property transfers and court filings, depending on the country) require it or exclude e-signatures entirely. Check which level your document types need before you pick a provider, since not every API offers every level.

Across jurisdictions, the evidence that holds up is the same: who signed, how they were identified, when it happened, and proof the document hasn't changed since. That's the audit trail and the completion certificate, which is why Step 6 stores both.

If you're evaluating providers for a workflow like this, the questions that matter at the integration level are mostly not on the pricing page:.

Recent findings suggest that the send call is one line. The reliability comes from everything around it: keeping the raw body for verification, checking timestamps and comparing in constant time, acknowledging fast and deduplicating by event ID, downloading files before their links expire, and running a reconciliation job for the events that never arrive. Get those right and contract signing becomes something your app does in the background, with no one chasing signatures or copying PDFs between folders.

For the Firma.dev-specific details used here (event names, header format, rate limits), see the webhooks guide.

Trump is deploying a special ‘Tiger Team’ for Thanksgiving air travel. Here’s why

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1403 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent chaos is making Americans wary of braving air travel this holiday season, but the Trump administration says it has a plan.
  • Recent chaos is making Americans wary of braving air travel this holiday season, but the Trump administration indicates it has a initiative.
  • According to recent reports, the White House recently revealed the formation of a “tiger team” dedicated to preventing major mess-ups like the recent multi-hour ground stop, which snarled airports nationwide as a mountain of delayed and rescheduled flights piled up.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent chaos is making Americans wary of braving air travel this holiday season, but the Trump administration says it has a plan. The White House recently announced the formation of a “tiger team” dedicated to preventing major mess-ups like the recent multi-hour ground stop, which snarled airports nationwide as a mountain of delayed and rescheduled flights piled up. The mid-November incident lasted more than four hours, grounding planes all over the country as the federal government scrambled to get the standard lines of communications for air traffic controllers back online. Trump’s special interagency group known as the “Transportation Technology Transformation Tiger Team” will bring together representatives from the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), the Department of Transportation, the Department of Defense, and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence, according to the White House. “As millions of Americans prepare to travel for the Thanksgiving holiday, President Donald J. Trump is making sure the skies stay open and the systems run smoothly,” the White House mentioned in a press release. The FAA reported that 12,462 flights were canceled during the ground stop, which began mid-afternoon on Friday, November 13. The FAA is still investigating the technical hiccup that prompted thousands of planes to be grounded, but a routine router upgrade completed by federal contractor L3Harris Technologies in Arkansas is believed to be at fault. Tiger teams in action The term “tiger team” is sometimes used in corporate settings, but it is more commonly used to describe small highly skilled teams convened to solve difficult problems in government and military operations. The most famous tiger team in history is credited with guiding NASA’s Apollo 13 mission back to Earth safely, a feat that earned then-Flight Director (and later NASA Mission Operations Director) Gene Kranz and his specialized group a Presidential Medal of Freedom. Other U.S. agencies use tiger teams for specialized problem-solving, including the U.S. Department of Labor. The Trump administration appears to have a particular affinity for the term and also formed a self-described tiger team across the Department of Energy and the Department of the Interior last year to “unleash” the American energy industry. That group later became bogged down wrestling with oil prices and inflation tied to the war in Iran. Aside from its tongue-twister of a name (try saying it five times fast), very little is known about Trump’s Transportation Technology Transformation Tiger Team. A White House official told The Daily Wire that the FAA is looking into “near-term” network configuration options and other short-term ways to boost the stability of current air traffic control systems while slower modernization efforts move forward. “President Trump and Secretary Duffy have brought together the best and the brightest across the government to ensure what happened last Friday can never happen again,” White House spokeswoman Allison Schuster said. “This team has hit the ground running in modernizing and improving the reliability of the nation’s decades-old air traffic control system.”  Schuster claimed that American skies are already safer, thanks to the “tremendous progress” from the tiger team, but reassuring Americans skittish about air safety after a spate of recent scares may not be that easy. Modernizing the U.S. air traffic control system is a major long-term goal pursued by multiple administrations and scores of lawmakers. Yet the ground stop revealed that pushing technology fixes into an ancient system that never goes offline carries its own set of risks. Record holiday travel expected In a press release, the Transportation Department said it expects to see the “busiest holiday skies in 16 years,” with more than 417,000 flights forecast for the nine days beginning on Monday of Thanksgiving week. Tuesday is projected to be the busiest travel day of the period, with more than 52,000 flights scheduled. “From standing up a Tiger Team to ensure a seamless travel experience for fliers to using a successful new platform to predict and address congestion in the airspace, we’ve taken unprecedented action to limit flight delays and cancellations,” Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said. “The American people can rest assured we will be on the clock 24/7 to get families to their destinations safely and on time.”.

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (424 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Tomshardware

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that multiple nations worldwide have chip-making programs in their respective universities, a discipline that is seeing increasing demand by the day.
  • Each truck-mounted mobileFab container contains three machines: a photoresist coater, a maskless lithography machine, and a photoresist developer.
  • The three machines going into trucks are part of the larger Minimal Fab laboratories in place in some Japanese colleges.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that multiple nations worldwide have chip-making programs in their respective universities, a discipline that is seeing increasing demand by the day. Japan is one such nation, and it currently has a program in which students can design circuits to wire chip wafers with miniaturized lithography stations. That gear is now going on wheels to schools and companies thanks to mobileFab trucks.

Each truck-mounted mobileFab container contains three machines: a photoresist coater, a maskless lithography machine, and a photoresist developer. Students take pre-etched wafers made by Japan's NIAIST (Institute for Advanced Industrial Science and Technology) and go through the necessary steps to wire the transistors therein together and produce a finalized chip core. The procedures are analogous to getting a breadboard with some pre-mounted, unconnected components and turning that into a product.

The three machines going into trucks are part of the larger Minimal Fab laboratories in place in some Japanese colleges. They're going on the move so that other schools and companies can train students/employees in the art of chipmaking. For now, the 12.5-mm wafers come from the NIAIST, but they can come from other foundries. Each machine is roughly 30 cm wide, and the machines use localized cleaning and sealed between-machine transportation so as not to have to rely on large-scale cleanrooms.

According to recent reports, according to the press release by the Minimal Fab Promotion Organization, this system is not only meant for democratizing access to chip manufacturing education. The machines also allow for rapid prototyping and iteration of chip designs, and facilitate small-scale manufacturing — all with modest capital investment.

The "why" of this initiative is fairly predictable: the program's organizers predict that semiconductor fab engineers will be in high demand over the next 10 years, and there aren't even enough teachers going around, making systematic education difficult. Additionally, the division of labor in semiconductor fabs means that many engineers don't participate in all stages of the chip-making process, nor do they have opportunities to operate chip-making equipment themselves. The mobileFab will be on display at the SEMICON Japan 2026 conference in December.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that in our previous post, Exploring Quantization Backends in Diffusers, we dived into how various quantization techniques can shrink diffusion models like FLUX.1-dev, making them significantly more accessible for inference without drastically compromising performance.
  • Performing inference is cool, but to make these models truly our own, we also need to be able to fine-tune them.
  • We aim to fine-tune black-forest-labs/FLUX.1-dev to adopt the artistic style of Alphonse Mucha, using a small dataset.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that in our previous post, Exploring Quantization Backends in Diffusers, we dived into how various quantization techniques can shrink diffusion models like FLUX.1-dev, making them significantly more accessible for inference without drastically compromising performance. We saw how bitsandbytes, torchao, and others reduce memory footprints for generating images.

Performing inference is cool, but to make these models truly our own, we also need to be able to fine-tune them. Therefore, in this post, we tackle efficient fine-tuning of these models with peak memory use under ~10 GB of VRAM on a single GPU. This post will guide you through fine-tuning FLUX.1-dev using QLoRA with the diffusers library. We'll showcase results from an NVIDIA RTX 4090. We'll also highlight how FP8 training with torchao can further optimize speed on compatible hardware.

We aim to fine-tune black-forest-labs/FLUX.1-dev to adopt the artistic style of Alphonse Mucha, using a small dataset.

The model consists of three main components:.

In our QLoRA approach, we focus exclusively on fine-tuning the transformer component. The text encoders and VAE remain frozen throughout training.

We used a diffusers training script (slightly modified from here designed for DreamBooth-style LoRA fine-tuning of FLUX models. Also, a shortened version to reproduce the results in this blogpost (and used in the Google Colab) is available here. Let's examine the crucial parts for QLoRA and memory efficiency:.

LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) Deep Dive: LoRA makes model training more efficient by keeping track of the weight updates with low-rank matrices. Instead of updating the full weight matrix W W W, LoRA learns two smaller matrices A A A and B B B. The update to the weights for the model is ΔW=BA \Delta W = B A ΔW=BA, where A∈Rr×k A \in \mathbb{R}^{r \times k} A∈Rr×k and B∈Rd×r B \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times r} B∈Rd×r. The number r r r (called rank) is much smaller than the original dimensions, which means less parameters to update. Lastly, α \alpha α is a scaling factor for the LoRA activations. This affects how much LoRA affects the updates, and is often set to the same value as the r r r or a multiple of it. It helps balance the influence of the pre-trained model and the LoRA adapter. For a general introduction to the concept, check out our previous blog post: Using LoRA for Efficient Stable Diffusion Fine-Tuning.

It has been revealed that QLoRA: The Efficiency Powerhouse: QLoRA enhances LoRA by first loading the pre-trained base model in a quantized format (typically 4-bit via bitsandbytes), drastically cutting the base model's memory footprint. It then trains LoRA adapters (usually in FP16/BF16) on top of this quantized base. This dramatically lowers the VRAM needed to hold the base model.

It has been revealed that for instance, in the DreamBooth training script for HiDream 4-bit quantization with bitsandbytes reduces the peak memory usage of a LoRA fine-tune from ~60GB down to ~37GB with negligible-to-none quality degradation. The very same principle is what we apply here to fine-tune FLUX.1 on a consumer-grade hardware.

Sources indicate that 8-bit Optimizer (AdamW): Standard AdamW optimizer maintains first and second moment estimates for each parameter in 32-bit (FP32), which consumes a lot of memory. The 8-bit AdamW uses block-wise quantization to store optimizer states in 8-bit precision, while maintaining training stability. This technique can reduce optimizer memory usage by ~75% compared to standard FP32 AdamW. Enabling it in the script is straightforward:.

According to recent reports, gradient Checkpointing: During forward pass, intermediate activations are typically stored for backward pass gradient computation. Gradient checkpointing trades computation for memory by only storing certain checkpoint activations and recomputing others during backpropagation.

Sources indicate that cache Latents: This optimization technique pre-processes all training images through the VAE encoder before the beginning of the training. It stores the resulting latent representations in memory. During the training, instead of encoding images on-the-fly, the cached latents are directly used. This approach offers two main benefits:.

Before we launch the QLoRA fine-tune we can save a huge chunk of VRAM and wall-clock time by caching outputs of text encoders once.

At training time the dataloader simply reads the cached embeddings instead of re-encoding the caption, so the CLIP/T5 encoder never has to sit in GPU memory.

By combining this with cached VAE latents (--cache_latents) you whittle the active model down to just the quantized transformer + LoRA adapters, keeping the whole fine-tune comfortably under 10 GB of GPU memory.

According to recent reports, for this demonstration, we leveraged an NVIDIA RTX 4090 (24GB VRAM) to explore its performance. The full training command using accelerate is shown below.

According to recent reports, configuration for RTX 4090: On our RTX 4090, we used a train_batch_size of 1, gradient_accumulation_steps of 4, mixed_precision="bf16", gradient_checkpointing=True, use_8bit_adam=True, a LoRA rank of 4, and resolution of 512x768. Latents were cached with cache_latents=True.

Training Time (RTX 4090): Fine-tuning for 700 steps on the Alphonse Mucha dataset took approximately 41 minutes on the RTX 4090 with train_batch_size of 1 and resolution of 512x768.

Output Quality: The ultimate measure is the generated art. Here are samples from our QLoRA fine-tuned model on the derekl35/alphonse-mucha-style dataset:.

This table compares the primary bf16 precision results. The goal of the fine-tuning was to teach the model the distinct style of Alphonse Mucha.

The fine-tuned model nicely captured Mucha's iconic art nouveau style, evident in the decorative motifs and distinct color palette. The QLoRA process maintained excellent fidelity while learning the fresh style.

The results are nearly identical, showing that QLoRA performs effectively with both fp16 and bf16 mixed precision.

For owners with NVIDIA GPUs possessing compute capability 8.9 or greater (such as the H100, RTX 4090), even greater speed efficiencies can be achieved by leveraging FP8 training via the torchao library.

After training your LoRA adapters, you have two main approaches for inference.

One approach is to load your trained LoRA adapters on top of the base model.

For when you want maximum efficiency with a single style, you can merge the LoRA weights into the base model.

While we showcased results on an RTX 4090, the same code can be run on more accessible hardware like the T4 GPU available in Google Colab for free.

On a T4, you can expect the fine-tuning process to take significantly longer around 4 hours for the same number of steps. This is a trade-off for accessibility, but it makes custom fine-tuning possible without high-end hardware. Be mindful of usage limits if running on Colab, as a 4-hour training run might push them.

It has been revealed that QLoRA, coupled with the diffusers library, significantly democratizes the ability to customize state-of-the-art models like FLUX.1-dev. As demonstrated on an RTX 4090, efficient fine-tuning is well within reach, yielding high-quality stylistic adaptations. Furthermore, for customers with the latest NVIDIA hardware, torchao enables even faster training through FP8 precision.

Sharing your fine-tuned LoRA adapters is a fantastic way to contribute to the open-source community. It allows others to easily try out your styles, build on your work, and helps create a vibrant ecosystem of creative AI tools.

The Jensen Huang saga poses the question: What happens when a leader becomes too big to fail?

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1887 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fastcompany

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Less than a week after Nvidia’s board said it would not reinstate Jensen Huang, it renamed him president and CEO.
  • Less than a week after Nvidia’s board mentioned it would not reinstate Jensen Huang, it renamed him president and CEO.
  • While Huang is a visionary leader who has delivered extraordinary results, putting him back at the helm despite an open, independent investigation of his conduct may put the company at even greater risk.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Less than a week after Nvidia’s board said it would not reinstate Jensen Huang, it renamed him president and CEO. President Donald Trump had intervened, showing his support for Huang publicly and reportedly even phoning in to a board meeting, urging Nvidia’s directors to reconsider their position. While Huang is a visionary leader who has delivered extraordinary results, putting him back at the helm despite an open, independent investigation of his conduct may put the firm at even greater risk. How will managers hold their teams accountable if the CEO is perceived to be able to violate the company’s code of conduct and lie about it to the board and employees without repercussions? As an executive and team coach, I’ve seen this situation time and again (albeit not to this extreme), and it creates a near-impossible situation for the rank and file. Leaders must now hold their teams accountable when employees have reason to question that the minimum standards are discretionary. Why people defend problematic high performers Compensation was the most submitted question that then-Interim CEO Colette Kress received during last week’s company-wide meeting. And it makes sense—the stock price dropped sharply when Huang announced his resignation. Yet it’s not just money that likely motivated more than 1,600 comments on an internal post, most supporting Huang’s return. There is also a sense of pride in being part of a winning team, one that was synonymous with Huang. In many ways, defending him may feel like defending what they’ve helped build. Moreover, with approximately 60 employees reporting directly to Huang, there is no apparent successor—heightening the business risk of replacing him. That, coupled with external political and investor pressure from heavyweights such as Trump, Elon Musk, and Bill Ackman, likely fueled the sentiment that Huang should be reinstated. What happens when exceptions become precedents Employees may trust Huang’s business judgment but question how Nvidia handles misconduct. The implications of the board’s reversal will likely take time to fully materialize. For example, what happens when a less indispensable leader violates company policy, or new allegations emerge against Huang or another executive? Will employees become less willing to raise concerns if consequences depend on someone’s perceived value to the company? Huang’s personal missteps may also erode trust and credibility with employees, after reports that he misled company leaders about his affair with suspected Chinese spy Alice Huang have shown he is willing to deceive people in his personal and professional life. Employees may think, What else is he capable of? This may affect employees’ willingness to stake their own reputations behind him. Managers may also struggle to hold employees to certain expectations when those employees believe exceptions can be made. One client of mine, whom I’ll call Eliza, is a chief revenue officer who worked with an underperforming VP of sales with a long-standing friendship with the company’s CEO. Although the VP of sales did not perform the basic functions of his role, Eliza couldn’t hold him accountable because the CEO would not back her up. She was responsible for the company’s revenue goal without having the authority to deliver it. Ultimately, Eliza gave the CEO an ultimatum: It was either her or the VP. The CEO ended up moving the VP to another department, but the company nearly lost Eliza in the process. Managing a double standard When Huang returned to the office, an employee shouted, “We love you, Jensen!” And while his return may be welcome to many, it will create a disparity in expectations that managers will have to address. I once worked with a senior executive in a similar situation. His team’s frustration with the CEO’s decisions became all-consuming—and he agreed with them. He spent his nights and weekends agonizing, and he found himself adding to their list of grievances in team meetings. He felt awful, and so did his team. I told him he had a decision to make. He could continue with the status quo, or he could acknowledge the reality of the situation and decide whether he wanted to stay or leave the company. He ultimately decided to look for a new job, but in the interim he focused his team on what they could influence. While he didn’t disclose to his team that he was looking for work elsewhere, he did tell them that while they worked for this company, they were responsible for having productive conversations that moved the business forward. If anyone felt they couldn’t do that, he would support them if they decided to leave. This alleviated the burden he felt he was carrying by trying to “protect” his team. Managers who are in the thankless position of serving under a divisive leader are stuck between a rock and a hard place. They are caught between a leader they can’t remove and their employees. Their best bet is to be clear about where their authority begins and ends, and make it clear that their team, including themselves, will be held to a high standard. But the internal cost of doing this when the company’s leader is not held to the same standard is high, often creating a ripe breeding ground for talented managers and employees to leave. While it is rare for a company to be ensnared in a scandal of this magnitude, leaders often face pressure to overlook the behavior of someone who delivers exceptional results. Overlooking this behavior may seem like the easiest path for continuing to deliver exceptional results—but it comes with a cost: the well-being of the rest of the team. This is why adequate succession planning is so critical, so no one becomes “too massive to fail.”.

Google is upgrading the Gemini app on Mac with computer use capabilities that can work across local desktop applications and the web.

The existing Task (previously Gemini Spark) functionality in the Mac app could just access local files in conjunction with Connected Apps, like @Gmail or @Google Calendar.

Computer use lets Gemini for Mac click and type on your behalf to accomplish multi-step tasks in local desktop apps and the web, like navigating menus and filling out forms.

It has been revealed that gemini works in an “isolated background window with a live preview right in your chat,” while your main screen and cursor remain free to use. On the safety front, you can stop Gemini at any time with one click, while you choose what apps Gemini uses. Google will pause for logins and payments, with confirmation needed for sensitive actions.

According to recent reports, many everyday tasks span desktop apps and websites that don’t connect to each other. Computer use handles the tedious steps in the background so you can save time without giving up your screen or cursor.

To use, add @Computer use to your prompt. In Customize > Connectors, you’ll see newly introduced “Desktop” apps like Blender and Autodesk Fusion join the existing Git and Obsidian integrations.

#195305. Shared CXL memory pools come with steep software tax that could stall multi-server scaling

AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Tomshardware ↗ Open Full Page

Shared CXL memory pools come with steep software tax that could stall multi-server scaling

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1584 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tomshardware

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Researchers at the University of Texas at Arlington and Intel measured what happens when four servers share one pool of CXL memory on real hardware.
  • Recent findings suggest that locks work like traffic signals for shared data: a server has to claim the lock before it changes something in the pool, and the other servers wait until it releases it.
  • The setup comprises four 86-core Intel Xeon 6787P servers with 256GB of DRAM each, connected over PCIe 5.0 to one CXL memory box.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Researchers at the University of Texas at Arlington and Intel measured what happens when four servers share one pool of CXL memory on real hardware. In a presentation shared at Supercomputer 2026 (SC26), they found that because the hardware doesn’t automatically keep shared data updated across servers, necessary software overhead adds a 3-5µ (microsecond) delay per lock, each time servers access the same data. These minute delays effectively cancel out the benefits — a finding that comes as CXL memory pools are being proposed as a potential AI KV cache solution.

Recent findings suggest that locks work like traffic signals for shared data: a server has to claim the lock before it changes something in the pool, and the other servers wait until it releases it. This way, no two servers overwrite the same data at the same time. Within a given server, the CPU’s hardware handles that handoff in a fraction of a microsecond, but across these servers, software is in charge of enforcement.

The setup comprises four 86-core Intel Xeon 6787P servers with 256GB of DRAM each, connected over PCIe 5.0 to one CXL memory box. The switch, which UT Arlington’s Peiran Du called “the only commercially available product we can use,” caps their setup at four servers. The catch is that there is no cross-host cache coherence or atomic operations on “a real four-host CXL shared-memory system.”.

This means no synced CPU caches and no hardware atomics between servers to build locks on, so software has to handle both. Writers publish their cached copy out to the pool and wait for it to finish, while readers throw out stale copies before reading, with the locks built from plain reads and writes, such as Lamport’s fast mutex. CXL 3.0 defines a hardware fix for the caches, called Back-Invalidate, but the researchers hadn’t received vendor confirmation that their platform supports it.

Aside from the lock acquisition penalty, which is “roughly an order of magnitude higher than local hardware spin locks,” there is a visibility cost: “one-way cross-host visibility is about 1 µs.” This is 0.94 µs, one way, compared to 1.91 µs for an RDMA write on their 400Gb/s InfiniBand, so the link isn’t the cause. A local compare-and-swap takes about 100 ns and, across servers, a lock’s median is 3.7 µs if uncontended, but 132 µs at the 95th percentile with several servers on one lock.

The result: breadth-first search (BFS), a standard graph algorithm and a common benchmark, “gains nothing from adding a second host,” and was actually slower on four servers than on one, at 0.74s versus 0.55s. This was mostly not from the locks and barriers, which were only about 3.5% of its runtime, but due to the repeated flushing of shared state at every level.

Industry observers note that on the other hand, throughput for a hash table — using independent buckets and per-host allocators — grew almost linearly when adding hosts. Triangle counting, another standard graph benchmark, also had a runtime reduction of more than half when scaling from one to four hosts.

Sources indicate that those costs matter, in part, because shared CXL pools are emerging as a new home for KV cache — an AI model’s stored record of a conversation’s state — once it outgrows GPU memory and a server’s own DRAM. The CXL Consortium’s SC26 session description indicates cloud providers and GPU makers “have highlighted CXL memory pooling as an effective approach for improving KV cache access.”.

Sources indicate that SK hynix, which makes CXL memory modules, showed a design that hands KV cache between GPU servers through a shared pool and claims 2.6x faster time to first token than standard RDMA setups. Its abstract also claims 3.0x lower P99 latency and 1.9x higher throughput. Micron, at SC26’s CXL Pavilion, showed its Abaco reference design of pooled CXL memory shared across rack servers and GPUs. It claimed 10x to 30x agentic AI gains, with famfs support for apps like Nvidia’s Dynamo.

The need is real, even if efficiency gains have led to less cache needed per token. Vikram Sharma Mailthody of Nvidia Research noted at SC26’s Emerging Storage panel that his own analysis of open models on Hugging Face reveals KV per token falling “by 50% every twelve months” with “up to 78 times reduction so far,” giving the example that 128K context took “about 64 gigabytes” three years ago and now takes less than one. But context lengths are heading toward millions of tokens, and “the product of those two will keep increasing,” he said.

Agents also add to the demand. Earlier in the conference, a workshop talk by Argonne National Laboratory and RIT researchers, based on public AI serving traces, indicated that a “session calls again ~2 min later, once its tools return: a 160 GiB recency cache keeps 1% of its context,” needing the GPU to recompute the rest, or about 99%. Recomputation is significantly slower and more demanding, and memory is needed to cache more.

That makes it a capacity problem more than a speed problem. “Memory capacity is becoming a dominant factor. Memory latencies have not been seen as a primary problem yet,” Mailthody said. An agent’s context only has to survive a gap of a couple of minutes. It’s also ideal for any KV cache solution to be as inexpensive as possible, and given that a 128GB DIMM costs more than four times that of a 64GB DIMM last year. According to Intel’s Anil Godbole on SC26’s CXL panel, being able to add capacity past the DIMM slot limit — including reusing DDR4 — bolsters the case for CXL even further.

Recent findings suggest that it doesn’t hurt that the KV cache handoff is write-once, read-many, which is the type of pattern that actually scaled in testing, although UT Arlington did not specifically test KV cache. Researchers behind OCEAN, a CXL emulator, backed this idea in the same paper session as UT Arlington, saying that software coherence is fine for read-heavy work, with hardware essential as writes climb. Its abstract reports that hardware coherence, at least in emulation, can give an 11x improvement at full coverage on Tigon database workloads.

Sources indicate that limitations still exist, which is why SK hynix, for one, is relying on “novel locking and coherence protocols” for its design. Hardware isn’t quite there yet, and Back-Invalidate might “be pretty costly,” Du mentioned, suggesting that both hardware and software coherence may be required.

Industry observers note that micron, which built prototype KV cache sharing into Nvidia’s Dynamo, noted two primary failure cases in a CXL Consortium presentation last month: where the writer’s data never reaches the pool, and where the reader never sees the updates. The first can be fixed by producers flushing before blocks are published, so unflushed blocks can never be found. The second is fixed with a consumer flush, that is, invalidation of their cached lines, before reading. These are the fixes and costs that UT Arlington was measuring.

Micron cut its flushing cost by flushing each slot only once, which works because KV cache is content-addressed — a slot in the pool that hasn’t changed stays coherent after its first flush. Micron’s presentation also notes that neither failure causes a crash. Instead, the read returns plausible-looking data, and the output is wrong in subtle ways, with the wrong tokens on some requests under cache pressure.

Industry observers note that working against CXL as a solution is the fact that the memory pooling only reaches within a rack today, Godbole remarked; it doesn’t span a full data center. Marvell and Penguin Solutions, in collaboration and in addition to others like Lightelligence, have shown or announced memory expansion and pooling over optical links, which could stretch pooling past a single rack. CXL is also “not the protocol to ferry such major data,” Godbole added, as it’s built for smaller reads and writes, 64 bytes at a time, closer to how a CPU uses RAM. For bulk transfers, he said, RDMA is more efficient.

It has been revealed that A research system called Beluga, in a paper published on arXiv a year ago, had KV cache in “a commercial CXL switch-based memory pool” with time to first token cut by 89.6% and throughput raised 7.35x compared with an RDMA-based setup once its cache was filled. This suggests some optimization could improve the usefulness of the technology, too.

Sources indicate that CXL is clearly a hit or miss with how it is actually used being a main concern, with “a gap between the [CXL] spec and the implementation from different vendors,” according to UT Arlington’s Jia Rao. SK hynix’s second-generation CMM-DDR5, at 256GB and using CXL 3.2, has only been shown, and the device its KV cache design uses to select what to send is still what the tech giant’s Younghoon Min called a “research prototype.” These are early times, and the enterprise landscape is simultaneously changing promptly.

It has been revealed that on paper, shared CXL pools do fit the KV handoff idea, but until a commercial switch ships with confirmed coherence across servers, the best we have is KV cache numbers from vendor demos and research prototypes. Back-Invalidate should cut the software overhead UT Arlington measured, but Du expects it to add delays of its own; production systems would likely need a combination of hardware coherence and software approaches like Micron’s.

Shane Downing is a Contributing Writer for Tom’s Hardware, covering consumer storage, PC hardware, and AI.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that you Can See Everything may begin as a documentary about disgraced tech entrepreneur Elizabeth Holmes in the month before her prison sentence, but in the movie’s second half, an entirely different (and entirely meta) subject emerges: the deal between Holmes’s partner, Billy Evans, and studio A24 to give Evans a cut of the film’s profits, and codirector Nathan Fielder’s uncertainty about how much Holmes knows about the money. Given Evans’s status as the film’s quasi-villain, the thought that ticket buyers’ money would end up in his pockets had moviegoers squirming in their seats. Thankfully, the documentary ends with a title card saying that Evans “decided to give up his right to profit on the movie” shortly after filming concluded. But a upcoming investigation indicates that Evans didn’t fully forgo his payout from the film—it was just redirected to charity instead. Evans’s share of the profits Two anonymous sources told The Hollywood Reporter that Evans and A24 amended their agreement so his payout would go to an unnamed children’s charity, not directly into his bank account. An A24 representative later confirmed that this deal was made, though they didn’t say why that detail was omitted from the film’s final title card. The exact size of Evans’s payout remains unknown, but given You Can See Everything’s unprecedented success at the box office, his share is definitely more than small change. This week, the film crossed $100 million in global box-office revenue, making it the fifth-highest-grossing non-concert documentary of all time. In a separate interview for THR, Evans explained why he agreed to back out on his initial deal with A24. “They noted that it would help the project. Time and time again, when there’s things that I really didn’t want to do that they said would be helpful for making a better movie and helping people see Liz more clearly, I made those sacrifices or decisions to help the project,” Evans said. “I am totally stubborn, but if there’s anything that I can do to help Liz regardless of the cost, I will do it.” Why the directors disagree Though THR’s report frames You Can See Everything’s final title card as disingenuous, directors Fielder and Lance Oppenheim say the outlet’s story misses the mark. At a Q&A on November 21, Fielder and Oppenheim reportedly said the story’s wording was inaccurate and that none of the documentary’s subjects were paid, according to reporting by Semafor. A studio source later told Semafor that Evans fully relinquished his profit-sharing deal, and that the charitable donation was a separate, mutual agreement between Evans and A24. Meanwhile, THR’s editor-in-chief, Maer Roshan, defended the story over email, saying that A24’s perspective “seems like a pretty semantic argument.”.

You Can See Everything may begin as a documentary about disgraced tech entrepreneur Elizabeth Holmes in the month before her prison sentence, but in the movie’s second half, an entirely different (and entirely meta) subject emerges: the deal between Holmes’s partner, Billy Evans, and studio A24 to give Evans a cut of the film’s profits, and codirector Nathan Fielder’s uncertainty about how much Holmes knows about the money.

In a recent development, given Evans’s status as the film’s quasi-villain, the thought that ticket buyers’ money would end up in his pockets had moviegoers squirming in their seats. Thankfully, the documentary ends with a title card saying that Evans “decided to give up his right to profit on the movie” shortly after filming concluded.

But a upcoming investigation states that Evans didn’t fully forgo his payout from the film—it was just redirected to charity instead.

Sources indicate that two anonymous sources told The Hollywood Reporter that Evans and A24 amended their agreement so his payout would go to an unnamed children’s charity, not directly into his bank account. An A24 representative later confirmed that this deal was made, though they didn’t say why that detail was omitted from the film’s final title card.

Recent findings suggest that the exact size of Evans’s payout remains unknown, but given You Can See Everything’s unprecedented success at the box office, his share is definitely more than small change. This week, the film crossed $100 million in global box-office revenue, making it the fifth-highest-grossing non-concert documentary of all time.

In a separate interview for THR, Evans explained why he agreed to back out on his initial deal with A24.

According to recent reports, “They said that it would help the project. Time and time again, when there’s things that I really didn’t want to do that they said would be helpful for making a better movie and helping people see Liz more clearly, I made those sacrifices or decisions to help the project,” Evans said. “I am totally stubborn, but if there’s anything that I can do to help Liz regardless of the cost, I will do it.”.

Though THR’s report frames You Can See Everything’s final title card as disingenuous, directors Fielder and Lance Oppenheim say the outlet’s story misses the mark.

At a Q&A on November 21, Fielder and Oppenheim reportedly noted the story’s wording was inaccurate and that none of the documentary’s subjects were paid, according to reporting by Semafor.

A studio source later told Semafor that Evans fully relinquished his profit-sharing deal, and that the charitable donation was a separate, mutual agreement between Evans and A24.

Meanwhile, THR’s editor-in-chief, Maer Roshan, defended the story over email, saying that A24’s perspective “seems like a pretty semantic argument.”.

A frontend application can compile successfully and still fail when it communicates with the backend.

Imagine a backend developer changes an API response from:.

The backend works correctly. The frontend also builds without errors. However, a component expecting user.name now receives undefined.

This is an example of API contract drift: the frontend and backend no longer agree on the structure or behavior of an API.

The problem becomes more difficult when several developers or teams work on different parts of an application. A change made by one team may affect another team's assumptions without producing an obvious error during development.

Recent findings suggest that typeScript helps catch many programming mistakes, but its types do not automatically validate data received over HTTP. A type declaration can describe what the application expects without proving that the server actually returns it.

In this tutorial, we'll look at a practical way to make API contracts more reliable.

Consider a typical frontend API function:.

At first glance, this looks reasonable.

The function promises to return a User, so TypeScript allows the application to access properties such as name and email.

It has been revealed that the return value of response.json() is not automatically checked against the User interface. The interface only provides compile-time information; it does not validate the actual JSON received from the server.

the frontend may still treat the response as a User even though the data has a different structure.

This is particularly vital when working with:.

Independently deployed frontend and backend applications.

APIs maintained by different engineering teams.

The solution is to validate data at the boundary where it enters the application.

It has been revealed that zod is a TypeScript-first schema validation library. It allows developers to describe expected data structures and validate actual values against those definitions.

Now create a schema for the user response:.

There are two important parts here.

First, UserSchema describes the structure that the application expects at runtime.

Second, z.infer generates the corresponding TypeScript type from the schema.

This means developers do not need to maintain a separate interface and validation definition for the same data structure.

The response is initially treated as unknown, which prevents the application from assuming that untrusted data already has the expected structure.

UserSchema.parse() validates the actual response.

If the backend returns an unexpected property type or misses a required field, Zod throws a validation error instead of allowing invalid data to move silently through the application.

You can also use safeParse() when you prefer to handle validation errors without exceptions:.

This approach is useful when API responses are external or when a frontend must provide more controlled error handling.

One common mistake is placing API validation logic directly inside React components.

Sources indicate that for a small application, this may seem convenient. As the project grows, however, it becomes difficult to reuse validation rules and identify where data transformations happen.

A better approach is to separate API schemas, service functions, and UI components.

The responsibilities are straightforward:.

schemas/user.ts defines the expected user data.

api/client.ts handles common HTTP configuration.

api/users.ts contains user-related API requests.

hooks/useUser.ts manages data fetching for React.

components/UserProfile.tsx displays the validated data.

This structure makes it easier to change an API implementation without rewriting the UI.

It also makes testing more manageable because validation logic can be tested independently of React rendering.

For more ideas on organizing application code, see SitePoint's guide to modern JavaScript modules.

According to recent reports, runtime validation protects an application when data arrives. However, teams also need a shared description of what an API is supposed to accept and return.

This is where OpenAPI becomes useful.

OpenAPI provides a standard format for describing HTTP APIs, including:.

Request and response structures.

Data types and validation constraints.

For example, an endpoint can be described using an OpenAPI document:.

This document describes what the endpoint should return.

Both frontend and backend developers can refer to the same contract instead of relying on separate assumptions or outdated documentation.

Swagger Editor helps developers write and validate OpenAPI documents. It also provides a convenient way to inspect API definitions.

Swagger UI turns an OpenAPI document into interactive API documentation, allowing developers to explore endpoints and test requests.

Redoc provides another way to generate readable API documentation from an OpenAPI specification.

These tools are particularly useful when APIs are maintained by multiple developers or consumed by several applications.

Maintaining API types manually across frontend and backend repositories creates opportunities for inconsistencies.

For example, a backend developer might add a newly introduced optional property while the frontend continues using an older interface.

One way to reduce this duplication is to generate TypeScript definitions and API clients from an OpenAPI specification.

Orval is a useful tool for this workflow.

It can generate TypeScript clients and types from an OpenAPI document, helping frontend developers work with consistent endpoint definitions.

A simplified workflow looks like this:.

A typical configuration might look like this:.

The exact configuration depends on the Orval version and the structure of the OpenAPI document.

Once configured, the client can be regenerated when the API specification changes.

This reduces the amount of repetitive code developers need to maintain manually.

However, generated types should not be confused with runtime validation. They improve consistency during development, but an application may still need to validate responses received from external systems or services that cannot be fully trusted.

Frontend developers often need to build or test features before the corresponding backend endpoint is ready.

Waiting for a complete backend implementation can slow down development, particularly when multiple teams work independently.

Mock Service Worker (MSW) helps solve this problem by intercepting network requests and returning controlled responses.

You can define a mock handler for the user endpoint:.

The frontend can now make normal HTTP requests while MSW supplies predictable responses during development or testing.

You can also simulate an invalid response:.

This makes it possible to check whether the application's validation and error-handling logic behave as expected.

MSW is particularly valuable because it allows frontend tests to run without requiring a live backend environment.

Runtime validation and generated clients improve reliability, but they do not automatically guarantee that independently developed services remain compatible.

For systems with multiple services, contract testing can provide another layer of protection.

Pact is a contract-testing tool that allows consumers and providers to verify their expectations about API interactions.

Consider a frontend application that expects the user endpoint to return:.

The consumer defines the expected interaction.

The backend provider can then run verification against that contract to check whether its actual response satisfies the consumer's expectations.

This helps identify breaking changes before they reach production.

These tools solve different problems. A project does not necessarily need all of them, but larger applications can benefit from combining the approaches that match their architecture.

A contract is only useful if developers consistently check it when making changes.

A practical approach is to run validation and tests automatically whenever someone opens a pull request.

For example, a GitHub Actions workflow might look like this:.

The api:validate script should be configured to validate the project's OpenAPI document or run the relevant contract checks.

The test command should execute the application's automated tests.

For a production project, you may also want to include:.

Generated-client consistency checks.

Consumer-provider contract verification.

The objective is to detect incompatible changes before they are merged.

A failed pipeline gives developers an opportunity to investigate the change while the context is still fresh.

API contracts become harder to maintain when several teams contribute to the same system.

For example, a firm might have separate teams responsible for:.

Customer-facing frontend applications.

If nobody owns an API contract, small changes can create unexpected problems for other teams.

Assigning clear ownership helps establish who reviews changes, maintains documentation, and coordinates breaking updates.

Industry observers note that this becomes particularly key when an organization expands its engineering capacity across locations or adds several specialized teams. Companies planning that kind of growth may also need to consider enterprise IT recruitment as part of their wider engineering workforce strategy.

Regardless of how a team is assembled, its development process should establish clear responsibilities for API design, versioning, testing, and release coordination.

A few practical conventions can make a significant difference:.

Assign an owner to every vital API or service.

Document breaking changes before implementation.

Require contract-related tests in pull requests.

Keep generated clients synchronized with the API specification.

Communicate deprecations before removing existing fields.

Monitor production errors after deploying API changes.

These practices help prevent a growing engineering organization from becoming a collection of disconnected services.

In a recent development, API contract drift is not simply a TypeScript problem. It is a coordination problem that becomes visible when applications and services develop different expectations about the same data.

TypeScript provides useful compile-time checks, but it cannot guarantee that an HTTP response matches a declared interface.

A more reliable approach combines several techniques:.

Use Zod to validate incoming data.

Use OpenAPI to document API expectations.

Generate TypeScript clients with tools such as Orval.

Use MSW to test frontend behavior without a live backend.

Use Pact when consumer-provider contract verification is appropriate.

Run validation and tests automatically in CI/CD.

Sources indicate that you do not need to introduce every tool at once. Start by validating external API responses, document important endpoints, and gradually automate contract checks as the application grows.

The result is a codebase where developers can make changes with greater confidence and where frontend and backend teams have a shared understanding of how their systems communicate.

Transformers backend integration in SGLang

📅 23 Jun 2025 | ⏱️ 2 min read (451 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Hugging Face transformers library is the standard for working with state-of-the-art models — from experimenting with cutting-edge research to fine-tuning on custom data.
  • In a recent development, but once you're ready to move from notebooks to production, inference performance becomes mission-critical.
  • In a recent development, designed for high-throughput, low-latency inference, SGLang now offers seamless integration with transformers as a backend.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hugging Face transformers library is the standard for working with state-of-the-art models — from experimenting with cutting-edge research to fine-tuning on custom data. Its simplicity, flexibility, and expansive model zoo make it a powerful tool for rapid development.

In a recent development, but once you're ready to move from notebooks to production, inference performance becomes mission-critical. That’s where SGLang comes in.

In a recent development, designed for high-throughput, low-latency inference, SGLang now offers seamless integration with transformers as a backend. This means you can pair the flexibility of transformers with the raw performance of SGLang.

Let’s dive into what this integration enables and how you can use it.

SGLang now supports Hugging Face transformers as a backend, letting you run any transformers-compatible model with high-performance inference out of the box.

No native support needed — SGLang automatically falls back to Transformers when needed, or you can set impl="transformers" explicitly.

Let’s walk through a simple text generation example with meta-llama/Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct to compare both approaches.

transformers library is great for experimentation, small-scale tasks and training, but it's not optimized for high-volume or low-latency scenarios.

SGLang takes a different track, prioritizing efficiency with features like RadixAttention (a memory-efficient attention mechanism). Inference with SGLang is noticeably faster and more resource-efficient, especially under load. Here’s the same task in SGlang using an offline engine:.

Or you can spin a server and send requests:.

Note that SGLang also offers an OpenAI-compatible API, making it a drop-in replacement for external services.

In a recent development, with the fresh transformers backend integration, SGLang can now automatically fall back to using transformers models it doesn’t natively support. This means in practice:.

This unlocks faster inference and optimized deployment (e.g enabling RadixAttention) without sacrificing the simplicity and versatility of transformers ecosystem.

Note that specifying the impl parameter is optional. If the model is not natively supported by SGLang, it switches to transformers implementation on its own.

Any model on the Hugging Face Hub that works with transformers using trust_remote_code=True and properly implements attention is compatible with SGLang. You can find the exact requirements in the official documentation. If your custom model meets these criteria, all you need to do is set trust_remote_code=True when loading it.

Kyutai Team’s Helium isn’t yet natively supported by SGLang. This is where transformers backend shines, enabling optimized inference without waiting for native support.

There are several key areas we are actively working on to enhance this integration:.

Performance Improvements: transformer models currently lag behind the native integration in terms of performance.Our primary objective is to optimize and narrow this gap.

VLM Integration: we are also working toward adding support for Vision-Language Models (VLM) to broaden the range of capabilities and use cases.
